- [ ] Validate the captured MTRR state and combine it with PAT to establish effective cache types for target physical ranges before selecting cache indexes. Add reviewable emulator tests for mapping, unmapping, permission behavior, and frame reclamation before replacing the inherited CR3.
- [ ] Only after a mapping policy works, add a kernel heap with documented alignment, allocation/free semantics, deterministic exhaustion behavior, and an explicit rule for interrupt contexts.

### Required exception/descriptor validation

- [x] Source contains GDT/TSS/IDT setup and normalized stubs for architectural exception vectors 0–31; double fault uses IST1.
- [x] Target-assemble/link and inspect the stubs and descriptor setup; ELF disassembly confirms call-stack alignment and the error-code normalization paths, while compile-time size assertions pin the IDT, TSS, and exception-context layouts.
- [x] Add QEMU fault-injection tests for a controlled page fault and invalid opcode. `just fault-smoke` verifies vector diagnostics, the exact CR2 address, no shell prompt or return marker, and that QEMU remains halted until its timeout; it then restores the default release kernel and ISO.
- [x] Boot the descriptor setup and both tested exception paths in QEMU. These checks cover only the injected page fault and invalid opcode, not all vectors or physical hardware.

**Exit criteria:** the kernel owns and validates its page-table state, frame allocation/mapping invariants are tested, OOM/failure leaves memory state consistent, page faults are diagnosable, and the kernel remains bootable under emulator tests. Not met: page-table ownership/transition and heap work remain outstanding.

---

## Milestone 3 — IRQs, time, and kernel scheduling

Do not enable interrupts as a side effect of installing exception gates. IRQ delivery needs its own controller, acknowledgement, masking, ownership, and synchronization design.

### Planned work

- [ ] Select and document the initial interrupt controller policy for QEMU and target hardware (for example, legacy PIC compatibility versus local I/O APIC; do not enable both accidentally).
- [ ] Add IRQ vector allocation, controller masking/unmasking, end-of-interrupt acknowledgement, spurious-interrupt handling, and a policy for unexpected IRQs.
- [ ] Add a calibrated/verified timer source and monotonic timekeeping; test interval arithmetic and drift assumptions.
- [ ] Establish interrupt-safe lock primitives and rules for code callable from normal, exception, and IRQ contexts. No allocator or blocking console operation may run in an unsafe interrupt context.
- [ ] Add a minimal kernel-thread context and lifecycle model, stack ownership/guard policy, context-switch tests, and emulator scheduling tests.
- [ ] Add preemption only after lock, stack, timer, and interrupt-return invariants have deterministic tests.
- [ ] Keep application-processor startup/SMP as a separate sub-milestone after per-CPU state, TLB invalidation, and lock semantics exist.

**Exit criteria:** tested IRQ acknowledgement and timer behavior, deterministic thread lifecycle/context-switch tests, and bounded QEMU tests under repeated timer interrupts. No `sti` before the design and tests are ready.

---

## Milestone 4 — isolated processes and syscall ABI

Userspace begins only after page tables, exception handling, scheduling, and controlled memory allocation are trustworthy. The syscall ABI is a product interface and must not emerge accidentally from internal functions.

### Planned work

- [ ] Decide and document the x86_64 user-entry/syscall mechanism, register convention, selector/MSR setup, per-CPU state requirements, and safe return path.
- [ ] Add user/kernel page permissions and process-owned address spaces, including teardown and TLB invalidation rules.
- [ ] Implement copy-in/copy-out helpers that validate lengths, arithmetic, canonical ranges, permissions, and faults; never form a kernel reference directly from a user pointer.
- [ ] Specify version discovery, stable syscall numbers, argument layouts, error encoding, partial-I/O behavior, interruption/restart, and compatibility policy before exposing calls.
- [ ] Add initial process lifecycle and descriptor-table semantics: create/load, exit, wait, close, duplication/inheritance, and process cleanup.
- [ ] Load a deliberately small documented executable format with bounds/segment/permission checks; reject malformed binaries safely.
- [ ] Build adversarial tests for bad pointers, overflow, invalid mappings, process teardown, descriptor misuse, and failed exec.

### First user-visible target

A small controlled `init` process should start from a reproducible image, write through a descriptor, exit with a status, and be waited on by a kernel test harness. Do not claim userspace or process isolation from ring-0 tasks that merely use process-shaped structs.

**Exit criteria:** an isolated init process runs in user mode and uses a versioned, documented syscall subset; invalid user pointers and process teardown are tested without corrupting the kernel.

---

## Milestone 5 — VFS, storage, and device ownership

Keep the current RAM filesystem as a bootstrap/test implementation. Persistence and device drivers require explicit block ownership, error handling, and recovery behavior.

### Planned work

- [ ] Define VFS node, mount, path, metadata, and file-descriptor contracts independently of a particular disk format.
- [ ] Preserve volatile RAMFS as a test backend and add tests for mount/path errors, capacity, partial I/O, and object lifetime.
- [ ] Add a narrowly scoped block-device interface with request validation, timeout/error reporting, and a QEMU-supported initial device driver (such as virtio-blk after PCI discovery is ready).
- [ ] Choose and document the first on-disk filesystem format. Specify partition discovery, byte order, block size, metadata limits, corruption handling, and read-only/recovery behavior before writable support.
- [ ] Add persistent write/read/remount/reboot integration tests; never claim persistence from an in-memory cache alone.
- [ ] Add a driver ownership and DMA policy before any device can write into arbitrary kernel memory.
- [ ] Define file descriptors and basic process I/O semantics before exposing them to applications.

**Exit criteria:** a reproducible image mounts a documented on-disk filesystem, user-visible tools can create/read files across reboot, and corruption/I/O errors fail safely.

---

## Milestone 6 — initial userspace and command-line utilities

Crabshell is currently an in-kernel parser/frontend. The long-term terminal application should reuse its parser model without linking kernel internals or bypassing syscalls.

### Planned work

- [ ] Start a user-mode `init` process and establish executable search, environment, current directory, descriptor inheritance, and process startup rules.
- [ ] Port or adapt Crabshell into a userspace terminal application that uses only the documented syscall/VFS interfaces.
- [ ] Add a small utility set with explicit scope: file listing, text output, create/remove/copy/move, and system information.
- [ ] Add command-line quoting, escaping, history, redirection, and pipelines only with parser tests and process/descriptor/pipe semantics to support them.
- [ ] Add integration tests that launch tools from the filesystem image and exercise them through syscalls; keep unsupported features explicit.

**Exit criteria:** shell and basic tools run as isolated user processes from a reproducible image; no shell command directly calls kernel-private VFS internals.

---

## Milestone 7 — graphical console and GUI (long-term)

A GUI is intentionally downstream of stable memory management, interrupts/input, process isolation, drivers, and userspace. Keep Crabshell's parser independent so a graphical terminal frontend can reuse it.

### Planned work

- [ ] Add validated framebuffer discovery and memory ownership; implement a minimal text/graphics console without compromising serial panic diagnostics.
- [ ] Establish an input subsystem that separates raw device events from key mapping and terminal policy. Plan PS/2 and USB HID support separately; do not treat the current raw scancode poller as a keyboard driver stack.
- [ ] Define a graphics buffer ownership/presentation API, clipping rules, pixel format, and bounds/overflow checks.
- [ ] Implement a minimal compositor/windowing policy only after process isolation and input routing are ready.
- [ ] Run Crabshell as a terminal application in a GUI window using the same parser and userspace services as the serial/TTY path.
- [ ] Preserve serial as a headless recovery/debug console and add repeatable QEMU display/input tests.

**Exit criteria:** a documented GUI session starts from userspace, renders a terminal, accepts tested input, and does not require direct kernel-private VFS access.

---

## Milestone 8 — networking (long-term, after drivers and process isolation)

Networking is not implied by the current device drivers. The initial target should be a tightly scoped virtual-device path with clear ownership and bounded buffers.

### Planned work

- [ ] Complete PCI/device discovery and define DMA buffer ownership, address translation, cache synchronization, and reset/error behavior.
- [ ] Implement one virtual NIC driver with bounded queues and timeouts; test against QEMU user networking.
- [ ] Choose and document a minimal link/network protocol scope before implementation. Keep packet parsing length-checked and fuzzable on the host.
- [ ] Add interface configuration, routing, socket/descriptor ownership, and per-process access policy.
- [ ] Add adversarial packet tests and integration tests for link loss, malformed packets, queue exhaustion, and device reset.
- [ ] Add higher-level transports/services only when the required protocol semantics, entropy source, and security model are designed.

**Exit criteria:** documented user processes can communicate through a tested virtual NIC/network stack, with malformed input and resource exhaustion handled safely. Do not claim internet, TLS, or POSIX sockets merely from a packet driver.

---

## Cross-cutting acceptance gates

Every milestone should include the relevant subset of these gates:

1. **Design:** documented ownership, invariants, resource limits, error semantics, and unsupported cases.
2. **Tests:** host tests for pure policy and malformed/boundary input; integration tests for hardware-facing behavior.
3. **Safety:** review unsafe blocks, pointer provenance/access, integer overflow, privilege boundaries, concurrency, and cleanup/rollback paths.
4. **Build:** format, host tests, target check, and final ELF link as appropriate.
5. **Boot/integration:** QEMU tests for changes to boot, paging, descriptors, interrupts, drivers, processes, or persistence.
6. **Documentation/status:** update architecture and roadmap docs; never check off a criterion without evidence.
7. **Compatibility:** claim Unix/POSIX behavior only for the exact documented subset with conformance-style tests.

## Working rule

Prefer a small end-to-end vertical slice over broad, unbootable scaffolding. A source file, interface, or architecture document is not proof that the corresponding subsystem is operational. When a check cannot run, record the exact environment blocker and leave that acceptance gate pending.

# Rustix agent instructions

These instructions apply to every coding agent working in this repository. Read this file before changing code. For the architecture and detailed subsystem contracts, use the linked documents under `docs/`; this file summarizes the rules agents must preserve.

## Project mission

Rustix is an experimental 64-bit, Unix-like operating system with its own Rust kernel. Limine is the external boot protocol/loader only. Do not describe Limine, a host shell, or a userspace project as the Rustix kernel.

The kernel is `no_std` and targets `x86_64-unknown-none`. Rust is the implementation language for kernel and OS components. The repository currently uses a Python standard-library script only to assemble and smoke-test the boot image; it does not replace kernel or OS functionality.

Unix-like behavior is a long-term design goal, not a claim of POSIX compatibility. Make unsupported behavior explicit rather than approximating it silently.

## Current project status — read before planning

The source contains:

- A Limine-based x86_64 kernel entry, linker layout, serial diagnostics, and boot-memory reporting.
- A separate allocation-free `no_std` `crabshell` parser crate and a kernel-mode COM1 shell frontend.
- A volatile, fixed-capacity RAM filesystem used by the shell.
- A validated, fixed-capacity boot memory-map snapshot, CPUID/address-width reporting, and gated read-only EFER.NXE/IA32_PAT/MTRR reporting.
- A fixed-capacity physical frame allocator retained in `BootInfo`; Crabshell's `meminfo` command reports counts. No kernel service currently allocates frames for mappings or other services.
- Pure 4 KiB mapping-range validation, leaf-PTE bit encoding, PAT layout parsing, and a host-tested MTRR resolver in `src/paging.rs`; these helpers check alignment, address widths, canonical virtual ranges, W^X, NXE input, PAT indices, and supplied MTRR register values/overlap rules. Boot captures EFER.NXE, `IA32_PAT`, and a bounded MTRR register snapshot read-only when supported. It does not yet combine PAT/MTRR semantics for mappings. No code establishes frame ownership or mapping coverage, or modifies page tables.
- Bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT setup and fatal exception handlers for vectors 0–31. Double faults use an IST stack and page faults report CR2. Opt-in QEMU tests inject a page fault and invalid opcode and verify diagnostics plus fatal halt; maskable IRQs remain disabled and exceptions are not recoverable.

Important incomplete work:

- Milestone 0's local exit criteria were met on 2026-10-16: `just verify` passed from both the working tree and a clean detached worktree in WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04. The detached worktree had an empty `target` directory, so the run exercised fresh Limine download/host-tool compilation, formatting, 19 host tests, target check, optimized build, image creation, and the 20-second QEMU prompt smoke test. Hosted CI has not been observed.
- A separate interactive `just run` session exercised directory navigation and create/write/append/read/copy/move/list/remove operations; `cp` replaced an existing destination, `rmdir` rejected a nonempty directory and succeeded after its child was removed, and unsupported `memtest` was rejected as expected. Boot snapshot tests and QEMU boot-metadata reporting were exercised. Structural checks still cannot prove that a Limine-provided non-null pointer is mapped or readable; that remains a loader trust boundary.
- Milestone 0 is closed for local acceptance; hosted CI remains pending. Milestone 1's validation criteria are met for the current Limine path, subject to the documented pointer-readability trust boundary. Milestone 2 is **in progress**, not complete. The frame allocator specifies token ownership and preserves the token on failed deallocation; unique allocator-instance use is still caller-enforced. CPU address widths, physical map bounds, protocol-scoped HHDM range arithmetic, Limine executable image bases, page-aligned linker-defined kernel segment bounds, and gated read-only EFER.NXE/IA32_PAT/MTRR capture are checked; the QEMU serial report showed the MTRR summary on 2026-10-22. The segment bounds were reported in QEMU but do not prove inherited page-table coverage or permissions. The transition-critical mapping inventory is documented. `just fault-smoke` has validated controlled page-fault/CR2 and invalid-opcode diagnostics plus fatal halting in QEMU. Rustix still inherits Limine's page tables; CR3's root address is decoded but table entries and complete live mapping extents are not inspected, effective MTRR/PAT interactions are not validated, and there is no kernel-owned page-table manager, heap, or live frame-allocation caller.
- There is no scheduler, userspace, syscall ABI, persistent filesystem, user/kernel isolation, or general IRQ subsystem.

Never advance status or check off a roadmap item merely because source code or an interface exists. Update `docs/roadmap/README.md` only to reflect implementation and validation actually achieved.

## Source-of-truth documents

Consult the relevant documentation before modifying a subsystem:

- [`docs/index.md`](docs/index.md) — documentation entry point and current status.
- [`docs/roadmap/README.md`](docs/roadmap/README.md) — milestone sequencing and exit criteria.
- [`docs/architecture/overview.md`](docs/architecture/overview.md) — current architecture and intended layers.
- [`docs/architecture/boot.md`](docs/architecture/boot.md) — Limine requests, boot snapshot, and trust boundary.
- [`docs/architecture/memory.md`](docs/architecture/memory.md) — memory ownership, frame allocator, and paging direction.
- [`docs/architecture/crabshell.md`](docs/architecture/crabshell.md) — parser/kernel boundary and shell/VFS contract.
- [`docs/architecture/drivers.md`](docs/architecture/drivers.md) — current driver scope and limitations.
- [`docs/security.md`](docs/security.md) — unsafe boundaries and security policy.
- [`docs/development/building.md`](docs/development/building.md) and [`docs/development/testing.md`](docs/development/testing.md) — supported commands and validation expectations.

When code and documentation disagree, inspect the implementation, resolve the discrepancy deliberately, and update the relevant documentation in the same change.

## Repository map

- `src/main.rs` — freestanding entry, boot snapshot acquisition, panic path, and shell handoff.
- `src/boot.rs` — mutable Limine requests, structural response/range validation, owned `BootInfo`, and boot diagnostics.
- `src/memory.rs` — allocation-free memory-map, address-width, canonical-address, Limine HHDM-range, and linker-defined kernel segment validation.
- `src/frame.rs` — bounded physical-frame allocator core; it only uses validated `Usable` ranges, reserves the first MiB, and has fixed range metadata.
- `src/paging.rs` — pure checked range and 4 KiB leaf-PTE bit construction for future mappings; no table access or physical-memory dereference.
- `src/shell.rs` — serial line editor and kernel-side Crabshell executor.
- `src/vfs.rs` — fixed-capacity volatile RAM filesystem and host-side tests.
- `crates/crabshell/` — separate `no_std` parser crate. It has no terminal, filesystem, or kernel dependencies.
- `src/arch/x86_64/serial.rs` — polling COM1 driver for shell input/output.
- `src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs` — bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT, assembly stubs, and fatal exception diagnostics.
- `src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs` — CPUID identification and selected feature reporting.
- `src/arch/x86_64/keyboard.rs` — raw, non-blocking PS/2-compatible scancode polling; not an input subsystem.
- `src/arch/x86_64/io.rs` — narrow port-I/O wrappers.
- `linker.ld`, `.cargo/config.toml`, `rust-toolchain.toml` — target, linker, and toolchain configuration.
- `limine.conf`, `scripts/boot.py` — boot configuration and pinned image/emulator workflow.
- `justfile` — supported development commands.
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — CI validation workflow.

## Engineering rules

### Keep changes incremental and coherent

1. Inspect the relevant source, tests, docs, and call sites before editing.
2. State assumptions, invariants, and failure behavior for new kernel interfaces.
3. Prefer small vertical slices that compile and can be tested over broad scaffolding or placeholder APIs.
4. Update tests and documentation alongside behavior changes.
5. Do not change unrelated code, rename files gratuitously, add speculative features, or rewrite project history.
6. Do not commit or create branches unless the user explicitly asks.

### Rust and dependency policy

- Preserve the kernel's `no_std`/freestanding constraints. Do not introduce `std` into kernel code.
- Prefer `core` and existing in-tree abstractions. Do not add third-party Rust dependencies without a concrete need and compatibility/security review.
- Keep the Crabshell parser independent of kernel I/O and VFS implementation. Kernel execution belongs in `src/shell.rs` or an appropriate kernel service.
- Do not add allocation-dependent APIs before a real heap exists. Fixed-capacity structures must document their limits and exhaustion behavior.
- Respect the workspace structure and the host-testable `rustix-kernel` library versus freestanding `rustix` binary boundary.

### Unsafe and hardware code

Unsafe code is expected only at explicit hardware, boot-protocol, assembly, or raw-memory boundaries. Keep each unsafe block narrow and document the invariant that makes it sound. Do not add broad `unsafe impl`, mutable global references, unchecked pointer arithmetic, or unreviewed inline/global assembly.

Before changing boot or memory code, account for these facts:

- Limine fills response pointers before `_start`; the request records must remain writable in the ELF image.
- Rustix validates nullness, alignment, counts, arithmetic, and physical ranges, but cannot prove that a non-null bootloader pointer is readable.
- Physical ranges are half-open `[start, end)` and must use checked arithmetic.
- Only regions classified `Usable` may enter the frame allocator. ACPI, bootloader-reclaimable, framebuffer, reserved, unknown, and other types are not free frames.
- A `Frame` is a physical address, not a dereferenceable pointer. Do not access it through the HHDM or change CR3 until an explicit, reviewed mapping policy and ownership proof exist.
- The kernel currently inherits Limine's page tables. Do not casually replace or mutate them: preserve the executing kernel, boot stack, `BootInfo`, request/response data, exception stacks, and mappings needed to continue execution.
- The exception setup is fatal-only. It does not enable maskable interrupts, configure a PIC/APIC, or provide recovery. Do not call `sti` or claim interrupt support without an IRQ design and tests.
- The shell and VFS run in ring 0 and are not isolated or secure.

For hardware changes, document assumptions about CPU mode, selectors, stacks, page permissions, interrupt state, and failure handling. Avoid new architecture mechanisms that cannot be statically reviewed or validated.

### Shell and filesystem contract

- Crabshell is presently a kernel-mode serial shell, not a userspace program or a POSIX shell.
- Its parser is a separate `no_std`, allocation-free crate; retain that boundary.
- The RAM filesystem is volatile and bounded. Preserve explicit errors and test capacity, path, and mutation edge cases.
- Do not imply persistence, permissions, links, process launching, or shell features that do not exist.
- Update the parser tests and `docs/architecture/crabshell.md` when adding or changing commands.

## Validation workflow

Run the narrowest relevant checks first, then broaden them. From the repository root, the supported commands are:

```sh
just fmt
just test
just check
just build
just image
just smoke
just verify
```

`just test` runs host-side library tests (memory-map validation, frame allocator, VFS, and Crabshell parser). `just check` checks `x86_64-unknown-none`; `just build` links the optimized ELF. `just verify` includes formatting, host tests, target check, pinned Limine image creation, and QEMU prompt smoke test. Image/boot checks need Python, `xorriso`, QEMU, the Rust target, and network access for the first pinned Limine download; Linux/WSL also needs `cc` to build Limine's host utility.

For changes to `src/main.rs`, `src/boot.rs`, linker/request configuration, `src/arch/x86_64/`, `src/frame.rs`, or paging/heap code, the intended full validation is `just verify`. If the environment does not permit a check, report the exact blocker and leave the corresponding roadmap criterion pending.

Do not claim a check passed unless it was run and its successful result was observed. Editor diagnostics are useful but are not a substitute for `cargo test`, a target build, or QEMU. A target check is not a final link; a linked ELF is not proof of boot; a prompt smoke test is not proof of interactive shell behavior or physical-hardware correctness.

## Completion criteria for agent changes

Before reporting work complete:

- Ensure source, tests, docs, and call sites agree.
- Review unsafe and hardware assumptions, including error paths and capacity limits.
- Run appropriate formatting/tests/build/boot checks, or clearly state why they could not run.
- Report files changed, behavior delivered, validation actually observed, and remaining risks.
- Keep milestone status accurate. A subsystem is not complete just because it has code.

   293	/// Capture a bounded register snapshot using a caller-provided MSR reader.
   294	///
   295	/// This helper performs no hardware access itself. A false support flag returns
   296	/// without invoking the reader; an over-capacity count returns no partial data.
   297	pub fn capture_mtrr_registers(supported: bool, mut read_msr: impl FnMut(u32) -> u64) -> MtrrState {
   298	    if !supported {
   299	        return MtrrState::Unsupported;
   300	    }
   301	
   302	    let capability = read_msr(IA32_MTRRCAP);
   303	    let variable_register_count = (capability & 0xff) as u8;
   304	    if usize::from(variable_register_count) > MAX_CAPTURED_VARIABLE_MTRRS {
   305	        return MtrrState::VariableRangeCapacityExceeded {
   306	            reported_count: variable_register_count,
   307	        };
   308	    }
   309	
   310	    let default_type = read_msr(IA32_MTRR_DEF_TYPE);
   311	    let fixed_registers = if capability & MTRRCAP_FIXED_SUPPORTED != 0 {
   312	        let mut registers = [0; FIXED_MTRR_REGISTER_INDICES.len()];
   313	        for (register, index) in registers.iter_mut().zip(FIXED_MTRR_REGISTER_INDICES) {
   314	            *register = read_msr(index);
   315	        }
   316	        Some(registers)
   317	    } else {
   318	        None
   319	    };
   320	
   321	    let mut variable_registers =
   322	        [MtrrRegisterPair { base: 0, mask: 0 }; MAX_CAPTURED_VARIABLE_MTRRS];
   323	    for (range_index, registers) in variable_registers
   324	        .iter_mut()
   325	        .take(usize::from(variable_register_count))
   326	        .enumerate()
   327	    {
   328	        let base_index = IA32_MTRR_PHYSBASE0 + 2 * range_index as u32;
   329	        registers.base = read_msr(base_index);
   330	        registers.mask = read_msr(base_index + 1);
   331	    }
   332	
   333	    MtrrState::Captured(MtrrRegisters {
   334	        capability,
   335	        default_type,
   336	        fixed_registers,
   337	        variable_register_count,
   338	        variable_registers,
   339	    })
   340	}

     1	# Memory-management direction
     2	
     3	## What exists now
     4	
     5	`src/memory.rs` contains an allocation-free `MemoryMapBuilder` that copies Limine ranges into validated half-open physical regions. It rejects empty ranges, `base + length` overflow, overlapping ranges, empty maps, and maps exceeding the fixed 256-region capacity. Known Limine types remain distinct, and unknown type values are preserved. Host-side tests cover range validation/classification, canonical-address boundaries, physical-width bounds, and HHDM range arithmetic. `src/boot.rs` stores the resulting map in an owned boot snapshot and reports usable bytes.
     6	
     7	`src/frame.rs` provides a fixed-capacity allocator core with host-side tests. It only manages complete 4 KiB frames inside validated `Usable` regions, reserves the first MiB, and coalesces adjacent free ranges. The ownership contract assumes one allocator instance per physical map: within that instance, each eligible frame is owned either by its free-range table or by a non-copyable `Frame` token while allocated. The public constructor does not enforce unique instances, so callers must not initialize multiple allocators for the same physical map; the current boot path retains one allocator in `BootInfo`. `allocate` returns `None` when no free frame remains. `deallocate` consumes the token only on success; on any error, including free-range-table exhaustion, it returns a `DeallocationError` containing the original token and leaves allocator state unchanged. The range tables each have a fixed `MAX_FRAME_RANGES` capacity, so fragmentation can prevent a frame from being returned until nearby ranges coalesce. No kernel service currently allocates frames for mappings or other work.
     8	
     9	`Frame::address()` is a physical address value, not a dereferenceable pointer and not a proof that the frame is mapped. CPU diagnostics now read `CR4.LA57` to report the active linear-address width (48 or 57 bits) and query `CPUID.80000008H` for physical and maximum linear-address widths when available. Boot-protocol pointers are checked against the active width, with host tests for 48- and 57-bit canonical boundaries. These facts do not prove that any physical address is mapped.
    10	
    11	`src/paging.rs` adds pure, host-tested 4 KiB mapping groundwork and decodes the inherited CR3 root address plus its low-bit interpretation. The CR3 decoder validates the physical-address width and reserved bits and interprets the low 12 bits according to the active `CR4.PCIDE` state; it does not dereference the root. The mapping-range validator requires a known physical-address width, checked aligned bounds, canonical virtual endpoints in one canonical half, and rejects writable-executable permissions. A validated range can encode the raw bits of one 4 KiB leaf PTE, including supervisor/user and write permissions, NX when the caller confirms EFER.NXE, and a bounded three-bit PAT index. `PatLayout` parses a supplied `IA32_PAT` value and selects WB, UC, or WC indices. `MtrrMemoryType`, `VariableMtrr`, `FixedMtrrRanges`, and `MtrrLayout` parse caller-supplied register values and resolve the MTRR type at one physical address, including fixed-range priority and specified variable-overlap rules; undefined overlaps fail closed. `src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs` now captures supported MTRR capability, default-type, fixed-range, and variable-range registers read-only into a fixed-capacity diagnostic snapshot. It retains up to 32 variable pairs; if hardware reports more, it records the capacity condition without retaining a partial snapshot. The raw capture is not yet validated and combined with PAT to establish an effective cache type for a mapping. The CPU reads EFER.NXE only when NX is supported and reads `IA32_PAT` only when PAT is supported; these reads are diagnostic and do not modify CPU state. None of these helpers proves frame ownership or HHDM coverage, inspects table entries, or modifies hardware page tables. No page mapping operation or CR3 transition is implemented.
    12	
    13	The requested Limine base revision is 3. Its protocol maps only `Usable`, `BootloaderReclaimable`, `ExecutableAndModules`, and `Framebuffer` memory-map regions into the HHDM; reserved, ACPI, bad, and unknown regions are not in that mapping set. HHDM mappings use at least 4 KiB granularity and may cover page-aligned bytes beyond unaligned region boundaries. On x86_64, inherited HHDM mappings are supervisor RWX, normally write-back cached, with framebuffer mappings write-combining when PAT is available. Therefore an HHDM offset is not a blanket physical-memory access grant, and inherited HHDM permissions are not Rustix's future W^X policy. See the [Limine base revision 3 protocol](https://github.com/limine-bootloader/limine-protocol/blob/trunk/PROTOCOL.md#base-revision-3) and its memory-layout/caching sections.
    14	
    15	The boot snapshot now rejects physical map ranges beyond the reported CPUID physical-address width when that CPUID leaf is available. For base revision 3 HHDM-mapped types, it also validates the page-rounded physical span, checked `offset + address` arithmetic, and canonical endpoints in the active linear-address width. If the CPU does not report a physical width, the physical-bound check is skipped and no mapping caller may treat the bound as known. These checks are derived from metadata and Limine's protocol contract; they do not inspect page tables or prove that a non-null loader pointer is readable. Rustix still does not dereference physical memory through the HHDM. Rustix-owned mappings should be non-executable by default; executable kernel text must be explicit. MMIO requires an explicit device range and cache policy, and guard regions must remain unmapped. A page-table transition must preserve the kernel image, active stacks, boot data, descriptor tables, and any loader mappings still needed. Rustix does not reclaim bootloader memory, own or replace the inherited Limine page tables, or provide a heap. Bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT setup and fatal exception diagnostics live in `src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs`; they do not enable maskable IRQs.
    16	
    17	## Mapping inventory before a CR3 transition
    18	
    19	The current runtime has several mappings that a future page-table transition must preserve. The address sources and remaining gaps are:
    20	
    21	- **Kernel ELF image:** `linker.ld` places `.text`, `.rodata`, `.limine_requests`, `.data`, `.bss`, and `.got` in three `PT_LOAD` segments: RX text, read-only rodata, and RW data/BSS. It exports `__kernel_start` and `__kernel_end` around the complete loadable image, plus page-aligned bounds for each segment. `BootInfo` checks that Limine's reported virtual base matches the linker start, validates ordered contiguous segment bounds covering the rounded image, derives corresponding half-open physical ranges from the executable physical base with checked arithmetic, and validates canonical virtual and reported physical address widths. The release ELF and QEMU runtime report both showed the three aligned ranges on 2026-10-21. The RX, R/NX, and RW/NX labels describe the linker segment intent; these are linker/boot metadata, not proof that the inherited page tables map every page or enforce those permissions, nor proof that loader pointers are readable. The memory-map `ExecutableAndModules` entries remain illustrative, not an authoritative kernel-image extent.
    22	- **Active stack and `BootInfo`:** The assembly `_start` shim captures Limine's entry `RSP` before any Rust prologue. Under the SysV entry convention the synthetic return slot occupies 8 bytes, so `RSP + 8` is the exclusive stack top. The protocol guarantees at least 64 KiB (without a Stack Size request); `BootInfo` records that minimum virtual span, translates it through the HHDM, and requires it to fit within a single `BootloaderReclaimable` physical region. The full loader allocation may be larger, and neither its exact bounds nor a guard page are known. Preserve the inherited mapping; do not infer a guard page.
    23	- **Kernel static data:** `RAM_FILESYSTEM`, GDT, IDT, TSS, the ring-0 stack, and double-fault IST stack are static BSS/data in the kernel image. Exception entry also requires the handler code and the TSS/IDT references to remain mapped. Preserve the complete relevant data/BSS pages and stack pages.
    24	- **Limine request data:** request records are in the kernel's writable `.limine_requests` segment. Response objects and the memory-map pointer array are bootloader-reclaimable; `capture_boot_information` copies the values used later, and the shell does not retain those pointers. Keep them mapped until the copy and validation finish; any later reclaim must be explicit rather than reclaiming the whole bootloader-reclaimable class.
    25	- **Inherited page tables:** Limine places its page tables in bootloader-reclaimable memory, but their layout is unspecified. `BootInfo` captures raw CR3 and validates a decoded physical root address plus the low-bit interpretation selected by active `CR4.PCIDE`; this numeric decode does not make the root dereferenceable. Rustix does not inspect root entries or inventory the live mappings. Keep the old root and its backing pages intact while inspecting/building a replacement; do not reclaim them until a verified switch no longer depends on them.
    26	- **Devices:** COM1 uses x86 port I/O and needs no MMIO virtual mapping. Rustix does not currently request or use a framebuffer. Any future framebuffer or device-register mapping needs an explicit physical range and cache policy.
    27	
    28	## Initial kernel-owned mapping policy (design only)
    29	
    30	A first Rustix-owned x86_64 root should use 4 KiB pages only and require NX support; if NX is unavailable, abort before switching. Preserve ELF permissions exactly: text RX, rodata R/NX, and `.limine_requests`/data/BSS/GOT RW/NX. Reject W+X mappings. Exclude the complete physical kernel-image span from the generic HHDM in the first implementation so no writable direct-map alias can undermine text or rodata permissions. Ordinary RAM HHDM mappings should be RW/NX and WB.
    31	
    32	Preserve the inherited PAT/MTRR configuration during the first transition. The current boot report reads the active `IA32_PAT` value when PAT is supported and captures supported MTRR registers, but does not validate the raw snapshot or establish effective cache types for physical ranges. Under Limine base revision 3 on x86_64, use PAT index 0 for WB, index 3 for UC, and index 5 for WC only when the active configuration and effective MTRR interaction are verified. Map MMIO only from explicit device ranges and use UC by default; do not infer MMIO from generic reserved memory-map entries. A framebuffer may use WC only after its response and cache policy are explicitly validated. COM1 uses port I/O and requires no MMIO mapping.
    33	
    34	Do not use huge pages in the first root; add them only when physical coverage, permissions, and cache attributes are uniform across the entire huge-page extent. Future Rustix-owned downward-growing stacks should have at least one 4 KiB unmapped guard page below them. The Limine bootstrap stack has no known guard, so none may be assumed there.
    35	
    36	Never modify Limine's active page tables in place. Build a separate candidate root from owned frames, leave the inherited root and its backing memory intact, and do not switch CR3 until every transition-critical mapping has been preserved and checked. Any pre-switch failure must discard the candidate root and return its frames without changing the active root. This policy is not yet implemented; Rustix does not inspect the inherited root or replace CR3.
    37	
    38	## Planned memory layers
    39	
    40	1. **Validated physical regions:** implemented as a fixed-capacity owned snapshot; allocator ownership and reclaim policy remain future work.
    41	2. **Frame allocator integration:** the bounded core is initialized from `BootInfo`; add real allocation callers only after the page-mapping policy and ownership rules are implemented.
    42	3. **Kernel virtual memory:** Rustix still runs on inherited Limine page tables. Before replacing them, preserve the executing kernel, bootstrap/Ring-0 stacks, request/response data, and exception stacks; define the HHDM extent and explicit mapping permissions/cache attributes. Keep writable-executable mappings disallowed by default and reserve MMIO and guard regions.

11.5.2.2   Selecting Memory Types for Pentium III and More Recent Processor Families

The Intel Core 2 Duo, Intel Atom, Intel Core Duo, Intel Core Solo, Pentium M, Pentium 4, Intel Xeon, and Pentium  III

 processors use the PAT to select effective page-level memory types. Here, a memory type for a page is selected 

by the MTRRs and the value in a PAT entry that is selected with the PAT, PCD and PWT bits in a page-table or page- directory entry (see Section 11.12.3, “Selecting a Memory Type from the PAT”).  Table 11-7 describes the mapping  of MTRR memory types and PAT entry types to effective memory types, when normal caching is in effect (the CD  and NW flags in control register CR0 are clear).

     5	`src/memory.rs` contains an allocation-free `MemoryMapBuilder` that copies Limine ranges into validated half-open physical regions. It rejects empty ranges, `base + length` overflow, overlapping ranges, empty maps, and maps exceeding the fixed 256-region capacity. Known Limine types remain distinct, and unknown type values are preserved. Host-side tests cover range validation/classification, canonical-address boundaries, physical-width bounds, and HHDM range arithmetic. `src/boot.rs` stores the resulting map in an owned boot snapshot and reports usable bytes.
     6	
     7	`src/frame.rs` provides a fixed-capacity allocator core with host-side tests. It only manages complete 4 KiB frames inside validated `Usable` regions, reserves the first MiB, and coalesces adjacent free ranges. The ownership contract assumes one allocator instance per physical map: within that instance, each eligible frame is owned either by its free-range table or by a non-copyable `Frame` token while allocated. The public constructor does not enforce unique instances, so callers must not initialize multiple allocators for the same physical map; the current boot path retains one allocator in `BootInfo`. `allocate` returns `None` when no free frame remains. `deallocate` consumes the token only on success; on any error, including free-range-table exhaustion, it returns a `DeallocationError` containing the original token and leaves allocator state unchanged. The range tables each have a fixed `MAX_FRAME_RANGES` capacity, so fragmentation can prevent a frame from being returned until nearby ranges coalesce. No kernel service currently allocates frames for mappings or other work.
     8	
     9	`Frame::address()` is a physical address value, not a dereferenceable pointer and not a proof that the frame is mapped. CPU diagnostics now read `CR4.LA57` to report the active linear-address width (48 or 57 bits) and query `CPUID.80000008H` for physical and maximum linear-address widths when available. Boot-protocol pointers are checked against the active width, with host tests for 48- and 57-bit canonical boundaries. These facts do not prove that any physical address is mapped.
    10

The mapping-range validator requires a known physical-address width, checked aligned bounds, canonical virtual endpoints in one canonical half, and rejects writable-executable permissions.     12	
    13	The requested Limine base revision is 3. Its protocol maps only `Usable`, `BootloaderReclaimable`, `ExecutableAndModules`, and `Framebuffer` memory-map regions into the HHDM; reserved, ACPI, bad, and unknown regions are not in that mapping set. HHDM mappings use at least 4 KiB granularity and may cover page-aligned bytes beyond unaligned region boundaries. On x86_64, inherited HHDM mappings are supervisor RWX, normally write-back cached, with framebuffer mappings write-combining when PAT is available. Therefore an HHDM offset is not a blanket physical-memory access grant, and inherited HHDM permissions are not Rustix's future W^X policy. See the [Limine base revision 3 protocol](https://github.com/limine-bootloader/limine-protocol/blob/trunk/PROTOCOL.md#base-revision-3) and its memory-layout/caching sections.
    14	
    15	The boot snapshot now rejects physical map ranges beyond the reported CPUID physical-address width when that CPUID leaf is available. For base revision 3 HHDM-mapped types, it also validates the page-rounded physical span, checked `offset + address` arithmetic, and canonical endpoints in the active linear-address width. If the CPU does not report a physical width, the physical-bound check is skipped and no mapping caller may treat the bound as known. These checks are derived from metadata and Limine's protocol contract; they do not inspect page tables or prove that a non-null loader pointer is readable. Rustix still does not dereference physical memory through the HHDM. Rustix-owned mappings should be non-executable by default; executable kernel text must be explicit. MMIO requires an explicit device range and cache policy, and guard regions must remain unmapped. A page-table transition must preserve the kernel image, active stacks, boot data, descriptor tables, and any loader mappings still needed. Rustix does not reclaim bootloader memory, own or replace the inherited Limine page tables, or provide a heap. Bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT setup and fatal exception diagnostics live in `src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs`; they do not enable maskable IRQs.
    16	
    17	## Mapping inventory before a CR3 transition
    18	
    19	The current runtime has several mappings that a future page-table transition must preserve. The address sources and remaining gaps are:
    20	
    21	- **Kernel ELF image:** `linker.ld` places `.text`, `.rodata`, `.limine_requests`, `.data`, `.bss`, and `.got` in three `PT_LOAD` segments: RX text, read-only rodata, and RW data/BSS. It exports `__kernel_start` and `__kernel_end` around the complete loadable image, plus page-aligned bounds for each segment. `BootInfo` checks that Limine's reported virtual base matches the linker start, validates ordered contiguous segment bounds covering the rounded image, derives corresponding half-open physical ranges from the executable physical base with checked arithmetic, and validates canonical virtual and reported physical address widths. The release ELF and QEMU runtime report both showed the three aligned ranges on 2026-10-21. The RX, R/NX, and RW/NX labels describe the linker segment intent; these are linker/boot metadata, not proof that the inherited page tables map every page or enforce those permissions, nor proof that loader pointers are readable. The memory-map `ExecutableAndModules` entries remain illustrative, not an authoritative kernel-image extent.
    22	- **Active stack and `BootInfo`:** The assembly `_start` shim captures Limine's entry `RSP` before any Rust prologue. Under the SysV entry convention the synthetic return slot occupies 8 bytes, so `RSP + 8` is the exclusive stack top. The protocol guarantees at least 64 KiB (without a Stack Size request); `BootInfo` records that minimum virtual span, translates it through the HHDM, and requires it to fit within a single `BootloaderReclaimable` physical region. The full loader allocation may be larger, and neither its exact bounds nor a guard page are known. Preserve the inherited mapping; do not infer a guard page.
    23	- **Kernel static data:** `RAM_FILESYSTEM`, GDT, IDT, TSS, the ring-0 stack, and double-fault IST stack are static BSS/data in the kernel image. Exception entry also requires the handler code and the TSS/IDT references to remain mapped. Preserve the complete relevant data/BSS pages and stack pages.
    24	- **Limine request data:** request records are in the kernel's writable `.limine_requests` segment. Response objects and the memory-map pointer array are bootloader-reclaimable; `capture_boot_information` copies the values used later, and the shell does not retain those pointers. Keep them mapped until the copy and validation finish; any later reclaim must be explicit rather than reclaiming the whole bootloader-reclaimable class.
    25	- **Inherited page tables:** Limine places its page tables in bootloader-reclaimable memory, but their layout is unspecified. `BootInfo` captures raw CR3 and validates a decoded physical root address plus the low-bit interpretation selected by active `CR4.PCIDE`; this numeric decode does not make the root dereferenceable. Rustix does not inspect root entries or inventory the live mappings. Keep the old root and its backing pages intact while inspecting/building a replacement; do not reclaim them until a verified switch no longer depends on them.
    26	- **Devices:** COM1 uses x86 port I/O and needs no MMIO virtual mapping. Rustix does not currently request or use a framebuffer. Any future framebuffer or device-register mapping needs an explicit physical range and cache policy.
    27	
    28	## Initial kernel-owned mapping policy (design only)
    29	
    30	A first Rustix-owned x86_64 root should use 4 KiB pages only and require NX support; if NX is unavailable, abort before switching. Preserve ELF permissions exactly: text RX, rodata R/NX, and `.limine_requests`/data/BSS/GOT RW/NX. Reject W+X mappings. Exclude the complete physical kernel-image span from the generic HHDM in the first implementation so no writable direct-map alias can undermine text or rodata permissions. Ordinary RAM HHDM mappings should be RW/NX and WB.
    31	
    32	Preserve the inherited PAT/MTRR configuration during the first transition. The current boot report reads the active `IA32_PAT` value when PAT is supported and captures supported MTRR registers, but does not validate the raw snapshot or establish effective cache types for physical ranges. Under Limine base revision 3 on x86_64, use PAT index 0 for WB, index 3 for UC, and index 5 for WC only when the active configuration and effective MTRR interaction are verified. Map MMIO only from explicit device ranges and use UC by default; do not infer MMIO from generic reserved memory-map entries. A framebuffer may use WC only after its response and cache policy are explicitly validated. COM1 uses port I/O and requires no MMIO mapping.
    33	
    34	Do not use huge pages in the first root; add them only when physical coverage, permissions, and cache attributes are uniform across the entire huge-page extent. Future Rustix-owned downward-growing stacks should have at least one 4 KiB unmapped guard page below them. The Limine bootstrap stack has no known guard, so none may be assumed there.
    35	
    36	Never modify Limine's active page tables in place. Build a separate candidate root from owned frames, leave the inherited root and its backing memory intact, and do not switch CR3 until every transition-critical mapping has been preserved and checked. Any pre-switch failure must discard the candidate root and return its frames without changing the active root. This policy is not yet implemented; Rustix does not inspect the inherited root or replace CR3.
    37	
    38	## Planned memory layers
    39	
    40	1. **Validated physical regions:** implemented as a fixed-capacity owned snapshot; allocator ownership and reclaim policy remain future work.
    41	2. **Frame allocator integration:** the bounded core is initialized from `BootInfo`; add real allocation callers only after the page-mapping policy and ownership rules are implemented.
    42	3. **Kernel virtual memory:** Rustix still runs on inherited Limine page tables. Before replacing them, preserve the executing kernel, bootstrap/Ring-0 stacks, request/response data, and exception stacks; define the HHDM extent and explicit mapping permissions/cache attributes. Keep writable-executable mappings disallowed by default and reserve MMIO and guard regions.
    43	4. **Heap:** add a global allocator only after frame allocation and page mapping are initialized. Define allocation failure behavior for kernel and interrupt contexts.
    44	5. **Process address spaces:** isolate userspace; define copy-in/copy-out helpers and never treat user pointers as kernel references.
    45	
    46	## Invariants to preserve
    47	
    48	- Physical ranges use checked arithmetic and the half-open convention `[start, end)`.
    49	- Only complete frames in validated `Usable` regions enter the allocator; the first MiB remains reserved. Firmware and loader-reclaimable regions are not silently promoted to free memory.
    50	- Under the single-allocator-per-physical-map contract, a frame is represented by one allocator-free range or one caller-owned, non-copyable `Frame` token. Only a successful `deallocate` transfers the token back to the allocator; errors return the token and leave allocator ranges and accounting unchanged. The current public constructor relies on callers to enforce unique allocator instances.
    51	- `allocate` returns `None` on frame exhaustion. Metadata-capacity exhaustion is an explicit error, never silent loss of a frame.
    52	- A `Frame` address is physical, not directly dereferenceable. No HHDM translation, page-table mutation, or CR3 switch is permitted until address widths, mapping coverage, permissions/cache attributes, and transition-preservation requirements are established.
    53	- Mapping changes validate alignment, canonical addresses, ownership, and permissions before touching tables.
    54	- User-controlled addresses are validated on every syscall boundary; prior validation is not a substitute for access checks during later copies.
    55	- Tests cover unaligned edges, exact-boundary allocations, arithmetic overflow, overlaps, exhaustion, and unchanged state/ownership on failure.
    56	
    57	These are design requirements for future milestones, not functionality delivered by the current boot summary.

```rustix/docs/security.md
     1	# Security and unsafe-code policy
     2	
     3	Rustix is an early kernel prototype, not a security-reviewed operating system. It has no user/kernel separation implementation, process isolation, security boundary, or supported deployment profile today.
     4	
     5	## Current unsafe boundaries
     6	
     7	- `src/arch/x86_64/io.rs` issues privileged x86 port-I/O instructions behind narrow driver wrappers.
     8	- `src/arch/x86_64/serial.rs` configures and writes to the legacy COM1 UART. It is intended for early kernel context only.
     9	- `src/arch/x86_64/keyboard.rs` reads raw bytes from a legacy PS/2-compatible controller; callers must poll without blocking.
    10	- `src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs` executes CPUID for boot-time feature reporting and performs gated, read-only `RDMSR` reads of EFER.NXE, `IA32_PAT`, and supported MTRR registers. EFER and PAT reads are gated by their CPUID features; MTRR reads are skipped unless CPUID reports MTRR support and are bounded to the reported variable-register count, up to 32 pairs. These paths assume CPL 0 and architectural feature/MSR availability, and they do not write MSRs.
    11	- `src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs` loads the GDT/TSS/IDT and exception-entry assembly, reads CR2 on page faults, and halts after printing the saved context. The exception gates are kernel-only and maskable interrupts remain disabled.
    12	- `src/boot.rs` reads Limine response pointers and entries, then validates and copies range metadata into an owned boot snapshot. Nullness, alignment, count bounds, arithmetic, and range overlap are checked; the kernel still trusts Limine to make non-null response objects readable for the handoff lifetime.
    13	- `src/main.rs` uses `cli` and `hlt` to stop the bootstrap CPU after a fatal startup error.
    14	- `src/vfs.rs` and `src/shell.rs` provide a kernel-mode RAM filesystem and shell. They have no user/kernel isolation, permissions, persistence, or protection from kernel bugs; shell commands are trusted kernel code, not sandboxed applications.
    15	
    16	Unsafe blocks should remain as small as practical and state the assumptions that make each operation valid. Avoid widening `unsafe impl` or introducing raw-pointer-based public APIs without a documented safety argument. The PS/2 routine consumes bytes from the controller, including discarding auxiliary/error bytes, so it must only be used by a single owner of that controller until input serialization is designed. External boot inputs, user pointers, MMIO, and DMA must not be treated as trusted merely because current boot data is trusted.
    17	
    18	## Security requirements for future subsystems
    19	
    20	- Validate every physical range and checked address calculation before mapping or allocating it.
    21	- Enforce least privilege in page mappings; avoid writable-executable pages by default.
    22	- Keep user memory untrusted and use explicit copy-in/copy-out routines at syscall boundaries.
    23	- Define ownership and lifetime rules for descriptors, processes, shared memory, and device buffers.
    24	- Test malformed input and error paths as well as successful operation.
    25	- Do not claim isolation or security guarantees until those properties have end-to-end tests and review.

```

     1	# Testing and verification
     2	
     3	## Current checks
     4	
     5	`just verify` runs the standard development verification sequence:
     6	
     7	1. `just fmt` — fail on formatting differences across the workspace.
     8	2. `just test` — run host-side memory-map, mapping-range/PTE-bit policy, frame-allocator, RAM-filesystem, and Crabshell parser tests.
     9	3. `just check` — check the `x86_64-unknown-none` kernel target.
    10	4. `just smoke` — build the pinned hybrid ISO, boot it in QEMU, and check that Crabshell reaches its prompt within a deadline.
    11	
    12	`just fault-smoke` separately builds opt-in kernel variants that deliberately trigger a page fault and an invalid opcode. It requires each QEMU run to report the expected exception (and CR2 for the page fault), avoid the shell prompt, and remain halted until timeout. It then rebuilds and restores the default release kernel and ISO. These are fatal-path diagnostics, not exception recovery tests; both Cargo features are disabled by default and cannot be enabled together.
    13	
    14	Keep the Crabshell parser, VFS, memory-map validator, paging policy helpers, and frame allocator independent of hardware so syntax, path handling, address and leaf-PTE bit policy, supplied PAT-layout parsing, storage semantics, and frame ownership can be tested without booting. The pure PTE/PAT helpers do not access tables, read the active PAT MSR, combine PAT with MTRRs, or validate frame ownership. Boot separately captures MTRR registers for diagnostics; host tests exercise the fixed-capacity capture model with supplied register-reader values. The GDT/TSS/IDT and CPU-register paths are privileged kernel code; QEMU boot and fault-injection checks complement, but do not replace, static review and target builds. Add tests for boundaries and failure behavior when introducing new pure kernel helpers. The kernel binary is not a host test target.
    15	
    16	## What current checks do not prove
    17	
    18	- `cargo check` does not perform a final target link.
    19	- A successful ELF link does not prove the boot protocol is recognized or `_start` is reached.
    20	- Host unit tests do not validate privileged instructions, UART behavior, memory-map pointer validity, page tables, interrupts, or actual hardware. The QEMU boot path exercises the gated EFER/PAT reads and bounded MTRR capture and prints diagnostic summaries, but the prompt smoke assertion does not make those facts a mapping-safety proof.
    21	- The automated QEMU prompt smoke test checks only that the kernel reaches the shell. `just fault-smoke` separately exercises only the controlled page-fault and invalid-opcode fatal paths; it does not test every exception vector, recovery, or physical hardware.
    22	- A separate manual QEMU session exercised directory navigation and file create/write/append/read/copy/move/remove operations, including `cp` replacing an existing destination and rejection of `rmdir` on a nonempty directory. This is not exhaustive shell coverage and does not prove persistence across reboot.
    23	- There is no on-disk filesystem integration test, syscall/userspace test, fuzz target, or physical-hardware test.
    24	
    25	## Validation policy
    26	
    27	For changes to the kernel entry, linker script, boot requests, architecture code, shell, or VFS, run `just verify`. For memory-management and ABI code, add negative tests for overflow, malformed ranges, permission failures, and invalid user pointers before exposing those paths to userspace.
    28	
    29	Record commands actually run and any environment limitation in change summaries; never call an unexecuted build “passing.”

```

   452	            physical_address_bits,
   453	            memory_type,
   454	        }))
   455	    }

   477	        fixed_enabled: bool,

   479	        fixed_ranges: Option<&'a FixedMtrrRanges>,
   480	        variable_ranges: &'a [VariableMtrr],
   481	    ) -> Result<Self, MtrrError> {
   482	        if !(12..=MAX_MTRR_PHYSICAL_ADDRESS_BITS).contains(&physical_address_bits) {
   483	            return Err(MtrrError::InvalidPhysicalAddressWidth);
   484	        }
   485	        if enabled && fixed_enabled && fixed_ranges.is_none() {
   486	            return Err(MtrrError::FixedRangesUnavailable);
   487	        }
   488	        if variable_ranges
   489	            .iter()
   490	            .any(|range| range.physical_address_bits != physical_address_bits)
   491	        {
   492	            return Err(MtrrError::PhysicalAddressWidthMismatch);
   493	        }
   494	
   495	        Ok(Self {
   496	            physical_address_bits,
   497	            enabled,
   498	            fixed_enabled,
   499	            default_type,
   500	            fixed_ranges,
   501	            variable_ranges,
   502	        })
   503	    }

   505	    /// Resolve the MTRR type for one physical address, rejecting undefined overlaps.
   506	    pub fn memory_type_for(&self, address: u64) -> Result<MtrrMemoryType, MtrrError> {
   507	        if address >= (1u64 << self.physical_address_bits) {
   508	            return Err(MtrrError::PhysicalAddressOutOfRange);
   509	        }
   510	        if !self.enabled {
   511	            return Ok(MtrrMemoryType::Uncacheable);
   512	        }
   513	        if self.fixed_enabled {
   514	            if let Some(memory_type) = self
   515	                .fixed_ranges
   516	                .and_then(|ranges| ranges.type_for_address(address))
   517	            {
   518	                return Ok(memory_type);
   519	            }
   520	        }
   521	
   522	        let mut matched_types = 0u8;
   523	        for range in self.variable_ranges {
   524	            if range.matches(address) {
   525	                matched_types |= 1 << range.memory_type as u8;
   526	            }
   527	        }
   528	        if matched_types == 0 {
   529	            return Ok(self.default_type);
   530	        }
   531	        if matched_types & (1 << MtrrMemoryType::Uncacheable as u8) != 0 {
   532	            return Ok(MtrrMemoryType::Uncacheable);
   533	        }
   534	        if matched_types.count_ones() == 1 {
   535	            return MtrrMemoryType::from_raw(matched_types.trailing_zeros() as u8);
   536	        }
   537	        let write_back_and_through =
   538	            (1 << MtrrMemoryType::WriteBack as u8) | (1 << MtrrMemoryType::WriteThrough as u8);
   539	        if matched_types == write_back_and_through {
   540	            return Ok(MtrrMemoryType::WriteThrough);
   541	        }
   542	        Err(MtrrError::UndefinedOverlap)
   543	    }
   544	}

    32	pub fn identify() -> CpuInfo {

    38	    vendor[8..12].copy_from_slice(&basic.ecx.to_le_bytes());
    39	
    40	    let basic_features = if basic.eax >= 1 {
    41	        Some(__cpuid(1))
    42	    } else {
    43	        None
    44	    };
    45	    let extended = __cpuid(0x8000_0000);
    46	    let extended_features = if extended.eax >= 0x8000_0001 {
    47	        Some(__cpuid(0x8000_0001))
    48	    } else {
    49	        None
    50	    };
    51	    let structured_features = if basic.eax >= 7 {
    52	        Some(__cpuid_count(7, 0))

    55	    };

   104	/// Read the current raw CR3 value without changing page-table state.
   105	pub fn read_cr3_raw() -> u64 {
   106	    let cr3: u64;
   107	    // SAFETY: Rustix runs at CPL 0; reading CR3 is privileged but non-mutating.
   108	    unsafe { asm!("mov {}, cr3", out(reg) cr3, options(nomem, nostack, preserves_flags)) };
   109	    cr3
   110	}
   111	
   112	/// Read a model-specific register at CPL 0.
   113	///
   114	/// # Safety
   115	/// The caller must ensure the MSR exists on this CPU and that the current
   116	/// privilege level permits the read.
   117	unsafe fn read_msr(index: u32) -> u64 {
   118	    let low: u32;
   119	    let high: u32;
   120	    // SAFETY: The caller guarantees that this MSR is supported and accessible.
   121	    unsafe {
   122	        asm!(
   123	            "rdmsr",
   124	            in("ecx") index,
   125	            out("eax") low,
   126	            out("edx") high,
   127	            options(nomem, nostack)
   128	        );
   129	    }
   130	    (u64::from(high) << 32) | u64::from(low)
   131	}
   132	
   133	/// Read CR4 without changing paging state.
   134	fn read_cr4_raw() -> u64 {
   135	    let cr4: u64;
   136	    // SAFETY: Rustix runs at CPL 0; reading CR4 is privileged but non-mutating.
   137	    unsafe { asm!("mov {}, cr4", out(reg) cr4, options(nomem, nostack, preserves_flags)) };
   138	    cr4
   139	}

11.5.2.2   Selecting Memory Types for Pentium III and More Recent Processor Families

The Intel Core 2 Duo, Intel Atom, Intel Core Duo, Intel Core Solo, Pentium M, Pentium 4, Intel Xeon, and Pentium  III

 processors use the PAT to select effective page-level memory types. Here, a memory type for a page is selected 

by the MTRRs and the value in a PAT entry that is selected with the PAT, PCD and PWT bits in a page-table or page- directory entry (see Section 11.12.3, “Selecting a Memory Type from the PAT”).  Table 11-7 describes the mapping  of MTRR memory types and PAT entry types to effective memory types, when normal caching is in effect (the CD  and NW flags in control register CR0 are clear).

MEMORY CACHE CONTROL

11.5.2.3   Writing Values Across Pages with Different Memory Types

If two adjoining pages in memory have different memory types, and a word or longer operand is written to a  memory location that crosses the page boundary between those two pages, the operand might be written to  memory twice. This action does not present a problem for writes to actual memory; however, if a device is mapped  the memory space assigned to the pages, the device might malfunction.

11.5.3 Preventing 

Caching

To disable the L1, L2, and L3 caches after they have been enabled and have received cache fills, perform the  following steps: 1. Enter the no-fill cache mode. (Set the CD flag in control register CR0 to 1 and the NW flag to 0. 2. Flush all caches using the WBINVD instruction. 3. Disable the MTRRs and set the default memory type to uncached or set all MTRRs for the uncached memory 

type (see the discussion of the discussion of the TYPE field and the E flag  in Section 11.11.2.1, “IA32_MTRR_DEF_TYPE MSR”).

The caches must be flushed (step 2) after the CD flag is set to insure system memory coherency. If the caches are  not flushed, cache hits on reads will still occur and data will be read from valid cache lines. The intent of the three separate steps listed above address three distinct requirements: (i) discontinue new data  replacing existing data in the cache (ii) ensure data already in the cache are evicted to memory, (iii) ensure subse- quent memory references observe UC memory type semantics. Different processor implementation of caching  control hardware may allow some variation of software implementation of these three requirements. See note  below.

NOTES

Setting the CD flag in control register CR0 modifies the processor’s caching behaviour as indicated  in  Table 11-5, but setting the CD flag alone may not be sufficient across all processor families to  force the effective memory type for all physical memory to be UC nor does it force strict memory  ordering, due to hardware implementation variations across different processor families. To force  the UC memory type and strict memory ordering on all of physical memory, it is sufficient to either  program the MTRRs for all physical memory to be UC memory type or disable all MTRRs. For the Pentium 4 and Intel Xeon processors, after the sequence of steps given above has been  executed, the cache lines containing the code between the end of the WBINVD instruction and  before the MTRRS have actually been disabled may be retained in the cache hierarchy. Here, to

Correct effective memory type for a WC MTRR on a region with a PAT entry
UC- from UC to WC.

As per Intel SDM section "Selecting Memory Types for Pentium III and More

# 13. PAT (Page Attribute Table)¶

x86 Page Attribute Table (PAT) allows for setting the memory attribute at the page level granularity. PAT is complementary to the MTRR settings which allows for setting of memory types over physical address ranges. However, PAT is more flexible than MTRR due to its capability to set attributes at page level and also due to the fact that there are no hardware limitations on number of such attribute settings allowed. Added flexibility comes with guidelines for not having memory type aliasing for the same physical memory with multiple virtual addresses.

PAT allows for different types of memory attributes. The most commonly used ones that will be supported at this time are:
| 

WB | 

Write-back |
| 

UC | 

Uncached |
| 

WC | 

Write-combined |
| 

WT | 

Write-through |
| 

UC- | 

Uncached Minus |

## 13.1. PAT APIs¶

There are many different APIs in the kernel that allows setting of memory attributes at the page level. In order to avoid aliasing, these interfaces should be used thoughtfully. Below is a table of interfaces available, their intended usage and their memory attribute relationships. Internally, these APIs use a `reserve_memtype()`/ `free_memtype()` interface on the physical address range to avoid any aliasing.

## 13.2. Advanced APIs for drivers¶

A. Exporting pages to users with remap_pfn_range, io_remap_pfn_range, vmf_insert_pfn.

Drivers wanting to export some pages to userspace do it by using mmap interface and a combination of:
- 

`pgprot_noncached()`
- 

`io_remap_pfn_range()` or `remap_pfn_range()` or `vmf_insert_pfn()`

With PAT support, a new API pgprot_writecombine is being added. So, drivers can continue to use the above sequence, with either `pgprot_noncached()` or `pgprot_writecombine()` in step 1, followed by step 2.

In addition, step 2 internally tracks the region as UC or WC in memtype list in order to ensure no conflicting mapping.

Note that this set of APIs only works with IO (non RAM) regions. If driver wants to export a RAM region, it has to do `set_memory_uc()` or `set_memory_wc()`as step 0 above and also track the usage of those pages and use `set_memory_wb()`before the page is freed to free pool.

## 13.3. MTRR effects on PAT / non-PAT systems¶

The following table provides the effects of using write-combining MTRRs when using ioremap*() calls on x86 for both non-PAT and PAT systems. Ideally `mtrr_add()` usage will be phased out in favor of `arch_phys_wc_add()` which will be a no-op on PAT enabled systems. The region over which a `arch_phys_wc_add()`is made, should already have been ioremapped with WC attributes or PAT entries, this can be done by using `ioremap_wc()` / `set_memory_wc()`.  Devices which combine areas of IO memory desired to remain uncacheable with areas where write-combining is desirable should consider use of `ioremap_uc()` followed by `set_memory_wc()` to white-list effective write-combined areas.  Such use is nevertheless discouraged as the effective memory type is considered implementation defined, yet this strategy can be used as last resort on devices with size-constrained regions where otherwise MTRR write-combining would otherwise not be effective.

```
====  =======  ===  =========================  =====================
MTRR  Non-PAT  PAT  Linux ioremap value        Effective memory type
====  =======  ===  =========================  =====================
      PAT                                        Non-PAT |  PAT
      |PCD                                               |
      ||PWT                                              |
      |||                                                |
WC    000      WB   _PAGE_CACHE_MODE_WB             WC   |   WC
WC    001      WC   _PAGE_CACHE_MODE_WC             WC*  |   WC
WC    010      UC-  _PAGE_CACHE_MODE_UC_MINUS       WC*  |   UC
WC    011      UC   _PAGE_CACHE_MODE_UC             UC   |   UC
====  =======  ===  =========================  =====================

(*) denotes implementation defined and is discouraged

```

Note

-- in the above table mean “Not suggested usage for the API”. Some of the --‘s are strictly enforced by the kernel. Some others are not really enforced today, but may be enforced in future.

For ioremap and pci access through /sys or /proc - The actual type returned can be more restrictive, in case of any existing aliasing for that address. For example: If there is an existing uncached mapping, a new ioremap_wc can return uncached mapping in place of write-combine requested.

set_memory_[uc|wc|wt] and set_memory_wb should be used in pairs, where driver will first make a region uc, wc or wt and switch it back to wb after use.

Over time writes to /proc/mtrr will be deprecated in favor of using PAT based interfaces. Users writing to /proc/mtrr are suggested to use above interfaces.

Drivers should use ioremap_[uc|wc] to access PCI BARs with [uc|wc] access types.

Drivers should use set_memory_[uc|wc|wt] to set access type for RAM ranges.

## 13.4. PAT debugging¶

With CONFIG_DEBUG_FS enabled, PAT memtype list can be examined by:

```
# mount -t debugfs debugfs /sys/kernel/debug
# cat /sys/kernel/debug/x86/pat_memtype_list
PAT memtype list:
uncached-minus @ 0x7fadf000-0x7fae0000
uncached-minus @ 0x7fb19000-0x7fb1a000
uncached-minus @ 0x7fb1a000-0x7fb1b000
uncached-minus @ 0x7fb1b000-0x7fb1c000
uncached-minus @ 0x7fb1c000-0x7fb1d000
uncached-minus @ 0x7fb1d000-0x7fb1e000
uncached-minus @ 0x7fb1e000-0x7fb25000
uncached-minus @ 0x7fb25000-0x7fb26000
uncached-minus @ 0x7fb26000-0x7fb27000
uncached-minus @ 0x7fb27000-0x7fb28000
uncached-minus @ 0x7fb28000-0x7fb2e000
uncached-minus @ 0x7fb2e000-0x7fb2f000
uncached-minus @ 0x7fb2f000-0x7fb30000
uncached-minus @ 0x7fb31000-0x7fb32000
uncached-minus @ 0x80000000-0x90000000

```

This list shows physical address ranges and various PAT settings used to access those physical address ranges.

Another, more verbose way of getting PAT related debug messages is with “debugpat” boot parameter. With this parameter, various debug messages are printed to dmesg log.
