//! CPU feature and gated, read-only MSR reporting for x86_64 boot diagnostics.

use core::arch::asm;
use core::arch::x86_64::{__cpuid, __cpuid_count};
use rustix_kernel::paging::{capture_mtrr_registers, MtrrState};

const IA32_EFER: u32 = 0xc000_0080;
const IA32_PAT: u32 = 0x0000_0277;
const EFER_NXE: u64 = 1 << 11;

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct CpuInfo {
    pub vendor: [u8; 12],
    pub max_basic_leaf: u32,
    pub max_extended_leaf: u32,
    pub has_sse2: bool,
    pub has_nx: bool,
    pub nx_enabled: bool,
    pub normal_caching: bool,
    pub has_pat: bool,
    pub pat_msr_value: Option<u64>,
    pub mtrr: MtrrState,
    pub has_1g_pages: bool,
    pub has_long_mode: bool,
    pub has_la57: bool,
    pub physical_address_bits: Option<u8>,
    pub max_linear_address_bits: Option<u8>,
    pub active_linear_address_bits: u8,
    pub pcid_enabled: bool,
}

/// Read CPUID identity, selected feature bits, and supported read-only MSR state.
pub fn identify() -> CpuInfo {
    // CPUID is part of the x86_64 architectural baseline.
    let basic = __cpuid(0);
    let mut vendor = [0; 12];
    vendor[0..4].copy_from_slice(&basic.ebx.to_le_bytes());
    vendor[4..8].copy_from_slice(&basic.edx.to_le_bytes());
    vendor[8..12].copy_from_slice(&basic.ecx.to_le_bytes());

    let basic_features = if basic.eax >= 1 {
        Some(__cpuid(1))
    } else {
        None
    };
    let extended = __cpuid(0x8000_0000);
    let extended_features = if extended.eax >= 0x8000_0001 {
        Some(__cpuid(0x8000_0001))
    } else {
        None
    };
    let structured_features = if basic.eax >= 7 {
        Some(__cpuid_count(7, 0))
    } else {
        None
    };
    let address_widths = if extended.eax >= 0x8000_0008 {
        Some(__cpuid(0x8000_0008).eax)
    } else {
        None
    };
    let cr0 = read_cr0_raw();
    let cr4 = read_cr4_raw();
    let has_nx = extended_features.is_some_and(|features| features.edx & (1 << 20) != 0);
    let nx_enabled = if has_nx {
        // SAFETY: EFER is available in x86_64 long mode; CPUID confirms NX support,
        // and this boot-time code executes at CPL 0. The read does not change state.
        unsafe { read_msr(IA32_EFER) & EFER_NXE != 0 }
    } else {
        false
    };
    let has_pat = basic_features.is_some_and(|features| features.edx & (1 << 16) != 0);
    let pat_msr_value = if has_pat {
        // SAFETY: CPUID reports PAT support and boot-time kernel code runs at CPL 0.
        Some(unsafe { read_msr(IA32_PAT) })
    } else {
        None
    };
    let has_mtrr = basic_features.is_some_and(|features| features.edx & (1 << 12) != 0);
    let mtrr = capture_mtrr_registers(has_mtrr, |index| {
        // SAFETY: CPUID reports MTRR support; the capture helper only requests
        // architectural MTRR MSRs after that feature check.
        unsafe { read_msr(index) }
    });

    CpuInfo {
        vendor,
        max_basic_leaf: basic.eax,
        max_extended_leaf: extended.eax,
        has_sse2: basic_features.is_some_and(|features| features.edx & (1 << 26) != 0),
        has_nx,
        nx_enabled,
        normal_caching: cr0 & ((1 << 30) | (1 << 29)) == 0,
        has_pat,
        pat_msr_value,
        mtrr,
        has_1g_pages: extended_features.is_some_and(|features| features.edx & (1 << 26) != 0),
        has_long_mode: extended_features.is_some_and(|features| features.edx & (1 << 29) != 0),
        has_la57: structured_features.is_some_and(|features| features.ecx & (1 << 16) != 0),
        physical_address_bits: address_widths.map(|eax| (eax & 0xff) as u8),
        max_linear_address_bits: address_widths.map(|eax| ((eax >> 8) & 0xff) as u8),
        active_linear_address_bits: if cr4 & (1 << 12) != 0 { 57 } else { 48 },
        pcid_enabled: cr4 & (1 << 17) != 0,
    }
}

/// Read the current raw CR3 value without changing page-table state.
pub fn read_cr3_raw() -> u64 {
    let cr3: u64;
    // SAFETY: Rustix runs at CPL 0; reading CR3 is privileged but non-mutating.
    unsafe { asm!("mov {}, cr3", out(reg) cr3, options(nomem, nostack, preserves_flags)) };
    cr3
}

/// Read a model-specific register at CPL 0.
///
/// # Safety
/// The caller must ensure the MSR exists on this CPU and that the current
/// privilege level permits the read.
unsafe fn read_msr(index: u32) -> u64 {
    let low: u32;
    let high: u32;
    // SAFETY: The caller guarantees that this MSR is supported and accessible.
    unsafe {
        asm!(
            "rdmsr",
            in("ecx") index,
            out("eax") low,
            out("edx") high,
            options(nomem, nostack)
        );
    }
    (u64::from(high) << 32) | u64::from(low)
}

/// Read CR0 without changing processor state.
fn read_cr0_raw() -> u64 {
    let cr0: u64;
    // SAFETY: Rustix runs at CPL 0; reading CR0 is privileged but non-mutating.
    unsafe { asm!("mov {}, cr0", out(reg) cr0, options(nomem, nostack, preserves_flags)) };
    cr0
}

/// Read CR4 without changing paging state.
fn read_cr4_raw() -> u64 {
    let cr4: u64;
    // SAFETY: Rustix runs at CPL 0; reading CR4 is privileged but non-mutating.
    unsafe { asm!("mov {}, cr4", out(reg) cr4, options(nomem, nostack, preserves_flags)) };
    cr4
}

/// Owned snapshot of bootloader data and CPU state consumed by the kernel.
pub struct BootInfo {
    pub hhdm_revision: u64,
    pub hhdm_offset: u64,
    pub inherited_cr3_raw: u64,
    pub inherited_cr3_root: Result<Cr3Root, Cr3Error>,
    pub executable_address_revision: u64,
    pub kernel_physical_base: u64,
    pub kernel_physical_end: u64,
    pub kernel_virtual_base: u64,
    pub kernel_virtual_end: u64,
    pub kernel_image_segments: KernelImageSegments,
    pub boot_stack_physical_start: u64,
    pub boot_stack_physical_end: u64,
    pub boot_stack_virtual_start: u64,
    pub boot_stack_virtual_end: u64,
    pub memory_map_revision: u64,
    pub memory_map: MemoryMap,
    pub frame_allocator: FrameAllocator,
    pub cpu_info: crate::arch::x86_64::cpu::CpuInfo,
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum BootInfoError {
    MissingHhdmResponse,
    InvalidHhdmResponsePointer,
    InvalidHhdmOffset,
    MissingExecutableAddressResponse,
    InvalidExecutableAddressResponsePointer,
    InvalidKernelImageRange,
    InvalidKernelImageSegments,
    InvalidInitialStackBounds,
    InvalidInitialStackHhdmRange,
    InitialStackNotBootloaderReclaimable,
    MissingMemoryMapResponse,
    InvalidMemoryMapResponsePointer,
    MemoryMapCountDoesNotFit,
    TooManyMemoryRegions,
    EmptyMemoryMap,
    InvalidEntriesPointer,
    EntriesAddressOverflow,
    InvalidEntryPointer { index: usize },
    InvalidPhysicalRange { index: usize },
    InvalidHhdmMappingRange { index: usize },
    InvalidMemoryMap(MemoryMapError),
    FrameAllocator(FrameError),
}

/// Copy and validate the boot data needed by the current kernel.
///
/// Structural checks can reject malformed pointers and ranges, but cannot prove
/// that a loader-provided pointer is mapped and readable. That remains part of
/// the documented Limine handoff trust boundary until the kernel owns its maps.
pub fn capture_boot_information(entry_rsp: u64) -> Result<BootInfo, BootInfoError> {
    let cpu_info = crate::arch::x86_64::cpu::identify();
    let inherited_cr3_raw = crate::arch::x86_64::cpu::read_cr3_raw();
    let inherited_cr3_root = parse_cr3_root(
        inherited_cr3_raw,
        cpu_info.physical_address_bits,
        cpu_info.pcid_enabled,
    );
    let virtual_address_bits = cpu_info.active_linear_address_bits;
    let (boot_stack_virtual_start, boot_stack_virtual_end) =
        limine_x86_64_stack_bounds(entry_rsp, virtual_address_bits)
            .ok_or(BootInfoError::InvalidInitialStackBounds)?;
    let hhdm_request = core::ptr::addr_of_mut!(HHDM_REQUEST);
    // SAFETY: Limine has completed writing the request response before `_start`.
    let hhdm_pointer =
        unsafe { core::ptr::read_volatile(core::ptr::addr_of!((*hhdm_request).response)) };
    if hhdm_pointer.is_null() {
        return Err(BootInfoError::MissingHhdmResponse);
    }
    if !is_valid_pointer(hhdm_pointer, virtual_address_bits) {
        return Err(BootInfoError::InvalidHhdmResponsePointer);
    }
    // SAFETY: The Limine response pointer is trusted to refer to a readable
    // response object; its nullness and alignment are checked above.
    let hhdm = unsafe { hhdm_pointer.read_volatile() };
    if hhdm.offset & 0xfff != 0 || !is_canonical_virtual_address(hhdm.offset, virtual_address_bits)
    {
        return Err(BootInfoError::InvalidHhdmOffset);
    }

    let executable_address_request = core::ptr::addr_of_mut!(EXECUTABLE_ADDRESS_REQUEST);
    // SAFETY: Limine has completed writing the request response before `_start`.
    let executable_address_pointer = unsafe {
        core::ptr::read_volatile(core::ptr::addr_of!((*executable_address_request).response))
    };
    if executable_address_pointer.is_null() {
        return Err(BootInfoError::MissingExecutableAddressResponse);
    }
    if !is_valid_pointer(executable_address_pointer, virtual_address_bits) {
        return Err(BootInfoError::InvalidExecutableAddressResponsePointer);
    }
    // SAFETY: Limine's response pointer is trusted to refer to a readable object;
    // nullness, alignment, and active-width canonicality were checked above.
    let executable_address = unsafe { executable_address_pointer.read_volatile() };
    // `linker.ld` defines these symbols as the boundaries of the loaded image.
    let (linked_virtual_start, linked_virtual_end) = (
        core::ptr::addr_of!(__kernel_start) as u64,
        core::ptr::addr_of!(__kernel_end) as u64,
    );
    let kernel_physical_end = kernel_image_physical_end(
        executable_address.physical_base,
        executable_address.virtual_base,
        linked_virtual_start,
        linked_virtual_end,
        cpu_info.physical_address_bits,
        virtual_address_bits,
    )
    .ok_or(BootInfoError::InvalidKernelImageRange)?;
    let linked_segments = KernelImageVirtualSegments {
        text: (
            core::ptr::addr_of!(__kernel_text_mapping_start) as u64,
            core::ptr::addr_of!(__kernel_text_mapping_end) as u64,
        ),
        rodata: (
            core::ptr::addr_of!(__kernel_rodata_mapping_start) as u64,
            core::ptr::addr_of!(__kernel_rodata_mapping_end) as u64,
        ),
        data: (
            core::ptr::addr_of!(__kernel_data_mapping_start) as u64,
            core::ptr::addr_of!(__kernel_data_mapping_end) as u64,
        ),
    };
    let kernel_image_segments = kernel_image_segments(
        executable_address.physical_base,
        executable_address.virtual_base,
        linked_virtual_start,
        linked_virtual_end,
        linked_segments,
        cpu_info.physical_address_bits,
        virtual_address_bits,
    )
    .ok_or(BootInfoError::InvalidKernelImageSegments)?;

    let memory_map_request = core::ptr::addr_of_mut!(MEMORY_MAP_REQUEST);
    // SAFETY: Limine has completed writing the request response before `_start`.
    let memory_map_pointer =
        unsafe { core::ptr::read_volatile(core::ptr::addr_of!((*memory_map_request).response)) };
    if memory_map_pointer.is_null() {
        return Err(BootInfoError::MissingMemoryMapResponse);
    }
    if !is_valid_pointer(memory_map_pointer, virtual_address_bits) {
        return Err(BootInfoError::InvalidMemoryMapResponsePointer);
    }
    // SAFETY: The Limine response pointer is trusted to refer to a readable
    // response object; its nullness and alignment are checked above.
    let response = unsafe { memory_map_pointer.read_volatile() };
    let entry_count = usize::try_from(response.entry_count)
        .map_err(|_| BootInfoError::MemoryMapCountDoesNotFit)?;
    if entry_count > MAX_MEMORY_REGIONS {
        return Err(BootInfoError::TooManyMemoryRegions);
    }
    if entry_count == 0 {
        return Err(BootInfoError::EmptyMemoryMap);
    }
    if response.entries.is_null() {
        return Err(BootInfoError::InvalidEntriesPointer);
    }
    if !is_valid_pointer(response.entries, virtual_address_bits) {
        return Err(BootInfoError::InvalidEntriesPointer);
    }
    let entry_bytes = entry_count
        .checked_mul(size_of::<*const MemoryMapEntry>())
        .ok_or(BootInfoError::EntriesAddressOverflow)?;
    let entries_start = response.entries as usize;
    let entries_end = entries_start
        .checked_add(entry_bytes)
        .ok_or(BootInfoError::EntriesAddressOverflow)?;
    if !is_canonical_virtual_address(entries_start as u64, virtual_address_bits)
        || !is_canonical_virtual_address((entries_end - 1) as u64, virtual_address_bits)
    {
        return Err(BootInfoError::InvalidEntriesPointer);
    }

    let mut builder = MemoryMapBuilder::new();
    for index in 0..entry_count {
        // SAFETY: Limine promises an array of `entry_count` pointers. The count
        // is capped and pointer alignment/address arithmetic are checked above.
        let entry_pointer = unsafe { response.entries.add(index).read_volatile() };
        if !is_valid_pointer(entry_pointer, virtual_address_bits) {
            return Err(BootInfoError::InvalidEntryPointer { index });
        }
        // SAFETY: Limine promises each non-null entry pointer is readable.
        let entry = unsafe { entry_pointer.read_volatile() };
        builder
            .push(entry.base, entry.length, entry.kind)
            .map_err(BootInfoError::InvalidMemoryMap)?;
    }

    let memory_map = builder.finish().map_err(|error| match error {
        MemoryMapError::EmptyMap => BootInfoError::EmptyMemoryMap,
        other => BootInfoError::InvalidMemoryMap(other),
    })?;
    for (index, region) in memory_map.regions().iter().enumerate() {
        if let Some(physical_bits) = cpu_info.physical_address_bits {
            if !physical_range_fits_address_width(region.start(), region.end(), physical_bits) {
                return Err(BootInfoError::InvalidPhysicalRange { index });
            }
        }
        if region.kind().is_mapped_by_limine_v3_hhdm()
            && !limine_v3_hhdm_range_is_valid(
                hhdm.offset,
                region.start(),
                region.end(),
                cpu_info.physical_address_bits,
                virtual_address_bits,
            )
        {
            return Err(BootInfoError::InvalidHhdmMappingRange { index });
        }
    }
    let boot_stack_physical_start = boot_stack_virtual_start
        .checked_sub(hhdm.offset)
        .ok_or(BootInfoError::InvalidInitialStackHhdmRange)?;
    let boot_stack_physical_end = boot_stack_virtual_end
        .checked_sub(hhdm.offset)
        .ok_or(BootInfoError::InvalidInitialStackHhdmRange)?;
    if !limine_v3_hhdm_range_is_valid(
        hhdm.offset,
        boot_stack_physical_start,
        boot_stack_physical_end,
        cpu_info.physical_address_bits,
        virtual_address_bits,
    ) {
        return Err(BootInfoError::InvalidInitialStackHhdmRange);
    }
    if !memory_map.range_is_within_region_kind(
        boot_stack_physical_start,
        boot_stack_physical_end,
        RegionKind::BootloaderReclaimable,
    ) {
        return Err(BootInfoError::InitialStackNotBootloaderReclaimable);
    }
    let frame_allocator =
        FrameAllocator::from_memory_map(&memory_map).map_err(BootInfoError::FrameAllocator)?;

    Ok(BootInfo {
        hhdm_revision: hhdm.revision,
        hhdm_offset: hhdm.offset,
        inherited_cr3_raw,
        inherited_cr3_root,
        executable_address_revision: executable_address.revision,
        kernel_physical_base: executable_address.physical_base,
        kernel_physical_end,
        kernel_virtual_base: executable_address.virtual_base,
        kernel_virtual_end: linked_virtual_end,
        kernel_image_segments,
        boot_stack_physical_start,
        boot_stack_physical_end,
        boot_stack_virtual_start,
        boot_stack_virtual_end,
        memory_map_revision: response.revision,
        memory_map,
        frame_allocator,
        cpu_info,
    })
}

/// Print a report from the copied snapshot; no loader pointers are used here.
pub fn report_boot_information(boot_info: &BootInfo) {
    crate::kprintln!(
        "HHDM: offset {:#018x}, response revision {}",
        boot_info.hhdm_offset,
        boot_info.hhdm_revision
    );
    crate::kprintln!(
        "inherited CR3: raw {:#018x} (page-table contents not inspected)",
        boot_info.inherited_cr3_raw
    );
    match boot_info.inherited_cr3_root {
        Ok(root) => crate::kprintln!(
            "inherited CR3 root: physical {:#018x}, low bits {:?}",
            root.physical_address(),
            root.low_bits()
        ),
        Err(error) => crate::kprintln!("inherited CR3 root could not be decoded: {:?}", error),
    }
    crate::kprintln!(
        "kernel image: physical [{:#018x}, {:#018x}), virtual [{:#018x}, {:#018x}), response revision {}",
        boot_info.kernel_physical_base,
        boot_info.kernel_physical_end,
        boot_info.kernel_virtual_base,
        boot_info.kernel_virtual_end,
        boot_info.executable_address_revision
    );
    let segments = &boot_info.kernel_image_segments;
    crate::kprintln!(
        "kernel mapping text RX: physical [{:#018x}, {:#018x}), virtual [{:#018x}, {:#018x})",
        segments.text.physical_start,
        segments.text.physical_end,
        segments.text.virtual_start,
        segments.text.virtual_end
    );
    crate::kprintln!(
        "kernel mapping rodata R/NX: physical [{:#018x}, {:#018x}), virtual [{:#018x}, {:#018x})",
        segments.rodata.physical_start,
        segments.rodata.physical_end,
        segments.rodata.virtual_start,
        segments.rodata.virtual_end
    );
    crate::kprintln!(
        "kernel mapping data RW/NX: physical [{:#018x}, {:#018x}), virtual [{:#018x}, {:#018x})",
        segments.data.physical_start,
        segments.data.physical_end,
        segments.data.virtual_start,
        segments.data.virtual_end
    );
    crate::kprintln!(
        "boot stack (minimum protocol span): physical [{:#018x}, {:#018x}), virtual [{:#018x}, {:#018x})",
        boot_info.boot_stack_physical_start,
        boot_info.boot_stack_physical_end,
        boot_info.boot_stack_virtual_start,
        boot_info.boot_stack_virtual_end
    );
    crate::kprintln!(
        "memory map: {} validated regions, {} MiB usable RAM, response revision {}",
        boot_info.memory_map.regions().len(),
        boot_info.memory_map.usable_bytes() / (1024 * 1024),
        boot_info.memory_map_revision
    );
    crate::kprintln!(
        "physical frames: {} managed, {} free (4 KiB each)",
        boot_info.frame_allocator.managed_frames(),
        boot_info.frame_allocator.free_frames()
    );
    for region in boot_info.memory_map.regions() {
        crate::kprintln!(
            "  [{:#018x}, {:#018x}) {:?}",
            region.start(),
            region.end(),
            region.kind()
        );
    }
    crate::kprintln!("console: COM1 serial (polling)");

    let cpu = &boot_info.cpu_info;
    let vendor = core::str::from_utf8(&cpu.vendor).unwrap_or("unknown");
    let mtrr_supported = !matches!(&cpu.mtrr, MtrrState::Unsupported);
    crate::kprintln!(
        "CPU: {} (basic leaf {}, extended leaf {:#x})",
        vendor,
        cpu.max_basic_leaf,
        cpu.max_extended_leaf
    );
    crate::kprintln!(
        "CPU feature support: SSE2={}, NX={}, NXE-enabled={}, normal-caching={}, PAT={}, MTRR={}, 1GiB-pages={}, long-mode={}, LA57-supported={}, PCID-enabled={}",
        cpu.has_sse2,
        cpu.has_nx,
        cpu.nx_enabled,
        cpu.normal_caching,
        cpu.has_pat,
        mtrr_supported,
        cpu.has_1g_pages,
        cpu.has_long_mode,
        cpu.has_la57,
        cpu.pcid_enabled
    );
    match cpu.pat_msr_value {
        Some(value) => match PatLayout::from_msr_value(value) {
            Ok(layout) => crate::kprintln!(
                "PAT: IA32_PAT={:#018x}, WB index={:?}, UC index={:?}, WC index={:?}",
                value,
                layout.index_for(CachePolicy::WriteBack),
                layout.index_for(CachePolicy::Uncacheable),
                layout.index_for(CachePolicy::WriteCombining)
            ),
            Err(error) => crate::kprintln!(
                "PAT: IA32_PAT={:#018x} has unsupported layout: {:?}",
                value,
                error
            ),
        },
        None => crate::kprintln!("PAT: unsupported"),
    }
    match &cpu.mtrr {
        MtrrState::Unsupported => {
            crate::kprintln!("MTRR: unsupported")
        }
        MtrrState::VariableRangeCapacityExceeded { reported_count } => {
            crate::kprintln!(
                "MTRR: {} variable pairs exceed the snapshot capacity {}; no partial state retained",
                reported_count,
                MAX_CAPTURED_VARIABLE_MTRRS
            )
        }
        MtrrState::Captured(registers) => {
            crate::kprintln!(
                "MTRR snapshot: MTRRCAP={:#018x}, DEF_TYPE={:#018x}, enabled={}, fixed-enabled={}, fixed-supported={}, WC-supported={}, variable-pairs={}",
                registers.capability,
                registers.default_type,
                registers.default_type & (1 << 11) != 0,
                registers.default_type & (1 << 10) != 0,
                registers.capability & (1 << 8) != 0,
                registers.capability & (1 << 10) != 0,
                registers.variable_register_count
            )
        }
    }
    match (&cpu.mtrr, cpu.pat_msr_value, cpu.physical_address_bits) {
        (MtrrState::Captured(registers), Some(pat_value), Some(address_bits)) => {
            match (
                registers.validated_layout(address_bits),
                PatLayout::from_msr_value(pat_value),
            ) {
                (Ok(mtrr), Ok(pat)) => crate::kprintln!(
                    "MTRR/PAT: validated; effective type at PA 0x0 using PAT[0]={:?}",
                    mtrr.effective_memory_type_for(0, pat, 0, cpu.normal_caching)
                ),
                (Err(error), _) => {
                    crate::kprintln!("MTRR/PAT: rejected captured MTRR state: {:?}", error)
                }
                (_, Err(error)) => {
                    crate::kprintln!("MTRR/PAT: rejected captured PAT state: {:?}", error)
                }
            }
        }
        _ => crate::kprintln!("MTRR/PAT: effective type unavailable (missing state or address width)"),
    }
    crate::kprintln!(
        "CPU address widths (bits): physical={:?}, max-linear={:?}, active-linear={} (LA57 active={})",
        cpu.physical_address_bits,
        cpu.max_linear_address_bits,
        cpu.active_linear_address_bits,
        cpu.active_linear_address_bits == 57
    );
}

fn is_valid_pointer<T>(pointer: *const T, virtual_address_bits: u8) -> bool {
    let start = pointer as usize;
    let Some(end) = start.checked_add(size_of::<T>()) else {
        return false;
    };
    !pointer.is_null()
        && start & (align_of::<T>() - 1) == 0
        && is_canonical_virtual_address(start as u64, virtual_address_bits)
        && is_canonical_virtual_address((end - 1) as u64, virtual_address_bits)
}

```

```
- `src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs` executes CPUID for boot-time feature reporting and performs gated, read-only `RDMSR` reads of EFER.NXE, `IA32_PAT`, and supported MTRR registers. ```

    /// Resolve the Intel SDM PAT/MTRR table for one address and PAT index.
    /// `normal_caching` must reflect CR0.CD=0 and CR0.NW=0.
    pub fn effective_memory_type_for(
        &self,
        address: u64,
        pat: PatLayout,
        pat_index: u8,
        normal_caching: bool,
    ) -> Result<EffectiveMemoryType, EffectiveMemoryTypeError> {
        if !normal_caching {
            return Err(EffectiveMemoryTypeError::NonNormalCachingMode);
        }
        let mtrr_type = self
            .memory_type_for(address)
            .map_err(EffectiveMemoryTypeError::Mtrr)?;
        let pat_type = pat.memory_type_at(pat_index)?;
        Ok(combine_mtrr_pat_types(mtrr_type, pat_type))
    }
```

```rustix/docs/architecture/boot.md
     1	# Boot protocol and kernel entry
     2	
     3	## Current boot contract
     4	
     5	Rustix currently expects a Limine-compatible x86_64 handoff. Limine is an external loader; it does not implement Rustix's kernel services. The kernel requests protocol base revision 3, the higher-half direct-map (HHDM) offset, the executable physical/virtual base addresses, and the memory map.
     6	
     7	Requests are kept in `.limine_requests_start`, `.limine_requests`, and `.limine_requests_end` by `linker.ld`. The response-bearing request records are mutable and the output `.limine_requests` section is placed in a writable load segment because Limine fills their response pointers before entering Rustix. The ELF entry symbol is `_start`.
     8	
     9	### Entry sequence
    10	
    11	1. Limine loads the ELF and transfers control to the assembly `_start` shim under the x86_64 Limine protocol. The shim captures the entry `RSP`, aligns the stack for a SysV call, and invokes `rustix_start`.
    12	2. `rustix_start` configures the legacy COM1 UART for polling output and input.
    13	3. The kernel disables maskable interrupts and installs its bootstrap GDT, TSS, and fatal-exception IDT. This does not initialize IRQ delivery.
    14	4. The kernel reads CPU address widths, active `CR4.PCIDE`, and raw CR3. It decodes CR3's physical root address and low-bit meaning against those CPU properties, without dereferencing the root. It reads EFER.NXE only when CPUID reports NX, `IA32_PAT` only when CPUID reports PAT, and MTRR registers only when CPUID reports MTRR support; these MSR reads do not change CPU state. The MTRR snapshot is bounded to 32 variable pairs and reports an explicit capacity-exceeded state without retaining partial registers. It copies the HHDM, executable-address, and memory-map responses into an owned `BootInfo` snapshot, validates pointers against the active linear width, derives and validates the linker-defined kernel image span and its page-aligned text/rodata/data segment spans from Limine's executable bases, and derives the protocol-guaranteed minimum initial-stack span from the captured entry `RSP`. It validates physical bounds, stack HHDM arithmetic/coverage, and page-rounded HHDM arithmetic for protocol-mapped memory types. It then builds a frame allocator only from validated usable ranges and rejects malformed metadata before starting the shell.
    15	5. The kernel reports raw CR3 and its decoded physical root/low bits when the reported width permits, physical and virtual kernel-image spans, linker-defined text RX, rodata R/NX, and data RW/NX segment spans, minimum protocol-guaranteed stack span, validated memory ranges, frame counts, CPU features/address widths, NXE state, the active PAT value plus recognized WB/UC/WC indices, and a summary of captured MTRR state, then seeds a volatile RAM filesystem and enters Crabshell on the serial console.
    16	6. The shell busy-polls COM1 because no scheduler or UART interrupt handler exists yet. The kernel does not return to the loader.
    17	
    18	The linker exports page-aligned virtual bounds for each of the kernel's three load segments. Boot validates their order, contiguity, coverage of the rounded image span, and derived physical ranges, then reports them with the permissions intended by `linker.ld`. Boot also decodes CR3's root physical address and active low-bit interpretation. These are validated linker/boot metadata only: Rustix does not inspect the inherited page tables, so it has not established that the segments are mapped or that their live permissions match the ELF flags.
    19	
    20	The memory-map snapshot stores physical regions as checked half-open ranges `[start, end)` and retains Limine's known classifications plus unknown type values. It does not authorize Rustix to access every region, reclaim loader memory, or mutate the current page tables. Rustix checks physical bounds and calculates canonical HHDM ranges for memory types covered by the requested base revision, but does not dereference physical memory through the HHDM or verify the inherited page tables. These metadata checks cannot prove that a Limine-provided non-null pointer is readable; that remains an explicit handoff trust boundary.
    21	
    22	## Link and target configuration
    23	
    24	- Rust target: `x86_64-unknown-none`
    25	- Linker script: `linker.ld`
    26	- Kernel virtual base: `0xffffffff80000000`
    27	- Required code-generation constraints: kernel code model, static relocation, and disabled red zone
    28	- Rust panic strategy: abort; the panic handler logs and halts
    29	
    30	See [`../development/building.md`](../development/building.md) for commands and toolchain setup.
    31	
    32	## Failure behavior and limitations
    33	
    34	Missing responses, bad pointers/alignment, invalid HHDM values, invalid image or segment bounds, invalid initial-stack spans, excessive counts, null entries, address arithmetic overflow, and invalid or overlapping physical ranges reject the complete boot snapshot. `_start` halts before starting Crabshell rather than continuing with partial memory metadata. Structural checks cannot establish that a non-null loader pointer is mapped and readable; that remains an explicit trust assumption of the Limine handoff. The installed exception handlers print fatal context and halt; no fault recovery or maskable IRQ delivery is provided. COM1 writes use a bounded polling loop so a non-responsive UART does not block forever.
    35	
    36	The repository includes a Limine v12.9.3 binary archive pin with SHA-256 verification, a hybrid ISO recipe, and a bounded QEMU serial smoke test that checks Crabshell's prompt. On 2026-10-16, `just verify` passed in WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 on both the working tree and a clean detached worktree with an empty `target` directory; the clean run fetched and built the pinned Limine host utility, created the image, and QEMU reported boot metadata before reaching the prompt. Milestone 0's local exit criteria are met. Hosted CI has not been observed. There is still no framebuffer console, reboot/shutdown interface, or broader boot-protocol compatibility test. The available serial and keyboard drivers do not imply a general device model.
    37	
    38	## Future boot work
    39	
    40	The kernel now snapshots and validates the Limine map and preserves firmware and loader-reclaimable classifications without reclaiming them. No region is considered Rustix-owned or free for allocation yet. Loader-reclaimable memory must remain unavailable until Rustix has copied any needed boot data and explicitly reaches a documented reclaim point; ACPI reclaimable memory needs the ACPI tables to be copied or parsed first. Frame allocation, page-table replacement, and ownership transfer remain future work.

```

````rustix/docs/architecture/overview.md
     1	# Architecture overview
     2	
     3	## Goals
     4	
     5	Rustix is a from-scratch operating system project with its own kernel, written in Rust. The intended initial platform is 64-bit x86 (`x86_64`), with a Unix-like process and file-descriptor model. The kernel should eventually own machine initialization, physical and virtual memory management, interrupt handling, scheduling, system calls, and device policy. A bootloader is a transport into the kernel, not a replacement for those facilities.
     6	
     7	Unix-like is a compatibility direction. It does **not** mean the current kernel is POSIX-compliant, nor does it commit the project to a particular existing kernel's internals. Compatibility profiles and a userland should be defined only after the underlying process, descriptor, and syscall semantics are implemented and tested.
     8	
     9	## Current implementation
    10	
    11	1. Cargo builds a `no_std`, `no_main` ELF for `x86_64-unknown-none` and uses Limine for the boot handoff.
    12	2. `_start` initializes COM1 and exception diagnostics, captures a validated boot snapshot and frame-allocator state, reports memory/CPU information, initializes a fixed-capacity RAM filesystem, and enters Crabshell.
    13	3. Crabshell reads an ASCII command line from the serial UART and supports basic navigation, directory creation/listing, and text-file operations.
    14	4. The separately packaged `crabshell` `no_std` crate parses commands without allocation or dependence on kernel I/O, making that layer reusable by a future graphical frontend.
    15	5. The kernel library contains checked memory accounting and the bounded VFS implementation, both covered by host-side unit tests.
    16	
    17	The current shell and filesystem run in kernel mode. Files exist only in RAM and disappear at reboot. Bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT setup and fatal exception handlers for vectors 0–31 exist, but maskable IRQs remain disabled and exception recovery is not implemented. There is no heap, Rustix-owned page-table manager, general IRQ subsystem, scheduler, user/kernel isolation, syscall ABI, on-disk filesystem, network stack, or userspace process.
    18	
    19	## Intended layers (planned)
    20	
    21	```text
    22	User programs and system utilities
    23	        | versioned syscall ABI
    24	Kernel services: processes, descriptors, VFS, IPC, signals
    25	        | explicit ownership and authorization checks
    26	Core kernel: scheduler, virtual memory, physical frames, interrupts
    27	        | narrow architecture abstractions
    28	x86_64 platform: paging, exceptions, timers, AP startup, drivers
    29	        | Limine boot handoff only
    30	Firmware and hardware
    31	```
    32	
    33	The diagram is a target decomposition, not a claim that those layers are implemented. Architecture-independent policy should live in safe Rust where possible; privileged instructions and raw device access should stay in small, reviewed architecture modules.
    34	
    35	## Design constraints
    36	
    37	- **Freestanding:** kernel code does not link `std`; allocation must be introduced deliberately after a physical-frame and heap strategy exists.

# Memory-management direction

## What exists now

`src/memory.rs` contains an allocation-free `MemoryMapBuilder` that copies Limine ranges into validated half-open physical regions. It rejects empty ranges, `base + length` overflow, overlapping ranges, empty maps, and maps exceeding the fixed 256-region capacity. Known Limine types remain distinct, and unknown type values are preserved. Host-side tests cover range validation/classification, canonical-address boundaries, physical-width bounds, and HHDM range arithmetic. `src/boot.rs` stores the resulting map in an owned boot snapshot and reports usable bytes.

`src/frame.rs` provides a fixed-capacity allocator core with host-side tests. It only manages complete 4 KiB frames inside validated `Usable` regions, reserves the first MiB, and coalesces adjacent free ranges. The ownership contract assumes one allocator instance per physical map: within that instance, each eligible frame is owned either by its free-range table or by a non-copyable `Frame` token while allocated. The public constructor does not enforce unique instances, so callers must not initialize multiple allocators for the same physical map; the current boot path retains one allocator in `BootInfo`. `allocate` returns `None` when no free frame remains. `deallocate` consumes the token only on success; on any error, including free-range-table exhaustion, it returns a `DeallocationError` containing the original token and leaves allocator state unchanged. The range tables each have a fixed `MAX_FRAME_RANGES` capacity, so fragmentation can prevent a frame from being returned until nearby ranges coalesce. No kernel service currently allocates frames for mappings or other work.

`Frame::address()` is a physical address value, not a dereferenceable pointer and not a proof that the frame is mapped. CPU diagnostics now read `CR4.LA57` to report the active linear-address width (48 or 57 bits) and query `CPUID.80000008H` for physical and maximum linear-address widths when available. Boot-protocol pointers are checked against the active width, with host tests for 48- and 57-bit canonical boundaries. These facts do not prove that any physical address is mapped.

`src/paging.rs` adds pure, host-tested 4 KiB mapping groundwork and decodes the inherited CR3 root address plus its low-bit interpretation. The CR3 decoder validates the physical-address width and reserved bits and interprets the low 12 bits according to the active `CR4.PCIDE` state; it does not dereference the root. The mapping-range validator requires a known physical-address width, checked aligned bounds, canonical virtual endpoints in one canonical half, and rejects writable-executable permissions. A validated range can encode the raw bits of one 4 KiB leaf PTE, including supervisor/user and write permissions, NX when the caller confirms EFER.NXE, and a bounded three-bit PAT index. `PatLayout` parses a supplied `IA32_PAT` value and selects WB, UC, or WC indices. `MtrrMemoryType`, `VariableMtrr`, `FixedMtrrRanges`, and `MtrrLayout` resolve MTRR types at one physical address, including fixed-range priority and defined variable-overlap rules; undefined overlaps fail closed. `MtrrRegisters::validated_layout` additionally validates captured capability/default-type reserved bits, register counts and fixed-range presence, WC support, variable-mask shape, and base alignment before producing an owned `ValidatedMtrrLayout`. That layout combines the address-specific MTRR type with a selected PAT entry according to Intel SDM Table 11-7, but only when `CR0.CD` and `CR0.NW` are clear. Host tests cover all 30 documented MTRR/PAT type pairs and reject invalid indexes, malformed snapshots, out-of-range addresses, and non-normal caching mode. The boot path reads CR0 without modifying it, validates supported captured MTRR/PAT state, and reports a diagnostic resolution at physical address zero using PAT index 0; this does not inspect the inherited PTE or assert that the live mapping uses that index. The raw MTRR capture remains bounded to 32 variable pairs and reports capacity overflow without partial state. These helpers do not prove frame ownership or HHDM coverage, inspect table entries, or modify hardware page tables. No page mapping operation or CR3 transition is implemented.

The requested Limine base revision is 3. Its protocol maps only `Usable`, `BootloaderReclaimable`, `ExecutableAndModules`, and `Framebuffer` memory-map regions into the HHDM; reserved, ACPI, bad, and unknown regions are not in that mapping set. HHDM mappings use at least 4 KiB granularity and may cover page-aligned bytes beyond unaligned region boundaries. On x86_64, inherited HHDM mappings are supervisor RWX, normally write-back cached, with framebuffer mappings write-combining when PAT is available. Therefore an HHDM offset is not a blanket physical-memory access grant, and inherited HHDM permissions are not Rustix's future W^X policy. See the [Limine base revision 3 protocol](https://github.com/limine-bootloader/limine-protocol/blob/trunk/PROTOCOL.md#base-revision-3) and its memory-layout/caching sections.

The boot snapshot now rejects physical map ranges beyond the reported CPUID physical-address width when that CPUID leaf is available. For base revision 3 HHDM-mapped types, it also validates the page-rounded physical span, checked `offset + address` arithmetic, and canonical endpoints in the active linear-address width. If the CPU does not report a physical width, the physical-bound check is skipped and no mapping caller may treat the bound as known. These checks are derived from metadata and Limine's protocol contract; they do not inspect page tables or prove that a non-null loader pointer is readable. Rustix still does not dereference physical memory through the HHDM. Rustix-owned mappings should be non-executable by default; executable kernel text must be explicit. MMIO requires an explicit device range and cache policy, and guard regions must remain unmapped. A page-table transition must preserve the kernel image, active stacks, boot data, descriptor tables, and any loader mappings still needed. Rustix does not reclaim bootloader memory, own or replace the inherited Limine page tables, or provide a heap. Bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT setup and fatal exception diagnostics live in `src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs`; they do not enable maskable IRQs.

## Mapping inventory before a CR3 transition

The current runtime has several mappings that a future page-table transition must preserve. The address sources and remaining gaps are:

- **Kernel ELF image:** `linker.ld` places `.text`, `.rodata`, `.limine_requests`, `.data`, `.bss`, and `.got` in three `PT_LOAD` segments: RX text, read-only rodata, and RW data/BSS. It exports `__kernel_start` and `__kernel_end` around the complete loadable image, plus page-aligned bounds for each segment. `BootInfo` checks that Limine's reported virtual base matches the linker start, validates ordered contiguous segment bounds covering the rounded image, derives corresponding half-open physical ranges from the executable physical base with checked arithmetic, and validates canonical virtual and reported physical address widths. The release ELF and QEMU runtime report both showed the three aligned ranges on 2026-10-21. The RX, R/NX, and RW/NX labels describe the linker segment intent; these are linker/boot metadata, not proof that the inherited page tables map every page or enforce those permissions, nor proof that loader pointers are readable. The memory-map `ExecutableAndModules` entries remain illustrative, not an authoritative kernel-image extent.
- **Active stack and `BootInfo`:** The assembly `_start` shim captures Limine's entry `RSP` before any Rust prologue. Under the SysV entry convention the synthetic return slot occupies 8 bytes, so `RSP + 8` is the exclusive stack top. The protocol guarantees at least 64 KiB (without a Stack Size request); `BootInfo` records that minimum virtual span, translates it through the HHDM, and requires it to fit within a single `BootloaderReclaimable` physical region. The full loader allocation may be larger, and neither its exact bounds nor a guard page are known. Preserve the inherited mapping; do not infer a guard page.
- **Kernel static data:** `RAM_FILESYSTEM`, GDT, IDT, TSS, the ring-0 stack, and double-fault IST stack are static BSS/data in the kernel image. Exception entry also requires the handler code and the TSS/IDT references to remain mapped. Preserve the complete relevant data/BSS pages and stack pages.
- **Limine request data:** request records are in the kernel's writable `.limine_requests` segment. Response objects and the memory-map pointer array are bootloader-reclaimable; `capture_boot_information` copies the values used later, and the shell does not retain those pointers. Keep them mapped until the copy and validation finish; any later reclaim must be explicit rather than reclaiming the whole bootloader-reclaimable class.
- **Inherited page tables:** Limine places its page tables in bootloader-reclaimable memory, but their layout is unspecified. `BootInfo` captures raw CR3 and validates a decoded physical root address plus the low-bit interpretation selected by active `CR4.PCIDE`; this numeric decode does not make the root dereferenceable. Rustix does not inspect root entries or inventory the live mappings. Keep the old root and its backing pages intact while inspecting/building a replacement; do not reclaim them until a verified switch no longer depends on them.
- **Devices:** COM1 uses x86 port I/O and needs no MMIO virtual mapping. Rustix does not currently request or use a framebuffer. Any future framebuffer or device-register mapping needs an explicit physical range and cache policy.

## Initial kernel-owned mapping policy (design only)

A first Rustix-owned x86_64 root should use 4 KiB pages only and require NX support; if NX is unavailable, abort before switching. Preserve ELF permissions exactly: text RX, rodata R/NX, and `.limine_requests`/data/BSS/GOT RW/NX. Reject W+X mappings. Exclude the complete physical kernel-image span from the generic HHDM in the first implementation so no writable direct-map alias can undermine text or rodata permissions. Ordinary RAM HHDM mappings should be RW/NX and WB.

Preserve the inherited PAT/MTRR configuration during the first transition. The boot report now validates captured registers and computes a diagnostic effective type from the active PAT/MTRR values under normal caching, but it does not inspect inherited PTEs or establish cache types for a complete mapping range. The pure combination follows Intel SDM Table 11-7; it is not a generic rule for legacy PCD/PWT-only selection or model-specific combinations, and it does not validate cache-type aliases. Under Limine base revision 3 on x86_64, use PAT index 0 for WB, index 3 for UC, and index 5 for WC only after the target physical range and active PAT/MTRR interaction are verified. Map MMIO only from explicit device ranges and use UC by default; do not infer MMIO from generic reserved memory-map entries. A framebuffer may use WC only after its response and cache policy are explicitly validated. COM1 uses port I/O and requires no MMIO mapping.

Do not use huge pages in the first root; add them only when physical coverage, permissions, and cache attributes are uniform across the entire huge-page extent. Future Rustix-owned downward-growing stacks should have at least one 4 KiB unmapped guard page below them. The Limine bootstrap stack has no known guard, so none may be assumed there.

Never modify Limine's active page tables in place. Build a separate candidate root from owned frames, leave the inherited root and its backing memory intact, and do not switch CR3 until every transition-critical mapping has been preserved and checked. Any pre-switch failure must discard the candidate root and return its frames without changing the active root. This policy is not yet implemented; Rustix does not inspect the inherited root or replace CR3.

## Planned memory layers

1. **Validated physical regions:** implemented as a fixed-capacity owned snapshot; allocator ownership and reclaim policy remain future work.
2. **Frame allocator integration:** the bounded core is initialized from `BootInfo`; add real allocation callers only after the page-mapping policy and ownership rules are implemented.
3. **Kernel virtual memory:** Rustix still runs on inherited Limine page tables. Before replacing them, preserve the executing kernel, bootstrap/Ring-0 stacks, request/response data, and exception stacks; define the HHDM extent and explicit mapping permissions/cache attributes. Keep writable-executable mappings disallowed by default and reserve MMIO and guard regions.
4. **Heap:** add a global allocator only after frame allocation and page mapping are initialized. Define allocation failure behavior for kernel and interrupt contexts.
5. **Process address spaces:** isolate userspace; define copy-in/copy-out helpers and never treat user pointers as kernel references.

## Invariants to preserve

- Physical ranges use checked arithmetic and the half-open convention `[start, end)`.
- Only complete frames in validated `Usable` regions enter the allocator; the first MiB remains reserved. Firmware and loader-reclaimable regions are not silently promoted to free memory.
- Under the single-allocator-per-physical-map contract, a frame is represented by one allocator-free range or one caller-owned, non-copyable `Frame` token. Only a successful `deallocate` transfers the token back to the allocator; errors return the token and leave allocator ranges and accounting unchanged. The current public constructor relies on callers to enforce unique allocator instances.
- `allocate` returns `None` on frame exhaustion. Metadata-capacity exhaustion is an explicit error, never silent loss of a frame.
- A `Frame` address is physical, not directly dereferenceable. No HHDM translation, page-table mutation, or CR3 switch is permitted until address widths, mapping coverage, permissions/cache attributes, and transition-preservation requirements are established.
- Mapping changes validate alignment, canonical addresses, ownership, and permissions before touching tables.
- User-controlled addresses are validated on every syscall boundary; prior validation is not a substitute for access checks during later copies.
- Tests cover unaligned edges, exact-boundary allocations, arithmetic overflow, overlaps, exhaustion, and unchanged state/ownership on failure.

These are design requirements for future milestones, not functionality delivered by the current boot summary.

# Boot protocol and kernel entry

## Current boot contract

Rustix currently expects a Limine-compatible x86_64 handoff. Limine is an external loader; it does not implement Rustix's kernel services. The kernel requests protocol base revision 3, the higher-half direct-map (HHDM) offset, the executable physical/virtual base addresses, and the memory map.

Requests are kept in `.limine_requests_start`, `.limine_requests`, and `.limine_requests_end` by `linker.ld`. The response-bearing request records are mutable and the output `.limine_requests` section is placed in a writable load segment because Limine fills their response pointers before entering Rustix. The ELF entry symbol is `_start`.

### Entry sequence

1. Limine loads the ELF and transfers control to the assembly `_start` shim under the x86_64 Limine protocol. The shim captures the entry `RSP`, aligns the stack for a SysV call, and invokes `rustix_start`.
2. `rustix_start` configures the legacy COM1 UART for polling output and input.
3. The kernel disables maskable interrupts and installs its bootstrap GDT, TSS, and fatal-exception IDT. This does not initialize IRQ delivery.
4. The kernel reads CR0 caching-control state, CPU address widths, active `CR4.PCIDE`, and raw CR3. It decodes CR3's physical root address and low-bit meaning against those CPU properties, without dereferencing the root. It reads EFER.NXE only when CPUID reports NX, `IA32_PAT` only when CPUID reports PAT, and MTRR registers only when CPUID reports MTRR support; these reads do not change CPU state. The MTRR snapshot is bounded to 32 variable pairs and reports an explicit capacity-exceeded state without retaining partial registers. It copies the HHDM, executable-address, and memory-map responses into an owned `BootInfo` snapshot, validates pointers against the active linear width, derives and validates the linker-defined kernel image span and its page-aligned text/rodata/data segment spans from Limine's executable bases, and derives the protocol-guaranteed minimum initial-stack span from the captured entry `RSP`. It validates physical bounds, stack HHDM arithmetic/coverage, and page-rounded HHDM arithmetic for protocol-mapped memory types. It then builds a frame allocator only from validated usable ranges and rejects malformed metadata before starting the shell.
5. The kernel reports raw CR3 and its decoded physical root/low bits when the reported width permits, physical and virtual kernel-image spans, linker-defined text RX, rodata R/NX, and data RW/NX segment spans, minimum protocol-guaranteed stack span, validated memory ranges, frame counts, CPU features/address widths, NXE and normal-caching state, the active PAT value plus recognized WB/UC/WC indices, and a summary of captured MTRR state. It also reports whether the captured PAT/MTRR registers validate and a diagnostic effective type at physical address zero for PAT index 0; this is not a page-table inspection or a live mapping claim. It then seeds a volatile RAM filesystem and enters Crabshell on the serial console.
6. The shell busy-polls COM1 because no scheduler or UART interrupt handler exists yet. The kernel does not return to the loader.

The linker exports page-aligned virtual bounds for each of the kernel's three load segments. Boot validates their order, contiguity, coverage of the rounded image span, and derived physical ranges, then reports them with the permissions intended by `linker.ld`. Boot also decodes CR3's root physical address and active low-bit interpretation. These are validated linker/boot metadata only: Rustix does not inspect the inherited page tables, so it has not established that the segments are mapped or that their live permissions match the ELF flags.

The memory-map snapshot stores physical regions as checked half-open ranges `[start, end)` and retains Limine's known classifications plus unknown type values. It does not authorize Rustix to access every region, reclaim loader memory, or mutate the current page tables. Rustix checks physical bounds and calculates canonical HHDM ranges for memory types covered by the requested base revision, but does not dereference physical memory through the HHDM or verify the inherited page tables. These metadata checks cannot prove that a Limine-provided non-null pointer is readable; that remains an explicit handoff trust boundary.

## Link and target configuration

- Rust target: `x86_64-unknown-none`
- Linker script: `linker.ld`
- Kernel virtual base: `0xffffffff80000000`
- Required code-generation constraints: kernel code model, static relocation, and disabled red zone
- Rust panic strategy: abort; the panic handler logs and halts

See [`../development/building.md`](../development/building.md) for commands and toolchain setup.

## Failure behavior and limitations

Missing responses, bad pointers/alignment, invalid HHDM values, invalid image or segment bounds, invalid initial-stack spans, excessive counts, null entries, address arithmetic overflow, and invalid or overlapping physical ranges reject the complete boot snapshot. `_start` halts before starting Crabshell rather than continuing with partial memory metadata. Structural checks cannot establish that a non-null loader pointer is mapped and readable; that remains an explicit trust assumption of the Limine handoff. The installed exception handlers print fatal context and halt; no fault recovery or maskable IRQ delivery is provided. COM1 writes use a bounded polling loop so a non-responsive UART does not block forever.

The repository includes a Limine v12.9.3 binary archive pin with SHA-256 verification, a hybrid ISO recipe, and a bounded QEMU serial smoke test that checks Crabshell's prompt. On 2026-10-16, `just verify` passed in WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 on both the working tree and a clean detached worktree with an empty `target` directory; the clean run fetched and built the pinned Limine host utility, created the image, and QEMU reported boot metadata before reaching the prompt. Milestone 0's local exit criteria are met. Hosted CI has not been observed. There is still no framebuffer console, reboot/shutdown interface, or broader boot-protocol compatibility test. The available serial and keyboard drivers do not imply a general device model.

## Future boot work

The kernel now snapshots and validates the Limine map and preserves firmware and loader-reclaimable classifications without reclaiming them. No region is considered Rustix-owned or free for allocation yet. Loader-reclaimable memory must remain unavailable until Rustix has copied any needed boot data and explicitly reaches a documented reclaim point; ACPI reclaimable memory needs the ACPI tables to be copied or parsed first. Frame allocation, page-table replacement, and ownership transfer remain future work.

```

# Security and unsafe-code policy

Rustix is an early kernel prototype, not a security-reviewed operating system. It has no user/kernel separation implementation, process isolation, security boundary, or supported deployment profile today.

## Current unsafe boundaries

- `src/arch/x86_64/io.rs` issues privileged x86 port-I/O instructions behind narrow driver wrappers.
- `src/arch/x86_64/serial.rs` configures and writes to the legacy COM1 UART. It is intended for early kernel context only.
- `src/arch/x86_64/keyboard.rs` reads raw bytes from a legacy PS/2-compatible controller; callers must poll without blocking.
- `src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs` executes CPUID for boot-time feature reporting, reads CR0/CR4/CR3 without modifying them, and performs gated, read-only `RDMSR` reads of EFER.NXE, `IA32_PAT`, and supported MTRR registers. EFER and PAT reads are gated by their CPUID features; MTRR reads are skipped unless CPUID reports MTRR support and are bounded to the reported variable-register count, up to 32 pairs. These paths assume CPL 0 and architectural feature/MSR availability, and they do not write control registers or MSRs.
- `src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs` loads the GDT/TSS/IDT and exception-entry assembly, reads CR2 on page faults, and halts after printing the saved context. The exception gates are kernel-only and maskable interrupts remain disabled.
- `src/boot.rs` reads Limine response pointers and entries, then validates and copies range metadata into an owned boot snapshot. Nullness, alignment, count bounds, arithmetic, and range overlap are checked; the kernel still trusts Limine to make non-null response objects readable for the handoff lifetime.
- `src/main.rs` uses `cli` and `hlt` to stop the bootstrap CPU after a fatal startup error.
- `src/vfs.rs` and `src/shell.rs` provide a kernel-mode RAM filesystem and shell. They have no user/kernel isolation, permissions, persistence, or protection from kernel bugs; shell commands are trusted kernel code, not sandboxed applications.

Unsafe blocks should remain as small as practical and state the assumptions that make each operation valid. Avoid widening `unsafe impl` or introducing raw-pointer-based public APIs without a documented safety argument. The PS/2 routine consumes bytes from the controller, including discarding auxiliary/error bytes, so it must only be used by a single owner of that controller until input serialization is designed. External boot inputs, user pointers, MMIO, and DMA must not be treated as trusted merely because current boot data is trusted.

## Security requirements for future subsystems

- Validate every physical range and checked address calculation before mapping or allocating it.
- Enforce least privilege in page mappings; avoid writable-executable pages by default.
- Keep user memory untrusted and use explicit copy-in/copy-out routines at syscall boundaries.
- Define ownership and lifetime rules for descriptors, processes, shared memory, and device buffers.
- Test malformed input and error paths as well as successful operation.
- Do not claim isolation or security guarantees until those properties have end-to-end tests and review.

```

# Testing and verification

## Current checks

`just verify` runs the standard development verification sequence:

1. `just fmt` — fail on formatting differences across the workspace.
2. `just test` — run host-side memory-map, mapping-range/PTE-bit policy, frame-allocator, RAM-filesystem, and Crabshell parser tests.
3. `just check` — check the `x86_64-unknown-none` kernel target.
4. `just smoke` — build the pinned hybrid ISO, boot it in QEMU, and check that Crabshell reaches its prompt within a deadline.

`just fault-smoke` separately builds opt-in kernel variants that deliberately trigger a page fault and an invalid opcode. It requires each QEMU run to report the expected exception (and CR2 for the page fault), avoid the shell prompt, and remain halted until timeout. It then rebuilds and restores the default release kernel and ISO. These are fatal-path diagnostics, not exception recovery tests; both Cargo features are disabled by default and cannot be enabled together.

Keep the Crabshell parser, VFS, memory-map validator, paging policy helpers, and frame allocator independent of hardware so syntax, path handling, address and leaf-PTE bit policy, PAT/MTRR policy, storage semantics, and frame ownership can be tested without booting. Pure tests validate captured MTRR register snapshots, resolve the Intel SDM Table 11-7 PAT/MTRR combinations for one physical address, and reject malformed state, invalid indexes, out-of-range addresses, and non-normal caching mode. These helpers do not access tables, read the active PAT MSR, prove frame ownership, or validate live mapping/cache aliases. Boot separately captures the registers and CR0 caching mode read-only and reports a diagnostic resolution; this is not a page-table or mapping test. The GDT/TSS/IDT and CPU-register paths are privileged kernel code; QEMU boot and fault-injection checks complement, but do not replace, static review and target builds. Add tests for boundaries and failure behavior when introducing new pure kernel helpers. The kernel binary is not a host test target.

## What current checks do not prove

- `cargo check` does not perform a final target link.
- A successful ELF link does not prove the boot protocol is recognized or `_start` is reached.
- Host unit tests do not validate privileged instructions, UART behavior, memory-map pointer validity, page tables, interrupts, or actual hardware. The QEMU boot path exercises the gated EFER/PAT reads and bounded MTRR capture and prints diagnostic summaries, but the prompt smoke assertion does not make those facts a mapping-safety proof.
- The automated QEMU prompt smoke test checks only that the kernel reaches the shell. `just fault-smoke` separately exercises only the controlled page-fault and invalid-opcode fatal paths; it does not test every exception vector, recovery, or physical hardware.
- A separate manual QEMU session exercised directory navigation and file create/write/append/read/copy/move/remove operations, including `cp` replacing an existing destination and rejection of `rmdir` on a nonempty directory. This is not exhaustive shell coverage and does not prove persistence across reboot.
- There is no on-disk filesystem integration test, syscall/userspace test, fuzz target, or physical-hardware test.

## Validation policy

For changes to the kernel entry, linker script, boot requests, architecture code, shell, or VFS, run `just verify`. For memory-management and ABI code, add negative tests for overflow, malformed ranges, permission failures, and invalid user pointers before exposing those paths to userspace.

Record commands actually run and any environment limitation in change summaries; never call an unexecuted build “passing.”

   325	/// Capture a bounded register snapshot using a caller-provided MSR reader.
   326	///
   327	/// This helper performs no hardware access itself. A false support flag returns
   328	/// without invoking the reader; an over-capacity count returns no partial data.
   329	pub fn capture_mtrr_registers(supported: bool, mut read_msr: impl FnMut(u32) -> u64) -> MtrrState {
   330	    if !supported {
   331	        return MtrrState::Unsupported;
   332	    }
   333	
   334	    let capability = read_msr(IA32_MTRRCAP);
   335	    let variable_register_count = (capability & 0xff) as u8;
   336	    if usize::from(variable_register_count) > MAX_CAPTURED_VARIABLE_MTRRS {
   337	        return MtrrState::VariableRangeCapacityExceeded {
   338	            reported_count: variable_register_count,
   339	        };
   340	    }
   341	
   342	    let default_type = read_msr(IA32_MTRR_DEF_TYPE);
   343	    let fixed_registers = if capability & MTRRCAP_FIXED_SUPPORTED != 0 {
   344	        let mut registers = [0; FIXED_MTRR_REGISTER_INDICES.len()];
   345	        for (register, index) in registers.iter_mut().zip(FIXED_MTRR_REGISTER_INDICES) {
   346	            *register = read_msr(index);
   347	        }
   348	        Some(registers)
   349	    } else {
   350	        None
   351	    };
   352	
   353	    let mut variable_registers =
   354	        [MtrrRegisterPair { base: 0, mask: 0 }; MAX_CAPTURED_VARIABLE_MTRRS];
   355	    for (range_index, registers) in variable_registers
   356	        .iter_mut()
   357	        .take(usize::from(variable_register_count))
   358	        .enumerate()
   359	    {
   360	        let base_index = IA32_MTRR_PHYSBASE0 + 2 * range_index as u32;
   361	        registers.base = read_msr(base_index);
   362	        registers.mask = read_msr(base_index + 1);
   363	    }
   364	
   365	    MtrrState::Captured(MtrrRegisters {
   366	        capability,
   367	        default_type,
   368	        fixed_registers,
   369	        variable_register_count,
   370	        variable_registers,
   371	    })
   372	}

//! Pure validation for future x86_64 4 KiB mappings.
//!
//! This module validates address shape and permissions only. It does not prove
//! frame ownership or mapping coverage, access physical memory, or modify tables.

use crate::memory::{is_canonical_virtual_address, physical_range_fits_address_width};

/// Base page size supported by the initial Rustix mapping policy.
pub const PAGE_SIZE: u64 = 4096;

/// The physical root address and interpretation of CR3's low bits.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct Cr3Root {
    physical_address: u64,
    low_bits: Cr3LowBits,
}

impl Cr3Root {
    pub const fn physical_address(self) -> u64 {
        self.physical_address
    }

    pub const fn low_bits(self) -> Cr3LowBits {
        self.low_bits
    }
}

/// CR3's low bits are either a PCID or the paging-structure cache controls.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Cr3LowBits {
    Pcid(u16),
    CacheControls {
        page_level_write_through: bool,
        page_level_cache_disable: bool,
    },
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Cr3Error {
    UnknownPhysicalAddressWidth,
    InvalidPhysicalAddressWidth,
    ReservedBits,
}

/// Decode the currently active CR3 value without dereferencing its root table.
///
/// The caller supplies the reported physical-address width and whether CR4.PCIDE
/// is active, since those determine the valid address and low-bit encodings.
pub fn parse_cr3_root(
    raw: u64,
    physical_address_bits: Option<u8>,
    pcid_enabled: bool,
) -> Result<Cr3Root, Cr3Error> {
    let physical_address_bits =
        physical_address_bits.ok_or(Cr3Error::UnknownPhysicalAddressWidth)?;
    if !(12..=MAX_PTE_PHYSICAL_ADDRESS_BITS).contains(&physical_address_bits) {
        return Err(Cr3Error::InvalidPhysicalAddressWidth);
    }

    let physical_mask = ((1u64 << physical_address_bits) - 1) & !(PAGE_SIZE - 1);
    let low_mask = if pcid_enabled {
        PAGE_SIZE - 1
    } else {
        (1 << 3) | (1 << 4)
    };
    if raw & !(physical_mask | low_mask) != 0 {
        return Err(Cr3Error::ReservedBits);
    }

    let low_bits = if pcid_enabled {
        Cr3LowBits::Pcid((raw & (PAGE_SIZE - 1)) as u16)
    } else {
        Cr3LowBits::CacheControls {
            page_level_write_through: raw & (1 << 3) != 0,
            page_level_cache_disable: raw & (1 << 4) != 0,
        }
    };

    Ok(Cr3Root {
        physical_address: raw & physical_mask,
        low_bits,
    })
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct PagePermissions {
    pub writable: bool,
    pub executable: bool,
    pub user_accessible: bool,
}

/// A mapping range whose arithmetic, address widths, alignment, and W^X policy passed validation.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct ValidatedMappingRange {
    virtual_start: u64,
    virtual_end: u64,
    physical_start: u64,
    physical_end: u64,
    physical_address_bits: u8,
    permissions: PagePermissions,
}

impl ValidatedMappingRange {
    pub const fn virtual_start(self) -> u64 {
        self.virtual_start
    }

    pub const fn virtual_end(self) -> u64 {
        self.virtual_end
    }

    pub const fn physical_start(self) -> u64 {
        self.physical_start
    }

    pub const fn physical_end(self) -> u64 {
        self.physical_end
    }

    pub const fn permissions(self) -> PagePermissions {
        self.permissions
    }

    pub const fn length(self) -> u64 {
        self.virtual_end - self.virtual_start
    }

    /// Encode a single 4 KiB leaf PTE within this validated range.
    ///
    /// `pat_index` is the raw three-bit PAT index; the caller must have verified
    /// that the active PAT MSR gives it the intended cache semantics. `nx_enabled`
    /// must reflect EFER.NXE, not merely CPUID support. This only creates entry
    /// bits—it neither owns the frame nor writes a page table.
    pub fn leaf_4k_entry(
        self,
        page_offset: u64,
        pat_index: u8,
        nx_enabled: bool,
    ) -> Result<PageTableEntry, MappingError> {
        if page_offset & (PAGE_SIZE - 1) != 0 {
            return Err(MappingError::UnalignedPageOffset);
        }
        if page_offset >= self.length() {
            return Err(MappingError::PageOffsetOutOfRange);
        }
        if self.physical_address_bits > MAX_PTE_PHYSICAL_ADDRESS_BITS {
            return Err(MappingError::InvalidPhysicalAddressWidth);
        }
        if pat_index > 7 {
            return Err(MappingError::InvalidPatIndex);
        }
        if !self.permissions.executable && !nx_enabled {
            return Err(MappingError::NxNotEnabled);
        }

        let physical_address = self
            .physical_start
            .checked_add(page_offset)
            .ok_or(MappingError::AddressOverflow)?;
        let mut bits = physical_address | PTE_PRESENT;
        if self.permissions.writable {
            bits |= PTE_WRITABLE;
        }
        if self.permissions.user_accessible {
            bits |= PTE_USER;
        }
        if pat_index & 0b001 != 0 {
            bits |= PTE_WRITE_THROUGH;
        }
        if pat_index & 0b010 != 0 {
            bits |= PTE_CACHE_DISABLE;
        }
        if pat_index & 0b100 != 0 {
            bits |= PTE_PAT_4K;
        }
        if !self.permissions.executable {
            bits |= PTE_NO_EXECUTE;
        }

        Ok(PageTableEntry(bits))
    }
}

/// Maximum x86_64 physical-address width representable by a 4 KiB PTE.
pub const MAX_PTE_PHYSICAL_ADDRESS_BITS: u8 = 52;
const PTE_PRESENT: u64 = 1 << 0;
const PTE_WRITABLE: u64 = 1 << 1;
const PTE_USER: u64 = 1 << 2;
const PTE_WRITE_THROUGH: u64 = 1 << 3;
const PTE_CACHE_DISABLE: u64 = 1 << 4;
const PTE_PAT_4K: u64 = 1 << 7;
const PTE_NO_EXECUTE: u64 = 1 << 63;

/// Raw bits for one x86_64 4 KiB leaf page-table entry.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct PageTableEntry(u64);

impl PageTableEntry {
    pub const fn bits(self) -> u64 {
        self.0
    }
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum CachePolicy {
    WriteBack,
    Uncacheable,
    WriteCombining,
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum PatMemoryType {
    Uncacheable,
    WriteCombining,
    WriteThrough,
    WriteProtected,
    WriteBack,
    UncacheableMinus,
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum EffectiveMemoryType {
    Uncacheable,
    WriteCombining,
    WriteThrough,
    WriteProtected,
    WriteBack,
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum PatLayoutError {
    ReservedBits { index: u8 },
    ReservedMemoryType { index: u8, value: u8 },
}

/// Parsed PAT memory types from an `IA32_PAT` MSR value supplied by the caller.
///
/// Parsing does not read the MSR or establish that this is the active value. The
/// MTRR configuration may also affect the effective cache type for an address.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct PatLayout {
    memory_types: [u8; 8],
}

impl PatLayout {
    pub fn from_msr_value(value: u64) -> Result<Self, PatLayoutError> {
        let mut memory_types = [0; 8];
        for (index, memory_type) in memory_types.iter_mut().enumerate() {
            let entry = ((value >> (index * 8)) & 0xff) as u8;
            if entry & !0x07 != 0 {
                return Err(PatLayoutError::ReservedBits { index: index as u8 });
            }
            if entry == 0b010 || entry == 0b011 {
                return Err(PatLayoutError::ReservedMemoryType {
                    index: index as u8,
                    value: entry,
                });
            }
            *memory_type = entry;
        }
        Ok(Self { memory_types })
    }

    /// Return the first PAT index with the exact requested memory type.
    pub fn index_for(self, policy: CachePolicy) -> Option<u8> {
        let requested_type = match policy {
            CachePolicy::Uncacheable => 0b000,
            CachePolicy::WriteCombining => 0b001,
            CachePolicy::WriteBack => 0b110,
        };
        self.memory_types
            .iter()
            .position(|memory_type| *memory_type == requested_type)
            .map(|index| index as u8)
    }

    fn memory_type_at(self, index: u8) -> Result<PatMemoryType, EffectiveMemoryTypeError> {
        match self.memory_types.get(usize::from(index)).copied() {
            Some(0) => Ok(PatMemoryType::Uncacheable),
            Some(1) => Ok(PatMemoryType::WriteCombining),
            Some(4) => Ok(PatMemoryType::WriteThrough),
            Some(5) => Ok(PatMemoryType::WriteProtected),
            Some(6) => Ok(PatMemoryType::WriteBack),
            Some(7) => Ok(PatMemoryType::UncacheableMinus),
            Some(_) => unreachable!("PAT layouts reject reserved memory types"),
            None => Err(EffectiveMemoryTypeError::PatIndexOutOfRange { index }),
        }
    }
}

const IA32_MTRRCAP: u32 = 0x0000_00fe;
const IA32_MTRR_DEF_TYPE: u32 = 0x0000_02ff;
const IA32_MTRR_PHYSBASE0: u32 = 0x0000_0200;
const MTRRCAP_FIXED_SUPPORTED: u64 = 1 << 8;
const FIXED_MTRR_REGISTER_INDICES: [u32; 11] = [
    0x250, 0x258, 0x259, 0x268, 0x269, 0x26a, 0x26b, 0x26c, 0x26d, 0x26e, 0x26f,
];

/// Maximum variable MTRR pairs retained in the fixed-capacity boot snapshot.
pub const MAX_CAPTURED_VARIABLE_MTRRS: usize = 32;

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct MtrrRegisterPair {
    pub base: u64,
    pub mask: u64,
}

/// Raw MTRR state captured for diagnostics; values still require policy validation.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct MtrrRegisters {
    pub capability: u64,
    pub default_type: u64,
    pub fixed_registers: Option<[u64; 11]>,
    pub variable_register_count: u8,
    pub variable_registers: [MtrrRegisterPair; MAX_CAPTURED_VARIABLE_MTRRS],
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum MtrrState {
    Unsupported,
    VariableRangeCapacityExceeded { reported_count: u8 },
    Captured(MtrrRegisters),
}

/// Capture a bounded register snapshot using a caller-provided MSR reader.
///
/// This helper performs no hardware access itself. A false support flag returns
/// without invoking the reader; an over-capacity count returns no partial data.
pub fn capture_mtrr_registers(supported: bool, mut read_msr: impl FnMut(u32) -> u64) -> MtrrState {
    if !supported {
        return MtrrState::Unsupported;
    }

    let capability = read_msr(IA32_MTRRCAP);
    let variable_register_count = (capability & 0xff) as u8;
    if usize::from(variable_register_count) > MAX_CAPTURED_VARIABLE_MTRRS {
        return MtrrState::VariableRangeCapacityExceeded {
            reported_count: variable_register_count,
        };
    }

    let default_type = read_msr(IA32_MTRR_DEF_TYPE);
    let fixed_registers = if capability & MTRRCAP_FIXED_SUPPORTED != 0 {
        let mut registers = [0; FIXED_MTRR_REGISTER_INDICES.len()];
        for (register, index) in registers.iter_mut().zip(FIXED_MTRR_REGISTER_INDICES) {
            *register = read_msr(index);
        }
        Some(registers)
    } else {
        None
    };

    let mut variable_registers =
        [MtrrRegisterPair { base: 0, mask: 0 }; MAX_CAPTURED_VARIABLE_MTRRS];
    for (range_index, registers) in variable_registers
        .iter_mut()
        .take(usize::from(variable_register_count))
        .enumerate()
    {
        let base_index = IA32_MTRR_PHYSBASE0 + 2 * range_index as u32;
        registers.base = read_msr(base_index);
        registers.mask = read_msr(base_index + 1);
    }

    MtrrState::Captured(MtrrRegisters {
        capability,
        default_type,
        fixed_registers,
        variable_register_count,
        variable_registers,
    })
}

pub const FIXED_MTRR_TYPE_COUNT: usize = 88;
const MAX_MTRR_PHYSICAL_ADDRESS_BITS: u8 = 52;
const MTRR_VALID: u64 = 1 << 11;

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
#[repr(u8)]
pub enum MtrrMemoryType {
    Uncacheable = 0,
    WriteCombining = 1,
    WriteThrough = 4,
    WriteProtected = 5,
    WriteBack = 6,
}

impl MtrrMemoryType {
    pub fn from_raw(value: u8) -> Result<Self, MtrrError> {
        match value {
            0 => Ok(Self::Uncacheable),
            1 => Ok(Self::WriteCombining),
            4 => Ok(Self::WriteThrough),
            5 => Ok(Self::WriteProtected),
            6 => Ok(Self::WriteBack),
            value => Err(MtrrError::ReservedMemoryType { value }),
        }
    }
}
