# Rustix roadmap

This roadmap describes an incremental path from the current bare-metal kernel to a useful Unix-like operating system. It is a dependency plan, not a schedule or a claim of compatibility. Features become current only after the implementation, tests, and exit criteria below agree.

## How to read status

- A checked box means the source/design work exists; it does **not** imply the code compiled, linked, booted, or passed an integration test.
- A milestone is not complete until its stated exit criteria are met and the evidence is recorded.
- Hardware work needs target build and emulator evidence. Host tests cannot validate privileged instructions, bootloader pointers, page tables, device I/O, or exception-entry assembly.
- Future work is intentionally not represented by placeholder APIs or dummy implementations.

## Current status

- **Milestone 0: local exit criteria met from a clean detached worktree; hosted CI pending.** On 2026-10-16, `just verify` passed in WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 from both the working tree and a clean detached worktree with an empty `target` directory. The clean run downloaded and compiled the pinned Limine host utility, formatted and tested the workspace, checked and built the target, created the image, and passed the 20-second QEMU prompt smoke test. Hosted CI has not been observed.
- **Milestone 1: validation criteria met for the current Limine path.** The bounded boot snapshot, memory-range classification, and CPUID reporting were covered by host tests and QEMU reporting; the Limine pointer-readability trust boundary remains explicit.
- **Milestone 2: in progress, not complete.** A bounded frame allocator is retained in `BootInfo`, and bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT fatal exception handlers exist. Controlled page-fault and invalid-opcode diagnostics plus fatal halting passed QEMU fault-injection tests. The kernel still inherits Limine's page tables; there is no owned page-table manager, global heap, or live frame-allocation caller.
- **Milestones 3 and later: planned.** There is no general IRQ system, scheduler, userspace, syscall ABI, persistent filesystem, GUI, or networking stack.

## Dependency path

```text
Reliable boot
    -> validated boot state
    -> owned mappings + frame allocation + heap + fault diagnostics
    -> timer/IRQ model + scheduler
    -> isolated processes + syscall ABI
    -> VFS/storage + userland utilities
    -> graphical terminal and other optional services
```

Some device-driver work can proceed in parallel after the core ownership, locking, and testing rules exist. It must not bypass them with direct, unreviewed hardware access.

---

## Milestone 0 — repeatable Rust kernel boot (local exit criteria met)

### Implementation present

- [x] `no_std` Rust kernel binary for `x86_64-unknown-none` with its own ELF linker layout and `_start`.
- [x] Limine boot requests and documented external-loader boundary.
- [x] COM1 serial output/input, startup reporting, and panic/fatal halt path.
- [x] Narrow x86 port-I/O helpers and raw non-blocking PS/2-compatible scancode polling.
- [x] `just` tasks for formatting, host tests, target checks, ELF/image builds, and QEMU smoke/run workflows.
- [x] Pinned Limine v12.9.3 binary archive with SHA-256 verification, BIOS/UEFI hybrid image recipe, and CI workflow.
- [x] Separate allocation-free Crabshell parser, kernel serial frontend, and bounded volatile RAM filesystem.

### Validation evidence and remaining proof

- [x] Current source passed formatting, host tests, target check, and optimized build through `just verify`.
- [x] The pinned image built and the bounded QEMU smoke test reached the Crabshell prompt in WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 on 2026-10-16.
- [x] A separate interactive QEMU session exercised `help`, `ls`, `meminfo`, directory navigation, and file create/write/append/read/copy/move/remove operations; `cp` replaced an existing destination, `rmdir` refused a nonempty directory, and unsupported `memtest` was rejected as expected.
- [x] Repeat verification from a clean detached worktree with an empty `target` directory and uncached build/tool state; fresh Limine download/host-tool compilation, image creation, and QEMU prompt smoke test all passed on 2026-10-16.
- [ ] Observe the hosted CI workflow; it has not yet been run or verified.

The QEMU serial log showed the startup banner, HHDM offset, validated memory-map summary, frame counts, CPUID report, and initial prompt. The interactive command check is a focused manual test, not exhaustive shell coverage or a persistence test. `cat` returned `hello Rustix from QEMU`, `cp` replaced an existing destination with source data, `rmdir` refused a nonempty directory, and `pwd` returned to `/home/rustix` after cleanup. If a future smoke test fails, preserve `target/rustix-qemu-serial.log` as failure evidence.

**Exit criteria:** met locally. A clean detached worktree with uncached build/tool state built the image, reached `_start`, reported the expected startup state, and reached the Crabshell prompt in the automated QEMU test. Hosted CI remains unobserved, but is tracked separately from the local exit criteria.

- [x] Document that classifying a range does not transfer ownership or authorize access/reclamation.

**Exit criteria:** met for the current Limine path. Host tests and QEMU metadata/reporting were observed in the 2026-10-16 WSL2 `just verify` run, including the clean detached-worktree verification. ## Milestone 3 — IRQs, time, and kernel scheduling

Do not enable interrupts as a side effect of installing exception gates. IRQ delivery needs its own controller, acknowledgement, masking, ownership, and synchronization design.

### Planned work

- [ ] Select and document the initial interrupt controller policy for QEMU and target hardware (for example, legacy PIC compatibility versus local I/O APIC; do not enable both accidentally).
- [ ] Add IRQ vector allocation, controller masking/unmasking, end-of-interrupt acknowledgement, spurious-interrupt handling, and a policy for unexpected IRQs.
- [ ] Add a calibrated/verified timer source and monotonic timekeeping; test interval arithmetic and drift assumptions.
- [ ] Establish interrupt-safe lock primitives and rules for code callable from normal, exception, and IRQ contexts. No allocator or blocking console operation may run in an unsafe interrupt context.
- [ ] Add a minimal kernel-thread context and lifecycle model, stack ownership/guard policy, context-switch tests, and emulator scheduling tests.
- [ ] Add preemption only after lock, stack, timer, and interrupt-return invariants have deterministic tests.
- [ ] Keep application-processor startup/SMP as a separate sub-milestone after per-CPU state, TLB invalidation, and lock semantics exist.

**Exit criteria:** tested IRQ acknowledgement and timer behavior, deterministic thread lifecycle/context-switch tests, and bounded QEMU tests under repeated timer interrupts. No `sti` before the design and tests are ready.

---

## Milestone 4 — isolated processes and syscall ABI

Userspace begins only after page tables, exception handling, scheduling, and controlled memory allocation are trustworthy. The syscall ABI is a product interface and must not emerge accidentally from internal functions.

### Planned work

- [ ] Decide and document the x86_64 user-entry/syscall mechanism, register convention, selector/MSR setup, per-CPU state requirements, and safe return path.
- [ ] Add user/kernel page permissions and process-owned address spaces, including teardown and TLB invalidation rules.
- [ ] Implement copy-in/copy-out helpers that validate lengths, arithmetic, canonical ranges, permissions, and faults; never form a kernel reference directly from a user pointer.
- [ ] Specify version discovery, stable syscall numbers, argument layouts, error encoding, partial-I/O behavior, interruption/restart, and compatibility policy before exposing calls.
- [ ] Add initial process lifecycle and descriptor-table semantics: create/load, exit, wait, close, duplication/inheritance, and process cleanup.
- [ ] Load a deliberately small documented executable format with bounds/segment/permission checks; reject malformed binaries safely.
- [ ] Build adversarial tests for bad pointers, overflow, invalid mappings, process teardown, descriptor misuse, and failed exec.

### First user-visible target

A small controlled `init` process should start from a reproducible image, write through a descriptor, exit with a status, and be waited on by a kernel test harness. Do not claim userspace or process isolation from ring-0 tasks that merely use process-shaped structs.

**Exit criteria:** an isolated init process runs in user mode and uses a versioned, documented syscall subset; invalid user pointers and process teardown are tested without corrupting the kernel.

---

## Milestone 5 — VFS, storage, and device ownership

Keep the current RAM filesystem as a bootstrap/test implementation. Persistence and device drivers require explicit block ownership, error handling, and recovery behavior.

### Planned work

- [ ] Define VFS node, mount, path, metadata, and file-descriptor contracts independently of a particular disk format.
- [ ] Preserve volatile RAMFS as a test backend and add tests for mount/path errors, capacity, partial I/O, and object lifetime.
- [ ] Add a narrowly scoped block-device interface with request validation, timeout/error reporting, and a QEMU-supported initial device driver (such as virtio-blk after PCI discovery is ready).
- [ ] Choose and document the first on-disk filesystem format. Specify partition discovery, byte order, block size, metadata limits, corruption handling, and read-only/recovery behavior before writable support.
- [ ] Add persistent write/read/remount/reboot integration tests; never claim persistence from an in-memory cache alone.
- [ ] Add a driver ownership and DMA policy before any device can write into arbitrary kernel memory.
- [ ] Define file descriptors and basic process I/O semantics before exposing them to applications.

**Exit criteria:** a reproducible image mounts a documented on-disk filesystem, user-visible tools can create/read files across reboot, and corruption/I/O errors fail safely.

---

## Milestone 6 — initial userspace and command-line utilities

Crabshell is currently an in-kernel parser/frontend. The long-term terminal application should reuse its parser model without linking kernel internals or bypassing syscalls.

### Planned work

- [ ] Start a user-mode `init` process and establish executable search, environment, current directory, descriptor inheritance, and process startup rules.
- [ ] Port or adapt Crabshell into a userspace terminal application that uses only the documented syscall/VFS interfaces.
- [ ] Add a small utility set with explicit scope: file listing, text output, create/remove/copy/move, and system information.
- [ ] Add command-line quoting, escaping, history, redirection, and pipelines only with parser tests and process/descriptor/pipe semantics to support them.
- [ ] Add integration tests that launch tools from the filesystem image and exercise them through syscalls; keep unsupported features explicit.

**Exit criteria:** shell and basic tools run as isolated user processes from a reproducible image; no shell command directly calls kernel-private VFS internals.

---

## Milestone 7 — graphical console and GUI (long-term)

A GUI is intentionally downstream of stable memory management, interrupts/input, process isolation, drivers, and userspace. Keep Crabshell's parser independent so a graphical terminal frontend can reuse it.

### Planned work

- [ ] Add validated framebuffer discovery and memory ownership; implement a minimal text/graphics console without compromising serial panic diagnostics.
- [ ] Establish an input subsystem that separates raw device events from key mapping and terminal policy. Plan PS/2 and USB HID support separately; do not treat the current raw scancode poller as a keyboard driver stack.
- [ ] Define a graphics buffer ownership/presentation API, clipping rules, pixel format, and bounds/overflow checks.
- [ ] Implement a minimal compositor/windowing policy only after process isolation and input routing are ready.
- [ ] Run Crabshell as a terminal application in a GUI window using the same parser and userspace services as the serial/TTY path.
- [ ] Preserve serial as a headless recovery/debug console and add repeatable QEMU display/input tests.

**Exit criteria:** a documented GUI session starts from userspace, renders a terminal, accepts tested input, and does not require direct kernel-private VFS access.

---

## Milestone 8 — networking (long-term, after drivers and process isolation)

Networking is not implied by the current device drivers. The initial target should be a tightly scoped virtual-device path with clear ownership and bounded buffers.

### Planned work

- [ ] Complete PCI/device discovery and define DMA buffer ownership, address translation, cache synchronization, and reset/error behavior.
- [ ] Implement one virtual NIC driver with bounded queues and timeouts; test against QEMU user networking.
- [ ] Choose and document a minimal link/network protocol scope before implementation. Keep packet parsing length-checked and fuzzable on the host.
- [ ] Add interface configuration, routing, socket/descriptor ownership, and per-process access policy.
- [ ] Add adversarial packet tests and integration tests for link loss, malformed packets, queue exhaustion, and device reset.
- [ ] Add higher-level transports/services only when the required protocol semantics, entropy source, and security model are designed.

**Exit criteria:** documented user processes can communicate through a tested virtual NIC/network stack, with malformed input and resource exhaustion handled safely. Do not claim internet, TLS, or POSIX sockets merely from a packet driver.

---

## Cross-cutting acceptance gates

Every milestone should include the relevant subset of these gates:

1. **Design:** documented ownership, invariants, resource limits, error semantics, and unsupported cases.
2. **Tests:** host tests for pure policy and malformed/boundary input; integration tests for hardware-facing behavior.
3. **Safety:** review unsafe blocks, pointer provenance/access, integer overflow, privilege boundaries, concurrency, and cleanup/rollback paths.
4. **Build:** format, host tests, target check, and final ELF link as appropriate.
5. **Boot/integration:** QEMU tests for changes to boot, paging, descriptors, interrupts, drivers, processes, or persistence.
6. **Documentation/status:** update architecture and roadmap docs; never check off a criterion without evidence.
7. **Compatibility:** claim Unix/POSIX behavior only for the exact documented subset with conformance-style tests.

## Working rule

Prefer a small end-to-end vertical slice over broad, unbootable scaffolding. A source file, interface, or architecture document is not proof that the corresponding subsystem is operational. When a check cannot run, record the exact environment blocker and leave that acceptance gate pending.

# Testing and verification

## Current checks

`just verify` runs the standard development verification sequence:

1. `just fmt` — fail on formatting differences across the workspace.
2. `just test` — run host-side memory-map, mapping-range/PTE-bit policy, frame-allocator, RAM-filesystem, and Crabshell parser tests.
3. `just check` — check the `x86_64-unknown-none` kernel target.
4. `just smoke` — build the pinned hybrid ISO, boot it in QEMU, and check that Crabshell reaches its prompt within a deadline.

`just fault-smoke` separately builds opt-in kernel variants that deliberately trigger a page fault and an invalid opcode. It requires each QEMU run to report the expected exception (and CR2 for the page fault), avoid the shell prompt, and remain halted until timeout. It then rebuilds and restores the default release kernel and ISO. These are fatal-path diagnostics, not exception recovery tests; both Cargo features are disabled by default and cannot be enabled together.

Keep the Crabshell parser, VFS, memory-map validator, paging policy helpers, and frame allocator independent of hardware so syntax, path handling, address and leaf-PTE bit policy, PAT/MTRR policy, storage semantics, and frame ownership can be tested without booting. Pure tests validate captured MTRR register snapshots, resolve the Intel SDM Table 11-7 PAT/MTRR combinations for one physical address, select a PAT index that remains uniform across MTRR boundaries in an aligned range, and reject malformed state, unsupported discontinuous masks, invalid indexes/ranges, out-of-range addresses, and non-normal caching mode. These helpers do not access tables, read the active PAT MSR, prove frame ownership, or validate live mapping/cache aliases. Boot separately captures the registers and CR0 caching mode read-only and reports a diagnostic resolution; this is not a page-table or mapping test. The GDT/TSS/IDT and CPU-register paths are privileged kernel code; QEMU boot and fault-injection checks complement, but do not replace, static review and target builds. Add tests for boundaries and failure behavior when introducing new pure kernel helpers. The kernel binary is not a host test target.

## What current checks do not prove

- `cargo check` does not perform a final target link.
- A successful ELF link does not prove the boot protocol is recognized or `_start` is reached.
- Host unit tests do not validate privileged instructions, UART behavior, memory-map pointer validity, page tables, interrupts, or actual hardware. The QEMU boot path exercises the gated EFER/PAT reads and bounded MTRR capture and prints diagnostic summaries, but the prompt smoke assertion does not make those facts a mapping-safety proof.
- The automated QEMU prompt smoke test checks only that the kernel reaches the shell. `just fault-smoke` separately exercises only the controlled page-fault and invalid-opcode fatal paths; it does not test every exception vector, recovery, or physical hardware.
- A separate manual QEMU session exercised directory navigation and file create/write/append/read/copy/move/remove operations, including `cp` replacing an existing destination and rejection of `rmdir` on a nonempty directory. This is not exhaustive shell coverage and does not prove persistence across reboot.
- There is no on-disk filesystem integration test, syscall/userspace test, fuzz target, or physical-hardware test.

## Validation policy

For changes to the kernel entry, linker script, boot requests, architecture code, shell, or VFS, run `just verify`. For memory-management and ABI code, add negative tests for overflow, malformed ranges, permission failures, and invalid user pointers before exposing those paths to userspace.

Record commands actually run and any environment limitation in change summaries; never call an unexecuted build “passing.”

Rustix is a 64-bit, Rust-first, Unix-like operating-system project. This index separates current implementation facts from planned interfaces: roadmap items are proposals until the corresponding code and tests exist.

## Current status

The repository contains a bare-metal `no_std` Rust kernel for `x86_64-unknown-none`. After Limine handoff it validates and copies memory-map metadata into an owned snapshot, captures the executable's physical and virtual bases, complete linker-defined image span, and page-aligned text/rodata/data segment bounds, reports baseline CPUID features, active/maximum address widths, read-only CR0 caching state, gated EFER.NXE/IA32_PAT values, and a bounded MTRR snapshot, seeds a volatile RAM filesystem, and runs Crabshell over the COM1 serial console. Boot-protocol pointers are checked for canonicality using the active 4- or 5-level paging width; physical map bounds and protocol-scoped HHDM range arithmetic are also validated. Crabshell's allocation-free parser is a separate crate; the kernel handles command execution. On 2026-10-16, `just verify` passed in WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 both in the working tree and from a clean detached worktree with an empty `target` directory; the clean run downloaded and built the pinned Limine host utility, created the image, and passed the bounded QEMU boot to the shell prompt. The serial log showed memory-map and CPU reporting. Hosted CI has not been observed. A separate interactive QEMU session exercised `help`, `ls`, `meminfo`, directory navigation, and file create/write/append/read/copy/move/remove commands. Milestone 0's local exit criteria are met, and Milestone 1's validation criteria are met for the current Limine path. This is a kernel-mode shell, not a user process. A bounded physical-frame allocator core is initialized from the validated map and reported by `meminfo`; its owned frame token and failed-deallocation semantics are documented and host-tested, but no kernel service allocates or maps frames yet. The Limine base-revision 3 HHDM scope and a conservative initial mapping/alias/cache policy are documented. Pure host-tested helpers validate mapping ranges/PTE bits, parse PAT layouts, validate captured MTRR snapshots, combine PAT/MTRR types under normal caching according to Intel SDM Table 11-7, and select a PAT index only when it yields one effective type across an aligned physical range. Boot validates the captured state and prints a diagnostic effective type at PA 0; neither this report nor the range selector inspects inherited PTEs or cache aliases, and no live mapping consumes a selected index. `BootInfo` records raw CR3 and a validated decode of its root physical address and low-bit interpretation, but Rustix does not use the HHDM to access physical memory, inspect page-table contents, or own/replace the inherited tables. The complete linker-defined kernel-image span and the protocol-guaranteed minimum active boot-stack span are captured; Limine does not provide the exact initial stack allocation or guard status, so Rustix preserves only the known minimum span and does not infer a guard page. There is not yet a heap, a general IRQ subsystem, a scheduler, process isolation, a persistent filesystem, or a Unix compatibility layer. Fatal CPU exceptions have basic GDT/TSS/IDT diagnostics but no recovery. `just fault-smoke` validates a controlled page fault (including CR2) and invalid opcode in QEMU; broader exception coverage and physical-hardware validation remain pending. On 2026-10-21, `just verify` passed after adding CR3 decoding and the pure MTRR resolver, including host tests, target check, release build, ISO creation, and QEMU prompt smoke. On 2026-10-22, `just verify` passed after adding bounded read-only MTRR register capture and after adding validated PAT/MTRR policy resolution, including host tests, target check, release build, ISO creation, and QEMU prompt smoke. The QEMU log confirmed normal caching and a validated PA 0 diagnostic (`PAT[0]` resolved to WB). These checks do not inspect page-table entries or validate live mapping attributes/aliases.

## Documentation conventions

- **Implemented** means present in the repository and checked by current code or tests.
- **Planned** means an architectural direction, not a stable ABI or delivered capability.
- Any future ABI proposal must state versioning, error behavior, memory ownership, and compatibility expectations before it is treated as stable.

# Rustix agent instructions

These instructions apply to every coding agent working in this repository. Read this file before changing code. For the architecture and detailed subsystem contracts, use the linked documents under `docs/`; this file summarizes the rules agents must preserve.

## Project mission

Rustix is an experimental 64-bit, Unix-like operating system with its own Rust kernel. Limine is the external boot protocol/loader only. Do not describe Limine, a host shell, or a userspace project as the Rustix kernel.

The kernel is `no_std` and targets `x86_64-unknown-none`. Rust is the implementation language for kernel and OS components. The repository currently uses a Python standard-library script only to assemble and smoke-test the boot image; it does not replace kernel or OS functionality.

Unix-like behavior is a long-term design goal, not a claim of POSIX compatibility. Make unsupported behavior explicit rather than approximating it silently.

## Current project status — read before planning

The source contains:

- A Limine-based x86_64 kernel entry, linker layout, serial diagnostics, and boot-memory reporting.
- A separate allocation-free `no_std` `crabshell` parser crate and a kernel-mode COM1 shell frontend.
- A volatile, fixed-capacity RAM filesystem used by the shell.
- A validated, fixed-capacity boot memory-map snapshot, CPUID/address-width reporting, read-only CR0 caching-mode reporting, and gated read-only EFER.NXE/IA32_PAT/MTRR reporting.
- A fixed-capacity physical frame allocator retained in `BootInfo`; Crabshell's `meminfo` command reports counts. No kernel service currently allocates frames for mappings or other services.
- Pure 4 KiB mapping-range validation, leaf-PTE bit encoding, PAT layout parsing, and host-tested MTRR/PAT policy in `src/paging.rs`; these helpers check alignment, address widths, canonical virtual ranges, W^X, NXE input, PAT indices, captured-register validity, MTRR overlap rules, and Intel SDM Table 11-7 effective types under normal caching. Discontinuous variable-MTRR masks are explicitly unsupported. A pure selector chooses a PAT index only when its effective type remains uniform across all MTRR boundaries in an aligned physical range. Boot captures CR0 caching mode, EFER.NXE, `IA32_PAT`, and a bounded MTRR snapshot read-only when supported, validates the captured state, and reports a diagnostic PA 0 resolution. No code verifies inherited PTE attributes or cache aliases, uses the selector for live mappings, establishes frame ownership/mapping coverage, or modifies page tables.
- Bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT setup and fatal exception handlers for vectors 0–31. Double faults use an IST stack and page faults report CR2. Opt-in QEMU tests inject a page fault and invalid opcode and verify diagnostics plus fatal halt; maskable IRQs remain disabled and exceptions are not recoverable.

Important incomplete work:

- Milestone 0's local exit criteria were met on 2026-10-16: `just verify` passed from both the working tree and a clean detached worktree in WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04. The detached worktree had an empty `target` directory, so the run exercised fresh Limine download/host-tool compilation, formatting, 19 host tests, target check, optimized build, image creation, and the 20-second QEMU prompt smoke test. Hosted CI has not been observed.
- A separate interactive `just run` session exercised directory navigation and create/write/append/read/copy/move/list/remove operations; `cp` replaced an existing destination, `rmdir` rejected a nonempty directory and succeeded after its child was removed, and unsupported `memtest` was rejected as expected. Boot snapshot tests and QEMU boot-metadata reporting were exercised. Structural checks still cannot prove that a Limine-provided non-null pointer is mapped or readable; that remains a loader trust boundary.
- Milestone 0 is closed for local acceptance; hosted CI remains pending. Milestone 1's validation criteria are met for the current Limine path, subject to the documented pointer-readability trust boundary. Milestone 2 is **in progress**, not complete. The frame allocator specifies token ownership and preserves the token on failed deallocation; unique allocator-instance use is still caller-enforced. CPU address widths, physical map bounds, protocol-scoped HHDM range arithmetic, Limine executable image bases, page-aligned linker-defined kernel segment bounds, and gated read-only EFER.NXE/IA32_PAT/MTRR capture are checked; the QEMU serial report showed the MTRR summary on 2026-10-22. On 2026-10-22, validated MTRR/PAT policy resolution also passed host tests and QEMU boot diagnostics, but those checks do not prove inherited page-table coverage, permissions, cache aliases, or effective attributes of live mappings. The transition-critical mapping inventory is documented. `just fault-smoke` has validated controlled page-fault/CR2 and invalid-opcode diagnostics plus fatal halting in QEMU. Rustix still inherits Limine's page tables; CR3's root address is decoded but table entries and complete live mapping extents are not inspected, and there is no kernel-owned page-table manager, heap, or live frame-allocation caller.
- There is no scheduler, userspace, syscall ABI, persistent filesystem, user/kernel isolation, or general IRQ subsystem.

Never advance status or check off a roadmap item merely because source code or an interface exists. Update `docs/roadmap/README.md` only to reflect implementation and validation actually achieved.

## Source-of-truth documents

Consult the relevant documentation before modifying a subsystem:

- [`docs/index.md`](docs/index.md) — documentation entry point and current status.
- [`docs/roadmap/README.md`](docs/roadmap/README.md) — milestone sequencing and exit criteria.
- [`docs/architecture/overview.md`](docs/architecture/overview.md) — current architecture and intended layers.
- [`docs/architecture/boot.md`](docs/architecture/boot.md) — Limine requests, boot snapshot, and trust boundary.
- [`docs/architecture/memory.md`](docs/architecture/memory.md) — memory ownership, frame allocator, and paging direction.
- [`docs/architecture/crabshell.md`](docs/architecture/crabshell.md) — parser/kernel boundary and shell/VFS contract.
- [`docs/architecture/drivers.md`](docs/architecture/drivers.md) — current driver scope and limitations.
- [`docs/security.md`](docs/security.md) — unsafe boundaries and security policy.
- [`docs/development/building.md`](docs/development/building.md) and [`docs/development/testing.md`](docs/development/testing.md) — supported commands and validation expectations.

When code and documentation disagree, inspect the implementation, resolve the discrepancy deliberately, and update the relevant documentation in the same change.

## Repository map

- `src/main.rs` — freestanding entry, boot snapshot acquisition, panic path, and shell handoff.
- `src/boot.rs` — mutable Limine requests, structural response/range validation, owned `BootInfo`, and boot diagnostics.
- `src/memory.rs` — allocation-free memory-map, address-width, canonical-address, Limine HHDM-range, and linker-defined kernel segment validation.
- `src/frame.rs` — bounded physical-frame allocator core; it only uses validated `Usable` ranges, reserves the first MiB, and has fixed range metadata.
- `src/paging.rs` — pure checked range and 4 KiB leaf-PTE bit construction for future mappings; no table access or physical-memory dereference.
- `src/shell.rs` — serial line editor and kernel-side Crabshell executor.
- `src/vfs.rs` — fixed-capacity volatile RAM filesystem and host-side tests.
- `crates/crabshell/` — separate `no_std` parser crate. It has no terminal, filesystem, or kernel dependencies.
- `src/arch/x86_64/serial.rs` — polling COM1 driver for shell input/output.
- `src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs` — bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT, assembly stubs, and fatal exception diagnostics.
- `src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs` — CPUID identification and selected feature reporting.
- `src/arch/x86_64/keyboard.rs` — raw, non-blocking PS/2-compatible scancode polling; not an input subsystem.
- `src/arch/x86_64/io.rs` — narrow port-I/O wrappers.
- `linker.ld`, `.cargo/config.toml`, `rust-toolchain.toml` — target, linker, and toolchain configuration.
- `limine.conf`, `scripts/boot.py` — boot configuration and pinned image/emulator workflow.
- `justfile` — supported development commands.
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — CI validation workflow.

## Engineering rules

### Keep changes incremental and coherent

1. Inspect the relevant source, tests, docs, and call sites before editing.
2. State assumptions, invariants, and failure behavior for new kernel interfaces.
3. Prefer small vertical slices that compile and can be tested over broad scaffolding or placeholder APIs.
4. Update tests and documentation alongside behavior changes.
5. Do not change unrelated code, rename files gratuitously, add speculative features, or rewrite project history.
6. Do not commit or create branches unless the user explicitly asks.

### Rust and dependency policy

- Preserve the kernel's `no_std`/freestanding constraints. Do not introduce `std` into kernel code.
- Prefer `core` and existing in-tree abstractions. Do not add third-party Rust dependencies without a concrete need and compatibility/security review.
- Keep the Crabshell parser independent of kernel I/O and VFS implementation. Kernel execution belongs in `src/shell.rs` or an appropriate kernel service.
- Do not add allocation-dependent APIs before a real heap exists. Fixed-capacity structures must document their limits and exhaustion behavior.
- Respect the workspace structure and the host-testable `rustix-kernel` library versus freestanding `rustix` binary boundary.

### Unsafe and hardware code

Unsafe code is expected only at explicit hardware, boot-protocol, assembly, or raw-memory boundaries. Keep each unsafe block narrow and document the invariant that makes it sound. Do not add broad `unsafe impl`, mutable global references, unchecked pointer arithmetic, or unreviewed inline/global assembly.

Before changing boot or memory code, account for these facts:

- Limine fills response pointers before `_start`; the request records must remain writable in the ELF image.
- Rustix validates nullness, alignment, counts, arithmetic, and physical ranges, but cannot prove that a non-null bootloader pointer is readable.
- Physical ranges are half-open `[start, end)` and must use checked arithmetic.
- Only regions classified `Usable` may enter the frame allocator. ACPI, bootloader-reclaimable, framebuffer, reserved, unknown, and other types are not free frames.
- A `Frame` is a physical address, not a dereferenceable pointer. Do not access it through the HHDM or change CR3 until an explicit, reviewed mapping policy and ownership proof exist.
- The kernel currently inherits Limine's page tables. Do not casually replace or mutate them: preserve the executing kernel, boot stack, `BootInfo`, request/response data, exception stacks, and mappings needed to continue execution.
- The exception setup is fatal-only. It does not enable maskable interrupts, configure a PIC/APIC, or provide recovery. Do not call `sti` or claim interrupt support without an IRQ design and tests.
- The shell and VFS run in ring 0 and are not isolated or secure.

For hardware changes, document assumptions about CPU mode, selectors, stacks, page permissions, interrupt state, and failure handling. Avoid new architecture mechanisms that cannot be statically reviewed or validated.

### Shell and filesystem contract

- Crabshell is presently a kernel-mode serial shell, not a userspace program or a POSIX shell.
- Its parser is a separate `no_std`, allocation-free crate; retain that boundary.
- The RAM filesystem is volatile and bounded. Preserve explicit errors and test capacity, path, and mutation edge cases.
- Do not imply persistence, permissions, links, process launching, or shell features that do not exist.
- Update the parser tests and `docs/architecture/crabshell.md` when adding or changing commands.

## Validation workflow

Run the narrowest relevant checks first, then broaden them. From the repository root, the supported commands are:

```sh
just fmt
just test
just check
just build
just image
just smoke
just verify
```

`just test` runs host-side library tests (memory-map validation, frame allocator, VFS, and Crabshell parser). `just check` checks `x86_64-unknown-none`; `just build` links the optimized ELF. `just verify` includes formatting, host tests, target check, pinned Limine image creation, and QEMU prompt smoke test. Image/boot checks need Python, `xorriso`, QEMU, the Rust target, and network access for the first pinned Limine download; Linux/WSL also needs `cc` to build Limine's host utility.

For changes to `src/main.rs`, `src/boot.rs`, linker/request configuration, `src/arch/x86_64/`, `src/frame.rs`, or paging/heap code, the intended full validation is `just verify`. If the environment does not permit a check, report the exact blocker and leave the corresponding roadmap criterion pending.

Do not claim a check passed unless it was run and its successful result was observed. Editor diagnostics are useful but are not a substitute for `cargo test`, a target build, or QEMU. A target check is not a final link; a linked ELF is not proof of boot; a prompt smoke test is not proof of interactive shell behavior or physical-hardware correctness.

## Completion criteria for agent changes

Before reporting work complete:

- Ensure source, tests, docs, and call sites agree.
- Review unsafe and hardware assumptions, including error paths and capacity limits.
- Run appropriate formatting/tests/build/boot checks, or clearly state why they could not run.
- Report files changed, behavior delivered, validation actually observed, and remaining risks.
- Keep milestone status accurate. A subsystem is not complete just because it has code.

   666	/// Fully decoded MTRR state. Construction rejects malformed or incomplete
   667	/// captured register snapshots before they can influence a mapping policy.
   668	#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
   669	pub struct ValidatedMtrrLayout {
   670	    physical_address_bits: u8,
   671	    enabled: bool,
   672	    fixed_enabled: bool,
   673	    default_type: MtrrMemoryType,
   674	    fixed_ranges: Option<FixedMtrrRanges>,
   675	    variable_ranges: [VariableMtrr; MAX_CAPTURED_VARIABLE_MTRRS],
   676	}
   677	
   678	impl MtrrRegisters {
   679	    pub fn validated_layout(
   680	        &self,
   681	        physical_address_bits: u8,
   682	    ) -> Result<ValidatedMtrrLayout, MtrrError> {
   683	        if !(12..=MAX_MTRR_PHYSICAL_ADDRESS_BITS).contains(&physical_address_bits) {
   684	            return Err(MtrrError::InvalidPhysicalAddressWidth);
   685	        }
   686	        if self.capability & !MTRRCAP_KNOWN_BITS != 0 {
   687	            return Err(MtrrError::ReservedCapabilityBits);
   688	        }
   689	        if self.default_type & !0x0cff != 0 {
   690	            return Err(MtrrError::ReservedDefaultTypeBits);
   691	        }
   692	
   693	        let reported_count = (self.capability & 0xff) as usize;
   694	        if reported_count > MAX_CAPTURED_VARIABLE_MTRRS
   695	            || reported_count != usize::from(self.variable_register_count)
   696	        {
   697	            return Err(MtrrError::VariableRegisterCountMismatch);
   698	        }
   699	
   700	        let fixed_supported = self.capability & MTRRCAP_FIXED_SUPPORTED != 0;
   701	        if fixed_supported != self.fixed_registers.is_some() {
   702	            return Err(MtrrError::FixedRegisterSupportMismatch);
   703	        }
   704	        let enabled = self.default_type & MTRR_ENABLED != 0;
   705	        let fixed_enabled = self.default_type & MTRR_FIXED_ENABLED != 0;
   706	        if fixed_enabled && !fixed_supported {
   707	            return Err(MtrrError::FixedRangesUnavailable);
   708	        }
   709	
   710	        let default_type = MtrrMemoryType::from_raw((self.default_type & 0xff) as u8)?;
   711	        let write_combining_supported = self.capability & MTRRCAP_WRITE_COMBINING_SUPPORTED != 0;
   712	        if default_type == MtrrMemoryType::WriteCombining && !write_combining_supported {
   713	            return Err(MtrrError::WriteCombiningUnsupported);
   714	        }
   715	
   716	        let fixed_ranges = self
   717	            .fixed_registers
   718	            .map(FixedMtrrRanges::from_msr_values)
   719	            .transpose()?;
   720	        if fixed_ranges.as_ref().is_some_and(|ranges| {
   721	            ranges
   722	                .memory_types
   723	                .contains(&MtrrMemoryType::WriteCombining)
   724	        }) && !write_combining_supported
   725	        {
   726	            return Err(MtrrError::WriteCombiningUnsupported);
   727	        }
   728	
   729	        let mut variable_ranges =
   730	            [VariableMtrr::inactive(physical_address_bits); MAX_CAPTURED_VARIABLE_MTRRS];
   731	        for (index, pair) in self
   732	            .variable_registers
   733	            .iter()
   734	            .take(reported_count)
   735	            .enumerate()
   736	        {
   737	            if let Some(range) =
   738	                VariableMtrr::from_msr_values(pair.base, pair.mask, physical_address_bits)?
   739	            {
   740	                if range.memory_type == MtrrMemoryType::WriteCombining && !write_combining_supported
   741	                {
   742	                    return Err(MtrrError::WriteCombiningUnsupported);
   743	                }
   744	                variable_ranges[index] = range;
   745	            }
   746	        }
   747	
   748	        Ok(ValidatedMtrrLayout {
   749	            physical_address_bits,
   750	            enabled,
   751	            fixed_enabled,
   752	            default_type,
   753	            fixed_ranges,
   754	            variable_ranges,
   755	        })
   756	    }
   757	}
   758	
   759	impl ValidatedMtrrLayout {
   760	    fn as_layout(&self) -> MtrrLayout<'_> {
   761	        MtrrLayout {
   762	            physical_address_bits: self.physical_address_bits,
   763	            enabled: self.enabled,
   764	            fixed_enabled: self.fixed_enabled,
   765	            default_type: self.default_type,
   766	            fixed_ranges: self.fixed_ranges.as_ref(),
   767	            variable_ranges: &self.variable_ranges,
   768	        }
   769	    }
   770	
   771	    pub fn memory_type_for(&self, address: u64) -> Result<MtrrMemoryType, MtrrError> {
   772	        self.as_layout().memory_type_for(address)
   773	    }
   774	
   775	    /// Resolve the Intel SDM PAT/MTRR table for one address and PAT index.
   776	    /// `normal_caching` must reflect CR0.CD=0 and CR0.NW=0.
   777	    pub fn effective_memory_type_for(
   778	        &self,
   779	        address: u64,
   780	        pat: PatLayout,
   781	        pat_index: u8,
   782	        normal_caching: bool,
   783	    ) -> Result<EffectiveMemoryType, EffectiveMemoryTypeError> {
   784	        if !normal_caching {
   785	            return Err(EffectiveMemoryTypeError::NonNormalCachingMode);
   786	        }
   787	        let mtrr_type = self
   788	            .memory_type_for(address)
   789	            .map_err(EffectiveMemoryTypeError::Mtrr)?;
   790	        let pat_type = pat.memory_type_at(pat_index)?;
   791	        Ok(combine_mtrr_pat_types(mtrr_type, pat_type))
   792	    }
   793	
   794	    /// Select the lowest PAT index that yields one effective type across an
   795	    /// aligned physical range. This checks MTRR transition boundaries, not aliases.
   796	    pub fn select_pat_index_for_range(
   797	        &self,
   798	        physical_start: u64,
   799	        length: u64,
   800	        pat: PatLayout,
   801	        requested: EffectiveMemoryType,
   802	        normal_caching: bool,
   803	    ) -> Result<u8, EffectiveMemoryTypeError> {
   804	        if !normal_caching {
   805	            return Err(EffectiveMemoryTypeError::NonNormalCachingMode);
   806	        }
   807	        if length == 0 {
   808	            return Err(EffectiveMemoryTypeError::EmptyRange);
   809	        }
   810	        if (physical_start | length) & (PAGE_SIZE - 1) != 0 {
   811	            return Err(EffectiveMemoryTypeError::UnalignedRange);
   812	        }
   813	        let end = physical_start
   814	            .checked_add(length)
   815	            .ok_or(EffectiveMemoryTypeError::AddressOverflow)?;
   816	        if end > (1u64 << self.physical_address_bits) {
   817	            return Err(EffectiveMemoryTypeError::Mtrr(
   818	                MtrrError::PhysicalAddressOutOfRange,
   819	            ));
   820	        }
   821	
   822	        let layout = self.as_layout();
   823	        let mut candidates = u8::MAX;
   824	        let mut address = physical_start;
   825	        while address < end {
   826	            let mtrr_type = layout
   827	                .memory_type_for(address)
   828	                .map_err(EffectiveMemoryTypeError::Mtrr)?;
   829	            for index in 0..8 {
   830	                let pat_type = pat.memory_type_at(index)?;
   831	                if combine_mtrr_pat_types(mtrr_type, pat_type) != requested {
   832	                    candidates &= !(1 << index);
   833	                }
   834	            }
   835	            if candidates == 0 {
   836	                return Err(EffectiveMemoryTypeError::NoUniformPatIndex { requested });
   837	            }
   838	            address = layout.next_boundary_after(address, end);
   839	        }
   840	        Ok(candidates.trailing_zeros() as u8)
   841	    }
   842	}

## Context Compaction (Completed)

## Goal
Continue Rustix Milestone 2 safely: validate memory/cache policy before implementing page tables, then proceed toward mapping ownership and heap work. Do not change active page tables or CR3 without a reviewed preservation and ownership proof.

## State
- The previous slice added validated captured MTRR state, Intel SDM Table 11-7 PAT/MTRR resolution under normal caching, and a read-only CR0 caching-mode diagnostic. `just verify` passed, and QEMU reported normal caching and `PAT[0]` resolving to WB at PA 0.
- The current slice adds `ValidatedMtrrLayout::select_pat_index_for_range`: for a nonempty, page-aligned physical range, it selects the lowest PAT index that yields the requested effective type across all fixed/variable MTRR transition boundaries. It checks boundaries rather than iterating page by page and rejects ranges with no uniform index.
- Variable MTRR discontinuous masks are architecturally permitted on some CPUs but explicitly unsupported by Rustix; the decoder rejects them rather than approximating their coverage.
- Tests cover variable-boundary selection, fixed-MTRR transitions, no-uniform-index behavior, and invalid ranges. The roadmap records range selection as done; live PTE/alias checks and mapping tests remain pending.
- `just verify` passed after the range selector: formatting, 4 parser tests, 53 kernel-library tests, target check, release build, ISO creation, and QEMU prompt smoke. Diagnostics reported no errors or warnings. `git diff --check` produced only pre-existing LF/CRLF warnings.
- The working tree contains numerous pre-existing uncommitted changes. Preserve them; do not reset or commit.

## Context
- Relevant implementation: `src/paging.rs`; architecture read-only state and diagnostic: `src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs`, `src/boot.rs`.
- Relevant docs updated: `docs/architecture/memory.md`, `docs/development/testing.md`, `docs/roadmap/README.md`, `docs/index.md`, and `AGENTS.md`.
- Effective-type policy follows Intel SDM Vol. 3A §11.5.2.2, Table 11-7, under `CR0.CD=0` and `CR0.NW=0`: <https://cdrdv2-public.intel.com/671447/325384-sdm-vol-3abcd.pdf>. Its footnotes distinguish page-table UC and MTRR UC behavior; the helper does not validate aliases.

     1	# Memory-management direction
     2	
     3	## What exists now
     4	
     5	`src/memory.rs` contains an allocation-free `MemoryMapBuilder` that copies Limine ranges into validated half-open physical regions. It rejects empty ranges, `base + length` overflow, overlapping ranges, empty maps, and maps exceeding the fixed 256-region capacity. Known Limine types remain distinct, and unknown type values are preserved. Host-side tests cover range validation/classification, canonical-address boundaries, physical-width bounds, and HHDM range arithmetic. `src/boot.rs` stores the resulting map in an owned boot snapshot and reports usable bytes.
     6	
     7	`src/frame.rs` provides a fixed-capacity allocator core with host-side tests. It only manages complete 4 KiB frames inside validated `Usable` regions, reserves the first MiB, and coalesces adjacent free ranges. The ownership contract assumes one allocator instance per physical map: within that instance, each eligible frame is owned either by its free-range table or by a non-copyable `Frame` token while allocated. The public constructor does not enforce unique instances, so callers must not initialize multiple allocators for the same physical map; the current boot path retains one allocator in `BootInfo`. `allocate` returns `None` when no free frame remains. `deallocate` consumes the token only on success; on any error, including free-range-table exhaustion, it returns a `DeallocationError` containing the original token and leaves allocator state unchanged. The range tables each have a fixed `MAX_FRAME_RANGES` capacity, so fragmentation can prevent a frame from being returned until nearby ranges coalesce. No kernel service currently allocates frames for mappings or other work.
     8	
     9	`Frame::address()` is a physical address value, not a dereferenceable pointer and not a proof that the frame is mapped. CPU diagnostics now read `CR4.LA57` to report the active linear-address width (48 or 57 bits) and query `CPUID.80000008H` for physical and maximum linear-address widths when available. Boot-protocol pointers are checked against the active width, with host tests for 48- and 57-bit canonical boundaries. These facts do not prove that any physical address is mapped.
    10	
    11	`src/paging.rs` adds pure, host-tested 4 KiB mapping groundwork and decodes the inherited CR3 root address plus its low-bit interpretation. The CR3 decoder validates the physical-address width and reserved bits and interprets the low 12 bits according to the active `CR4.PCIDE` state; it does not dereference the root. The mapping-range validator requires a known physical-address width, checked aligned bounds, canonical virtual endpoints in one canonical half, and rejects writable-executable permissions. A validated range can encode the raw bits of one 4 KiB leaf PTE, including supervisor/user and write permissions, NX when the caller confirms EFER.NXE, and a bounded three-bit PAT index. `PatLayout` parses a supplied `IA32_PAT` value and selects WB, UC, or WC indices. `MtrrMemoryType`, `VariableMtrr`, `FixedMtrrRanges`, and `MtrrLayout` resolve MTRR types at one physical address, including fixed-range priority and defined variable-overlap rules; undefined overlaps fail closed. `MtrrRegisters::validated_layout` additionally validates captured capability/default-type reserved bits, register counts and fixed-range presence, WC support, and variable-mask shape/alignment before producing an owned `ValidatedMtrrLayout`. It supports contiguous power-of-two variable masks; Intel permits discontinuous masks on some CPUs, but Rustix rejects them explicitly as unsupported rather than approximating their coverage. The layout combines the address-specific MTRR type with a selected PAT entry according to Intel SDM Table 11-7, but only when `CR0.CD` and `CR0.NW` are clear. Host tests cover all 30 documented MTRR/PAT type pairs and reject invalid indexes, malformed snapshots, out-of-range addresses, and non-normal caching mode. A pure range selector now returns the lowest PAT index that produces one requested effective type throughout a nonempty, aligned physical range, checking fixed- and variable-MTRR transition boundaries rather than iterating every page. It rejects the range if no single index works throughout. Boot reads CR0 without modifying it, validates supported captured MTRR/PAT state, and reports a diagnostic resolution at physical address zero using PAT index 0; this does not inspect the inherited PTE or assert that the live mapping uses that index. The range selector does not inspect existing mappings or cache aliases. The raw MTRR capture remains bounded to 32 variable pairs and reports capacity overflow without partial state. These helpers do not prove frame ownership or HHDM coverage, inspect table entries, or modify hardware page tables. No page mapping operation or CR3 transition is implemented.
    12	
    13	The effective-type resolver follows [Intel SDM Vol. 3A §11.5.2.2, Table 11-7](https://cdrdv2-public.intel.com/671447/325384-sdm-vol-3abcd.pdf), which applies when normal caching is enabled (`CR0.CD=0`, `CR0.NW=0`). Its footnotes distinguish UC selected by an MTRR from UC selected by a page-table entry (the latter involves cache snooping and aliasing concerns); they also identify combinations that older manual editions called undefined but current processors supporting both PAT and MTRRs resolve as shown. The resolver does not cover legacy PCD/PWT-only selection or model-specific combinations outside that table.
    14	
    15	The requested Limine base revision is 3. Its protocol maps only `Usable`, `BootloaderReclaimable`, `ExecutableAndModules`, and `Framebuffer` memory-map regions into the HHDM; reserved, ACPI, bad, and unknown regions are not in that mapping set. HHDM mappings use at least 4 KiB granularity and may cover page-aligned bytes beyond unaligned region boundaries. On x86_64, inherited HHDM mappings are supervisor RWX, normally write-back cached, with framebuffer mappings write-combining when PAT is available. Therefore an HHDM offset is not a blanket physical-memory access grant, and inherited HHDM permissions are not Rustix's future W^X policy. See the [Limine base revision 3 protocol](https://github.com/limine-bootloader/limine-protocol/blob/trunk/PROTOCOL.md#base-revision-3) and its memory-layout/caching sections.
    16	
    17	The boot snapshot now rejects physical map ranges beyond the reported CPUID physical-address width when that CPUID leaf is available. For base revision 3 HHDM-mapped types, it also validates the page-rounded physical span, checked `offset + address` arithmetic, and canonical endpoints in the active linear-address width. If the CPU does not report a physical width, the physical-bound check is skipped and no mapping caller may treat the bound as known. These checks are derived from metadata and Limine's protocol contract; they do not inspect page tables or prove that a non-null loader pointer is readable. Rustix still does not dereference physical memory through the HHDM. Rustix-owned mappings should be non-executable by default; executable kernel text must be explicit. MMIO requires an explicit device range and cache policy, and guard regions must remain unmapped. A page-table transition must preserve the kernel image, active stacks, boot data, descriptor tables, and any loader mappings still needed. Rustix does not reclaim bootloader memory, own or replace the inherited Limine page tables, or provide a heap. Bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT setup and fatal exception diagnostics live in `src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs`; they do not enable maskable IRQs.
    18	
    19	## Mapping inventory before a CR3 transition
    20	
    21	The current runtime has several mappings that a future page-table transition must preserve. The address sources and remaining gaps are:
    22	
    23	- **Kernel ELF image:** `linker.ld` places `.text`, `.rodata`, `.limine_requests`, `.data`, `.bss`, and `.got` in three `PT_LOAD` segments: RX text, read-only rodata, and RW data/BSS. It exports `__kernel_start` and `__kernel_end` around the complete loadable image, plus page-aligned bounds for each segment. `BootInfo` checks that Limine's reported virtual base matches the linker start, validates ordered contiguous segment bounds covering the rounded image, derives corresponding half-open physical ranges from the executable physical base with checked arithmetic, and validates canonical virtual and reported physical address widths. The release ELF and QEMU runtime report both showed the three aligned ranges on 2026-10-21. The RX, R/NX, and RW/NX labels describe the linker segment intent; these are linker/boot metadata, not proof that the inherited page tables map every page or enforce those permissions, nor proof that loader pointers are readable. The memory-map `ExecutableAndModules` entries remain illustrative, not an authoritative kernel-image extent.
    24	- **Active stack and `BootInfo`:** The assembly `_start` shim captures Limine's entry `RSP` before any Rust prologue. Under the SysV entry convention the synthetic return slot occupies 8 bytes, so `RSP + 8` is the exclusive stack top. The protocol guarantees at least 64 KiB (without a Stack Size request); `BootInfo` records that minimum virtual span, translates it through the HHDM, and requires it to fit within a single `BootloaderReclaimable` physical region. The full loader allocation may be larger, and neither its exact bounds nor a guard page are known. Preserve the inherited mapping; do not infer a guard page.
    25	- **Kernel static data:** `RAM_FILESYSTEM`, GDT, IDT, TSS, the ring-0 stack, and double-fault IST stack are static BSS/data in the kernel image. Exception entry also requires the handler code and the TSS/IDT references to remain mapped. Preserve the complete relevant data/BSS pages and stack pages.
    26	- **Limine request data:** request records are in the kernel's writable `.limine_requests` segment. Response objects and the memory-map pointer array are bootloader-reclaimable; `capture_boot_information` copies the values used later, and the shell does not retain those pointers. Keep them mapped until the copy and validation finish; any later reclaim must be explicit rather than reclaiming the whole bootloader-reclaimable class.
    27	- **Inherited page tables:** Limine places its page tables in bootloader-reclaimable memory, but their layout is unspecified. `BootInfo` captures raw CR3 and validates a decoded physical root address plus the low-bit interpretation selected by active `CR4.PCIDE`; this numeric decode does not make the root dereferenceable. Rustix does not inspect root entries or inventory the live mappings. Keep the old root and its backing pages intact while inspecting/building a replacement; do not reclaim them until a verified switch no longer depends on them.
    28	- **Devices:** COM1 uses x86 port I/O and needs no MMIO virtual mapping. Rustix does not currently request or use a framebuffer. Any future framebuffer or device-register mapping needs an explicit physical range and cache policy.
    29	
    30	## Initial kernel-owned mapping policy (design only)
    31	
    32	A first Rustix-owned x86_64 root should use 4 KiB pages only and require NX support; if NX is unavailable, abort before switching. Preserve ELF permissions exactly: text RX, rodata R/NX, and `.limine_requests`/data/BSS/GOT RW/NX. Reject W+X mappings. Exclude the complete physical kernel-image span from the generic HHDM in the first implementation so no writable direct-map alias can undermine text or rodata permissions. Ordinary RAM HHDM mappings should be RW/NX and WB.
    33	
    34	Preserve the inherited PAT/MTRR configuration during the first transition. The boot report validates captured registers and computes a diagnostic effective type from the active PAT/MTRR values under normal caching. A separate pure selector can choose an index whose effective type remains uniform across an aligned physical range, but neither checks inherited PTEs nor detects cache-type aliases. The pure combination follows Intel SDM Table 11-7; it is not a generic rule for legacy PCD/PWT-only selection or model-specific combinations. Under Limine base revision 3 on x86_64, use PAT index 0 for WB, index 3 for UC, and index 5 for WC only after the target physical range and active PAT/MTRR interaction are verified. Map MMIO only from explicit device ranges and use UC by default; do not infer MMIO from generic reserved memory-map entries. A framebuffer may use WC only after its response and cache policy are explicitly validated. COM1 uses port I/O and requires no MMIO mapping.
    35	
    36	Do not use huge pages in the first root; add them only when physical coverage, permissions, and cache attributes are uniform across the entire huge-page extent. Future Rustix-owned downward-growing stacks should have at least one 4 KiB unmapped guard page below them. The Limine bootstrap stack has no known guard, so none may be assumed there.
    37	
    38	Never modify Limine's active page tables in place. Build a separate candidate root from owned frames, leave the inherited root and its backing memory intact, and do not switch CR3 until every transition-critical mapping has been preserved and checked. Any pre-switch failure must discard the candidate root and return its frames without changing the active root. This policy is not yet implemented; Rustix does not inspect the inherited root or replace CR3.
    39	
    40	## Planned memory layers
    41	
    42	1. **Validated physical regions:** implemented as a fixed-capacity owned snapshot; allocator ownership and reclaim policy remain future work.
    43	2. **Frame allocator integration:** the bounded core is initialized from `BootInfo`; add real allocation callers only after the page-mapping policy and ownership rules are implemented.
    44	3. **Kernel virtual memory:** Rustix still runs on inherited Limine page tables. Before replacing them, preserve the executing kernel, bootstrap/Ring-0 stacks, request/response data, and exception stacks; define the HHDM extent and explicit mapping permissions/cache attributes. Keep writable-executable mappings disallowed by default and reserve MMIO and guard regions.
    45	4. **Heap:** add a global allocator only after frame allocation and page mapping are initialized. Define allocation failure behavior for kernel and interrupt contexts.
    46	5. **Process address spaces:** isolate userspace; define copy-in/copy-out helpers and never treat user pointers as kernel references.
    47	
    48	## Invariants to preserve
    49	
    50	- Physical ranges use checked arithmetic and the half-open convention `[start, end)`.
    51	- Only complete frames in validated `Usable` regions enter the allocator; the first MiB remains reserved. Firmware and loader-reclaimable regions are not silently promoted to free memory.
    52	- Under the single-allocator-per-physical-map contract, a frame is represented by one allocator-free range or one caller-owned, non-copyable `Frame` token. Only a successful `deallocate` transfers the token back to the allocator; errors return the token and leave allocator ranges and accounting unchanged. The current public constructor relies on callers to enforce unique allocator instances.
    53	- `allocate` returns `None` on frame exhaustion. Metadata-capacity exhaustion is an explicit error, never silent loss of a frame.
    54	- A `Frame` address is physical, not directly dereferenceable. No HHDM translation, page-table mutation, or CR3 switch is permitted until address widths, mapping coverage, permissions/cache attributes, and transition-preservation requirements are established.
    55	- Mapping changes validate alignment, canonical addresses, ownership, and permissions before touching tables.

    57	- Tests cover unaligned edges, exact-boundary allocations, arithmetic overflow, overlaps, exhaustion, and unchanged state/ownership on failure.

   615	    /// Resolve the MTRR type for one physical address, rejecting undefined overlaps.
   616	    pub fn memory_type_for(&self, address: u64) -> Result<MtrrMemoryType, MtrrError> {
   617	        if address >= (1u64 << self.physical_address_bits) {
   618	            return Err(MtrrError::PhysicalAddressOutOfRange);
   619	        }
   620	        if !self.enabled {
   621	            return Ok(MtrrMemoryType::Uncacheable);
   622	        }
   623	        if self.fixed_enabled {
   624	            if let Some(memory_type) = self
   625	                .fixed_ranges
   626	                .and_then(|ranges| ranges.type_for_address(address))
   627	            {
   628	                return Ok(memory_type);
   629	            }
   630	        }
   631	
   632	        let mut matched_types = 0u8;
   633	        for range in self.variable_ranges {
   634	            if range.matches(address) {
   635	                matched_types |= 1 << range.memory_type as u8;
   636	            }
   637	        }
   638	        if matched_types == 0 {
   639	            return Ok(self.default_type);
   640	        }
   641	        if matched_types & (1 << MtrrMemoryType::Uncacheable as u8) != 0 {
   642	            return Ok(MtrrMemoryType::Uncacheable);
   643	        }
   644	        if matched_types.count_ones() == 1 {
   645	            return MtrrMemoryType::from_raw(matched_types.trailing_zeros() as u8);
   646	        }
   647	        let write_back_and_through =
   648	            (1 << MtrrMemoryType::WriteBack as u8) | (1 << MtrrMemoryType::WriteThrough as u8);
   649	        if matched_types == write_back_and_through {
   650	            return Ok(MtrrMemoryType::WriteThrough);
   651	        }
   652	        Err(MtrrError::UndefinedOverlap)
   653	    }
   654	}

   656	fn next_fixed_mtrr_boundary(address: u64) -> Option<u64> {
   657	    match address {
   658	        0..0x80_000 => Some((address / 0x1_0000 + 1) * 0x1_0000),
   659	        0x80_000..0xa0_000 => Some(0x80_000 + ((address - 0x80_000) / 0x4000 + 1) * 0x4000),
   660	        0xa0_000..0xc0_000 => Some(0xa0_000 + ((address - 0xa0_000) / 0x4000 + 1) * 0x4000),
   661	        0xc0_000..0x10_0000 => Some(0xc0_000 + ((address - 0xc0_000) / 0x1000 + 1) * 0x1000),
   662	        _ => None,
   663	    }

   716	        let fixed_ranges = self

   718	            .map(FixedMtrrRanges::from_msr_values)

   732	            .variable_registers
   733	            .iter()

   750	            enabled,
   751	            fixed_enabled,
   752	            default_type,
   753	            fixed_ranges,
   754	            variable_ranges,
   755	        })

   794	    /// Select the lowest PAT index that yields one effective type across an
   795	    /// aligned physical range. This checks MTRR transition boundaries, not aliases.
   796	    pub fn select_pat_index_for_range(
   797	        &self,
   798	        physical_start: u64,
   799	        length: u64,
   800	        pat: PatLayout,
   801	        requested: EffectiveMemoryType,
   802	        normal_caching: bool,
   803	    ) -> Result<u8, EffectiveMemoryTypeError> {
   804	        if !normal_caching {
   805	            return Err(EffectiveMemoryTypeError::NonNormalCachingMode);
   806	        }
   807	        if length == 0 {
   808	            return Err(EffectiveMemoryTypeError::EmptyRange);
   809	        }
   810	        if (physical_start | length) & (PAGE_SIZE - 1) != 0 {
   811	            return Err(EffectiveMemoryTypeError::UnalignedRange);
   812	        }
   813	        let end = physical_start
   814	            .checked_add(length)
   815	            .ok_or(EffectiveMemoryTypeError::AddressOverflow)?;
   816	        if end > (1u64 << self.physical_address_bits) {
   817	            return Err(EffectiveMemoryTypeError::Mtrr(
   818	                MtrrError::PhysicalAddressOutOfRange,
   819	            ));
   820	        }
   821	
   822	        let layout = self.as_layout();
   823	        let mut candidates = u8::MAX;
   824	        let mut address = physical_start;
   825	        while address < end {
   826	            let mtrr_type = layout
   827	                .memory_type_for(address)
   828	                .map_err(EffectiveMemoryTypeError::Mtrr)?;
   829	            for index in 0..8 {
   830	                let pat_type = pat.memory_type_at(index)?;
   831	                if combine_mtrr_pat_types(mtrr_type, pat_type) != requested {
   832	                    candidates &= !(1 << index);
   833	                }
   834	            }
   835	            if candidates == 0 {
   836	                return Err(EffectiveMemoryTypeError::NoUniformPatIndex { requested });
   837	            }
   838	            address = layout.next_boundary_after(address, end);
   839	        }
   840	        Ok(candidates.trailing_zeros() as u8)
   841	    }
   842	}

   891	fn combine_mtrr_pat_types(mtrr: MtrrMemoryType, pat: PatMemoryType) -> EffectiveMemoryType {
   892	    use MtrrMemoryType as M;
   893	    use PatMemoryType as P;
   894	
   895	    // Intel SDM Table 11-7; rows are MTRR UC/WC/WT/WB/WP, columns PAT UC/UC-/WC/WT/WB/WP.
   896	    let row = match mtrr {
   897	        M::Uncacheable => 0,
   898	        M::WriteCombining => 1,
   899	        M::WriteThrough => 2,
   900	        M::WriteBack => 3,
   901	        M::WriteProtected => 4,
   902	    };
   903	    let column = match pat {
   904	        P::Uncacheable => 0,
   905	        P::UncacheableMinus => 1,
   906	        P::WriteCombining => 2,
   907	        P::WriteThrough => 3,
   908	        P::WriteBack => 4,
   909	        P::WriteProtected => 5,
   910	    };
   911	    INTEL_PAT_MTRR_EFFECTIVE_TYPES[row][column]
   912	}

    57	/// A bounded allocator over only validated `Usable` memory-map ranges.
    58	///
    59	/// For a given physical map, callers must use only one allocator instance as
    60	/// the allocation authority; the type does not enforce this uniqueness. Within
    61	/// that instance, each eligible frame is owned by the allocator while free, or
    62	/// by the non-copyable `Frame` token returned by `allocate` while allocated. A
    63	/// frame address is an identifier only; this allocator does not map or access it.
    64	/// Both range tables are sorted, disjoint, page-aligned half-open ranges. The
    65	/// allocator returns `None` on frame exhaustion and reports metadata exhaustion
    66	/// explicitly without changing state or consuming the caller's frame token.
    67	pub struct FrameAllocator {
    68	    managed: [FrameRange; MAX_FRAME_RANGES],
    69	    managed_count: usize,
    70	    free: [FrameRange; MAX_FRAME_RANGES],

    79	        managed_count: 0,
    80	        free: [FrameRange::EMPTY; MAX_FRAME_RANGES],
    81	        free_count: 0,

    86	    /// Build allocator metadata without allocating or touching physical memory.
    87	    ///
    88	    /// The caller must ensure there is only one allocator instance per physical
    89	    /// map; constructing multiple instances would duplicate allocation authority.
    90	    pub fn from_memory_map(map: &MemoryMap) -> Result<Self, FrameError> {
    91	        let mut allocator = Self::EMPTY;
    92	        let page_mask = !(FRAME_SIZE - 1);
    93	
    94	        for region in map.regions() {
    95	            if region.kind() != RegionKind::Usable {
    96	                continue;
    97	            }
    98	
    99	            let start = region.start().max(LOW_MEMORY_RESERVED_END);
   100	            let Some(start) = start
   101	                .checked_add(FRAME_SIZE - 1)
   102	                .map(|address| address & page_mask)
   103	            else {
   104	                continue;
   105	            };
   106	            let end = region.end() & page_mask;
   107	            if start >= end {
   108	                continue;
   109	            }
   110	
   111	            let range = FrameRange { start, end };
   112	            Self::insert_range(&mut allocator.managed, &mut allocator.managed_count, range)?;
   113	            Self::insert_range(&mut allocator.free, &mut allocator.free_count, range)?;
   114	
   115	            let frames = (end - start) / FRAME_SIZE;
   116	            allocator.managed_frames = allocator
   117	                .managed_frames
   118	                .checked_add(frames)
   119	                .ok_or(FrameError::AccountingOverflow)?;
   120	            allocator.free_frames = allocator
   121	                .free_frames
   122	                .checked_add(frames)
   123	                .ok_or(FrameError::AccountingOverflow)?;
   124	        }
   125	
   126	        Ok(allocator)
   127	    }

   129	    /// Number of complete frames inside eligible usable regions.
   130	    pub const fn managed_frames(&self) -> u64 {
   131	        self.managed_frames
   132	    }
   133	
   134	    /// Number of currently unallocated frames.
   135	    pub const fn free_frames(&self) -> u64 {
   136	        self.free_frames
   137	    }
   138	
   139	    /// Allocate the lowest-address available frame, or return `None` on exhaustion.
   140	    pub fn allocate(&mut self) -> Option<Frame> {
   141	        if self.free_count == 0 {
   142	            return None;
   143	        }
   144	
   145	        let address = self.free[0].start;
   146	        self.free[0].start += FRAME_SIZE;
   147	        self.free_frames -= 1;

   154	    /// Return a frame to the allocator, merging adjacent free ranges.
   155	    ///
   156	    /// On error, the returned `DeallocationError` retains the frame token so the
   157	    /// caller can retry or otherwise preserve ownership. Failed returns do not
   158	    /// change allocator state.
   159	    pub fn deallocate(&mut self, frame: Frame) -> Result<(), DeallocationError> {

   161	        if address & (FRAME_SIZE - 1) != 0 {
   162	            return Err(DeallocationError {
   163	                error: FrameError::UnalignedFrame,
   164	                frame,
   165	            });
   166	        }

   168	            return Err(DeallocationError {
   169	                error: FrameError::NotManaged,
   170	                frame,
   171	            });
   172	        };
   173	        if !self
   174	            .managed
   175	            .iter()
   176	            .take(self.managed_count)
   177	            .any(|range| range.start <= address && end <= range.end)
   178	        {
   179	            return Err(DeallocationError {
   180	                error: FrameError::NotManaged,
   181	                frame,
   182	            });
   183	        }
   184	        if self
   185	            .free
   186	            .iter()
   187	            .take(self.free_count)
   188	            .any(|range| address < range.end && range.start < end)
   189	        {
   190	            return Err(DeallocationError {
   191	                error: FrameError::AlreadyFree,
   192	                frame,
   193	            });
   194	        }
   195	
   196	        let Some(new_free_count) = self.free_frames.checked_add(1) else {
   197	            return Err(DeallocationError {
   198	                error: FrameError::AccountingOverflow,
   199	                frame,
   200	            });
   201	        };
   202	        if let Err(error) = Self::insert_range(
   203	            &mut self.free,
   204	            &mut self.free_count,
   205	            FrameRange {
   206	                start: address,
   207	                end,
   208	            },
   209	        ) {
   210	            return Err(DeallocationError { error, frame });
   211	        }
   212	        self.free_frames = new_free_count;
   213	        Ok(())
   214	    }

   216	    fn insert_range(
   217	        ranges: &mut [FrameRange; MAX_FRAME_RANGES],
   218	        count: &mut usize,
   219	        incoming: FrameRange,
   220	    ) -> Result<(), FrameError> {
   221	        let mut index = 0;
   222	        while index < *count && ranges[index].start < incoming.start {
   223	            index += 1;
   224	        }
   225	
   226	        if (index > 0 && ranges[index - 1].end > incoming.start)
   227	            || (index < *count && incoming.end > ranges[index].start)
   228	        {
   229	            return Err(FrameError::RangeOverlap);
   230	        }
   231	
   232	        let joins_previous = index > 0 && ranges[index - 1].end == incoming.start;
   233	        let joins_next = index < *count && incoming.end == ranges[index].start;
   234	        match (joins_previous, joins_next) {
   235	            (true, true) => {
   236	                ranges[index - 1].end = ranges[index].end;
   237	                Self::remove_range(ranges, count, index);
   238	            }
   239	            (true, false) => ranges[index - 1].end = incoming.end,
   240	            (false, true) => ranges[index].start = incoming.start,
   241	            (false, false) => {
   242	                if *count == MAX_FRAME_RANGES {
   243	                    return Err(FrameError::RangeTableFull);
   244	                }
   245	                for move_index in (index..*count).rev() {
   246	                    ranges[move_index + 1] = ranges[move_index];
   247	                }
   248	                ranges[index] = incoming;
   249	                *count += 1;
   250	            }
   251	        }
   252	        Ok(())
   253	    }
   254	
   255	    fn remove_range(ranges: &mut [FrameRange; MAX_FRAME_RANGES], count: &mut usize, index: usize) {
   256	        for move_index in index..(*count - 1) {
   257	            ranges[move_index] = ranges[move_index + 1];
   258	        }
   259	        *count -= 1;
   260	        ranges[*count] = FrameRange::EMPTY;
   261	    }
   262	}

    16	    }

    26	        u64::MAX >> address_bits
    27	    };

    29	}

   246	    pub fn from_msr_value(value: u64) -> Result<Self, PatLayoutError> {

   269	            CachePolicy::WriteBack => 0b110,
