## Milestone 3 — IRQs, time, and kernel scheduling

Do not enable interrupts as a side effect of installing exception gates. IRQ delivery needs its own controller, acknowledgement, masking, ownership, and synchronization design.

### Planned work

- [ ] Select and document the initial interrupt controller policy for QEMU and target hardware (for example, legacy PIC compatibility versus local I/O APIC; do not enable both accidentally).
- [ ] Add IRQ vector allocation, controller masking/unmasking, end-of-interrupt acknowledgement, spurious-interrupt handling, and a policy for unexpected IRQs.
- [ ] Add a calibrated/verified timer source and monotonic timekeeping; test interval arithmetic and drift assumptions.
- [ ] Establish interrupt-safe lock primitives and rules for code callable from normal, exception, and IRQ contexts. No allocator or blocking console operation may run in an unsafe interrupt context.
- [ ] Add a minimal kernel-thread context and lifecycle model, stack ownership/guard policy, context-switch tests, and emulator scheduling tests.
- [ ] Add preemption only after lock, stack, timer, and interrupt-return invariants have deterministic tests.
- [ ] Keep application-processor startup/SMP as a separate sub-milestone after per-CPU state, TLB invalidation, and lock semantics exist.

**Exit criteria:** tested IRQ acknowledgement and timer behavior, deterministic thread lifecycle/context-switch tests, and bounded QEMU tests under repeated timer interrupts. No `sti` before the design and tests are ready.

---

## Milestone 4 — isolated processes and syscall ABI

Userspace begins only after page tables, exception handling, scheduling, and controlled memory allocation are trustworthy. The syscall ABI is a product interface and must not emerge accidentally from internal functions.

### Planned work

- [ ] Decide and document the x86_64 user-entry/syscall mechanism, register convention, selector/MSR setup, per-CPU state requirements, and safe return path.
- [ ] Add user/kernel page permissions and process-owned address spaces, including teardown and TLB invalidation rules.
- [ ] Implement copy-in/copy-out helpers that validate lengths, arithmetic, canonical ranges, permissions, and faults; never form a kernel reference directly from a user pointer.
- [ ] Specify version discovery, stable syscall numbers, argument layouts, error encoding, partial-I/O behavior, interruption/restart, and compatibility policy before exposing calls.
- [ ] Add initial process lifecycle and descriptor-table semantics: create/load, exit, wait, close, duplication/inheritance, and process cleanup.
- [ ] Load a deliberately small documented executable format with bounds/segment/permission checks; reject malformed binaries safely.
- [ ] Build adversarial tests for bad pointers, overflow, invalid mappings, process teardown, descriptor misuse, and failed exec.

### First user-visible target

A small controlled `init` process should start from a reproducible image, write through a descriptor, exit with a status, and be waited on by a kernel test harness. Do not claim userspace or process isolation from ring-0 tasks that merely use process-shaped structs.

**Exit criteria:** an isolated init process runs in user mode and uses a versioned, documented syscall subset; invalid user pointers and process teardown are tested without corrupting the kernel.

---

## Milestone 5 — VFS, storage, and device ownership

Keep the current RAM filesystem as a bootstrap/test implementation. Persistence and device drivers require explicit block ownership, error handling, and recovery behavior.

### Planned work

- [ ] Define VFS node, mount, path, metadata, and file-descriptor contracts independently of a particular disk format.
- [ ] Preserve volatile RAMFS as a test backend and add tests for mount/path errors, capacity, partial I/O, and object lifetime.
- [ ] Add a narrowly scoped block-device interface with request validation, timeout/error reporting, and a QEMU-supported initial device driver (such as virtio-blk after PCI discovery is ready).
- [ ] Choose and document the first on-disk filesystem format. Specify partition discovery, byte order, block size, metadata limits, corruption handling, and read-only/recovery behavior before writable support.
- [ ] Add persistent write/read/remount/reboot integration tests; never claim persistence from an in-memory cache alone.
- [ ] Add a driver ownership and DMA policy before any device can write into arbitrary kernel memory.
- [ ] Define file descriptors and basic process I/O semantics before exposing them to applications.

**Exit criteria:** a reproducible image mounts a documented on-disk filesystem, user-visible tools can create/read files across reboot, and corruption/I/O errors fail safely.

---

## Milestone 6 — initial userspace and command-line utilities

Crabshell is currently an in-kernel parser/frontend. The long-term terminal application should reuse its parser model without linking kernel internals or bypassing syscalls.

### Planned work

- [ ] Start a user-mode `init` process and establish executable search, environment, current directory, descriptor inheritance, and process startup rules.
- [ ] Port or adapt Crabshell into a userspace terminal application that uses only the documented syscall/VFS interfaces.
- [ ] Add a small utility set with explicit scope: file listing, text output, create/remove/copy/move, and system information.
- [ ] Add command-line quoting, escaping, history, redirection, and pipelines only with parser tests and process/descriptor/pipe semantics to support them.
- [ ] Add integration tests that launch tools from the filesystem image and exercise them through syscalls; keep unsupported features explicit.

**Exit criteria:** shell and basic tools run as isolated user processes from a reproducible image; no shell command directly calls kernel-private VFS internals.

---

## Milestone 7 — graphical console and GUI (long-term)

A GUI is intentionally downstream of stable memory management, interrupts/input, process isolation, drivers, and userspace. Keep Crabshell's parser independent so a graphical terminal frontend can reuse it.

### Planned work

- [ ] Add validated framebuffer discovery and memory ownership; implement a minimal text/graphics console without compromising serial panic diagnostics.
- [ ] Establish an input subsystem that separates raw device events from key mapping and terminal policy. Plan PS/2 and USB HID support separately; do not treat the current raw scancode poller as a keyboard driver stack.
- [ ] Define a graphics buffer ownership/presentation API, clipping rules, pixel format, and bounds/overflow checks.
- [ ] Implement a minimal compositor/windowing policy only after process isolation and input routing are ready.
- [ ] Run Crabshell as a terminal application in a GUI window using the same parser and userspace services as the serial/TTY path.
- [ ] Preserve serial as a headless recovery/debug console and add repeatable QEMU display/input tests.

**Exit criteria:** a documented GUI session starts from userspace, renders a terminal, accepts tested input, and does not require direct kernel-private VFS access.

---

## Milestone 8 — networking (long-term, after drivers and process isolation)

Networking is not implied by the current device drivers. The initial target should be a tightly scoped virtual-device path with clear ownership and bounded buffers.

### Planned work

- [ ] Complete PCI/device discovery and define DMA buffer ownership, address translation, cache synchronization, and reset/error behavior.
- [ ] Implement one virtual NIC driver with bounded queues and timeouts; test against QEMU user networking.
- [ ] Choose and document a minimal link/network protocol scope before implementation. Keep packet parsing length-checked and fuzzable on the host.
- [ ] Add interface configuration, routing, socket/descriptor ownership, and per-process access policy.
- [ ] Add adversarial packet tests and integration tests for link loss, malformed packets, queue exhaustion, and device reset.
- [ ] Add higher-level transports/services only when the required protocol semantics, entropy source, and security model are designed.

**Exit criteria:** documented user processes can communicate through a tested virtual NIC/network stack, with malformed input and resource exhaustion handled safely. Do not claim internet, TLS, or POSIX sockets merely from a packet driver.

---

## Cross-cutting acceptance gates

Every milestone should include the relevant subset of these gates:

1. **Design:** documented ownership, invariants, resource limits, error semantics, and unsupported cases.
2. **Tests:** host tests for pure policy and malformed/boundary input; integration tests for hardware-facing behavior.
3. **Safety:** review unsafe blocks, pointer provenance/access, integer overflow, privilege boundaries, concurrency, and cleanup/rollback paths.
4. **Build:** format, host tests, target check, and final ELF link as appropriate.
5. **Boot/integration:** QEMU tests for changes to boot, paging, descriptors, interrupts, drivers, processes, or persistence.
6. **Documentation/status:** update architecture and roadmap docs; never check off a criterion without evidence.
7. **Compatibility:** claim Unix/POSIX behavior only for the exact documented subset with conformance-style tests.

## Working rule

Prefer a small end-to-end vertical slice over broad, unbootable scaffolding. A source file, interface, or architecture document is not proof that the corresponding subsystem is operational. When a check cannot run, record the exact environment blocker and leave that acceptance gate pending.

# Testing and verification

## Current checks

`just verify` runs the standard development verification sequence:

1. `just fmt` — fail on formatting differences across the workspace.
2. `just test` — run host-side memory-map, mapping-range/PTE-bit policy, frame-allocator, RAM-filesystem, and Crabshell parser tests.
3. `just check` — check the `x86_64-unknown-none` kernel target.
4. `just smoke` — build the pinned hybrid ISO, boot it in QEMU, and check that Crabshell reaches its prompt within a deadline.

`just fault-smoke` separately builds opt-in kernel variants that deliberately trigger a page fault and an invalid opcode. It requires each QEMU run to report the expected exception (and CR2 for the page fault), avoid the shell prompt, and remain halted until timeout. It then rebuilds and restores the default release kernel and ISO. These are fatal-path diagnostics, not exception recovery tests; both Cargo features are disabled by default and cannot be enabled together.

Keep the Crabshell parser, VFS, memory-map validator, paging policy helpers, and frame allocator independent of hardware so syntax, path handling, address and leaf-PTE bit policy, PAT/MTRR policy, storage semantics, and frame ownership can be tested without booting. Pure tests validate captured MTRR register snapshots, resolve the Intel SDM Table 11-7 PAT/MTRR combinations for one physical address, select a PAT index that remains uniform across MTRR boundaries in an aligned range, and bind that selection to validated mapping metadata before encoding leaves. They reject malformed state, unsupported discontinuous masks, invalid indexes/ranges, out-of-range addresses, mismatched physical widths, and non-normal caching mode. These helpers do not access tables, read the active PAT MSR, prove frame ownership, or validate live mapping/cache aliases. Boot separately captures the registers and CR0 caching mode read-only and reports a diagnostic resolution; this is not a page-table or mapping test. The GDT/TSS/IDT and CPU-register paths are privileged kernel code; QEMU boot and fault-injection checks complement, but do not replace, static review and target builds. Add tests for boundaries and failure behavior when introducing new pure kernel helpers. The kernel binary is not a host test target.

## What current checks do not prove

- `cargo check` does not perform a final target link.
- A successful ELF link does not prove the boot protocol is recognized or `_start` is reached.
- Host unit tests do not validate privileged instructions, UART behavior, memory-map pointer validity, page tables, interrupts, or actual hardware. The QEMU boot path exercises the gated EFER/PAT reads and bounded MTRR capture and prints diagnostic summaries, but the prompt smoke assertion does not make those facts a mapping-safety proof.
- The automated QEMU prompt smoke test checks only that the kernel reaches the shell. `just fault-smoke` separately exercises only the controlled page-fault and invalid-opcode fatal paths; it does not test every exception vector, recovery, or physical hardware.
- A separate manual QEMU session exercised directory navigation and file create/write/append/read/copy/move/remove operations, including `cp` replacing an existing destination and rejection of `rmdir` on a nonempty directory. This is not exhaustive shell coverage and does not prove persistence across reboot.
- There is no on-disk filesystem integration test, syscall/userspace test, fuzz target, or physical-hardware test.

## Validation policy

For changes to the kernel entry, linker script, boot requests, architecture code, shell, or VFS, run `just verify`. For memory-management and ABI code, add negative tests for overflow, malformed ranges, permission failures, and invalid user pointers before exposing those paths to userspace.

Record commands actually run and any environment limitation in change summaries; never call an unexecuted build “passing.”

```rustix/src/paging.rs
  1020	///
  1021	/// The physical-address width must be known; passing `None` is rejected rather
  1022	/// than treating an unknown bound as unbounded. Successful validation does not
  1023	/// establish that physical frames are owned by a caller or mapped in the HHDM.
  1024	pub fn validate_mapping_range(
  1025	    virtual_start: u64,
  1026	    physical_start: u64,
  1027	    length: u64,
  1028	    permissions: PagePermissions,
  1029	    physical_address_bits: Option<u8>,
  1030	    virtual_address_bits: u8,
  1031	) -> Result<ValidatedMappingRange, MappingError> {
  1032	    if virtual_address_bits == 0 || virtual_address_bits > 64 {
  1033	        return Err(MappingError::InvalidVirtualAddressWidth);
  1034	    }
  1035	    let physical_address_bits =
  1036	        physical_address_bits.ok_or(MappingError::UnknownPhysicalAddressWidth)?;
  1037	    if physical_address_bits == 0 || physical_address_bits > 64 {
  1038	        return Err(MappingError::InvalidPhysicalAddressWidth);
  1039	    }
  1040	    if length == 0 {
  1041	        return Err(MappingError::EmptyRange);
  1042	    }
  1043	    if (virtual_start | physical_start | length) & (PAGE_SIZE - 1) != 0 {
  1044	        return Err(MappingError::UnalignedRange);
```

    75	2. State assumptions, invariants, and failure behavior for new kernel interfaces.
    76	3. Prefer small vertical slices that compile and can be tested over broad scaffolding or placeholder APIs.
    77	4. Update tests and documentation alongside behavior changes.
    78	5. Do not change unrelated code, rename files gratuitously, add speculative features, or rewrite project history.
    79	6. Do not commit or create branches unless the user explicitly asks.
    80	
    81	### Rust and dependency policy
    82	
    83	- Preserve the kernel's `no_std`/freestanding constraints. Do not introduce `std` into kernel code.
    84	- Prefer `core` and existing in-tree abstractions. Do not add third-party Rust dependencies without a concrete need and compatibility/security review.
    85	- Keep the Crabshell parser independent of kernel I/O and VFS implementation. Kernel execution belongs in `src/shell.rs` or an appropriate kernel service.
    86	- Do not add allocation-dependent APIs before a real heap exists. Fixed-capacity structures must document their limits and exhaustion behavior.
    87	- Respect the workspace structure and the host-testable `rustix-kernel` library versus freestanding `rustix` binary boundary.
    88	
    89	### Unsafe and hardware code
    90	
    91	Unsafe code is expected only at explicit hardware, boot-protocol, assembly, or raw-memory boundaries. Keep each unsafe block narrow and document the invariant that makes it sound. Do not add broad `unsafe impl`, mutable global references, unchecked pointer arithmetic, or unreviewed inline/global assembly.
    92	
    93	Before changing boot or memory code, account for these facts:
    94	
    95	- Limine fills response pointers before `_start`; the request records must remain writable in the ELF image.
    96	- Rustix validates nullness, alignment, counts, arithmetic, and physical ranges, but cannot prove that a non-null bootloader pointer is readable.
    97	- Physical ranges are half-open `[start, end)` and must use checked arithmetic.
    98	- Only regions classified `Usable` may enter the frame allocator. ACPI, bootloader-reclaimable, framebuffer, reserved, unknown, and other types are not free frames.
    99	- A `Frame` is a physical address, not a dereferenceable pointer. Do not access it through the HHDM or change CR3 until an explicit, reviewed mapping policy and ownership proof exist.
   100	- The kernel currently inherits Limine's page tables. Do not casually replace or mutate them: preserve the executing kernel, boot stack, `BootInfo`, request/response data, exception stacks, and mappings needed to continue execution.
   101	- The exception setup is fatal-only. It does not enable maskable interrupts, configure a PIC/APIC, or provide recovery. Do not call `sti` or claim interrupt support without an IRQ design and tests.
   102	- The shell and VFS run in ring 0 and are not isolated or secure.
   103	
   104	For hardware changes, document assumptions about CPU mode, selectors, stacks, page permissions, interrupt state, and failure handling. Avoid new architecture mechanisms that cannot be statically reviewed or validated.
   105	
   106	### Shell and filesystem contract
   107	
   108	- Crabshell is presently a kernel-mode serial shell, not a userspace program or a POSIX shell.
   109	- Its parser is a separate `no_std`, allocation-free crate; retain that boundary.
   110	- The RAM filesystem is volatile and bounded. Preserve explicit errors and test capacity, path, and mutation edge cases.
   111	- Do not imply persistence, permissions, links, process launching, or shell features that do not exist.
   112	- Update the parser tests and `docs/architecture/crabshell.md` when adding or changing commands.
   113	
   114	## Validation workflow
   115	
   116	Run the narrowest relevant checks first, then broaden them. From the repository root, the supported commands are:
   117	
   118	```sh
   119	just fmt
   120	just test
   121	just check
   122	just build
   123	just image
   124	just smoke
   125	just verify
   126	```
   127	
   128	`just test` runs host-side library tests (memory-map validation, frame allocator, VFS, and Crabshell parser). `just check` checks `x86_64-unknown-none`; `just build` links the optimized ELF. `just verify` includes formatting, host tests, target check, pinned Limine image creation, and QEMU prompt smoke test. Image/boot checks need Python, `xorriso`, QEMU, the Rust target, and network access for the first pinned Limine download; Linux/WSL also needs `cc` to build Limine's host utility.
   129	
   130	For changes to `src/main.rs`, `src/boot.rs`, linker/request configuration, `src/arch/x86_64/`, `src/frame.rs`, or paging/heap code, the intended full validation is `just verify`. If the environment does not permit a check, report the exact blocker and leave the corresponding roadmap criterion pending.
   131	
   132	Do not claim a check passed unless it was run and its successful result was observed. Editor diagnostics are useful but are not a substitute for `cargo test`, a target build, or QEMU. A target check is not a final link; a linked ELF is not proof of boot; a prompt smoke test is not proof of interactive shell behavior or physical-hardware correctness.
   133	
   134	## Completion criteria for agent changes
   135	
   136	Before reporting work complete:
   137	
   138	- Ensure source, tests, docs, and call sites agree.
   139	- Review unsafe and hardware assumptions, including error paths and capacity limits.
   140	- Run appropriate formatting/tests/build/boot checks, or clearly state why they could not run.
   141	- Report files changed, behavior delivered, validation actually observed, and remaining risks.
   142	- Keep milestone status accurate. A subsystem is not complete just because it has code.

**Tool Call: Review safe paging transition path**
Status: Completed

## Verdict

**Newly allocated table frames:** Limine’s base-revision-3 HHDM contract is a plausible basis for accessing an allocator-issued frame through `hhdm_offset + frame.address()`: the allocator takes complete frames only from `Usable` regions, Limine’s HHDM includes `Usable` memory, and boot validation checks page-rounded HHDM arithmetic and canonicality for those regions. That is sufficient **only as an explicit trust premise on a compliant Limine handoff**, with a known physical-address width and a checked frame-to-HHDM conversion. It is not proof that the live page tables contain the mapping or that the observed permissions/cache attributes match the contract.

**The inherited root:** current checks are **not enough to dereference it**. `parse_cr3_root` validates the numeric CR3 encoding and physical width, but `BootInfo` retains its `Result` rather than rejecting an invalid root. The code does not check that the root page belongs to an HHDM-mapped memory-map region, walk its child tables, or verify their locations. The memory documentation says Limine places its tables in bootloader-reclaimable memory, but the source does not establish that for the captured root.

**I would not switch CR3 yet.** The current code has validation and PTE-bit helpers, not table access, table ownership, live mapping inspection, or a replacement root.

## What the current code establishes—and what it does not

- `MemoryMap` validates checked, non-overlapping physical ranges. `FrameAllocator` rounds `Usable` regions inward to complete 4 KiB frames and reserves the first MiB. It does not map or access a frame; `Frame` is only a physical-address token. The one-allocator-per-map rule is documented, not enforced. See [`src/frame.rs:57-90`](src/frame.rs) and [`src/frame.rs:94-127`](src/frame.md).
- For HHDM-mapped region types, boot checks physical bounds when known and page-rounded HHDM addition/canonicality. `limine_v3_hhdm_range_is_valid` explicitly does **not** check actual page-table presence. If CPUID does not provide a physical width, the physical-bound check is skipped. See [`src/boot.rs:321-337`](src/boot.rs) and [`src/memory.rs:251-307`](src/memory.rs).
- `BootInfo` stores raw CR3 and a decoded-root result. Decoding checks width and low-bit interpretation, but does not dereference or locate the root in the memory map. See [`src/boot.rs:179-188`](src/boot.rs) and [`src/paging.rs:45-83`](src/paging.rs).
- The paging module validates range shape and encodes leaf PTE bits. It does not establish frame ownership, HHDM coverage, or actual cache attributes, and never touches page tables. See [`src/paging.rs:212-217`](src/paging.rs) and [`src/paging.rs:1019-1079`](src/paging.rs).
- The policy documentation correctly describes the HHDM types and limitations, but explicitly says inherited page tables are not inspected and HHDM must not be treated as a blanket physical-memory grant. See [`docs/architecture/memory.md:11-17`](docs/architecture/memory.md).

For a table frame, the protocol premise can bridge the “mapping presence” gap for a **narrow, checked access** to an allocated `Usable` frame. It does not make arbitrary physical addresses dereferenceable. A future accessor should require an allocator-owned token, known physical width, membership in the expected `Usable` range, checked/canonical HHDM translation, and a documented reliance on Limine’s mapping guarantee. Do not let the token or accessor imply coverage for `Reserved`, ACPI, or unknown regions.

For the inherited root, at minimum first check that its complete 4 KiB page fits in a region the HHDM contract maps, verify the translation arithmetic, and fail closed if the physical width or CR3 decode is unknown/invalid. The same checks are needed for every child table before walking it. Merely validating the whole memory-map regions does not tie the CR3 address to one of them.

## Minimum transition-critical state

A later candidate root must cover, at the required virtual addresses and with suitable permissions:

1. **The complete kernel image:** linker-defined text RX; rodata R/NX; `.limine_requests`, data, BSS, and GOT RW/NX. This includes the current instruction stream and the code, data, and strings used by boot reporting, shell, and fatal handlers. The linker exports aligned segment bounds, and boot validates their metadata, but neither proves inherited PTE coverage or permissions. See [`linker.ld:14-57`](linker.ld) and [`docs/architecture/memory.md:21-26`](docs/architecture/memory.md).
2. **The active boot stack and `BootInfo`:** `BootInfo` is held on the current Rust stack and passed by reference into the shell. Preserve at least the recorded 64 KiB minimum span; the actual Limine stack allocation and any guard are unknown. The current code validates the span’s HHDM arithmetic and bootloader-reclaimable backing, not its live PTEs. See [`src/main.rs:44-69`](src/main.rs), [`src/boot.rs:339-381`](src/boot.rs), and [`src/memory.rs:228-249`](src/memory.rs).
3. **Descriptor and exception state:** the active GDT, IDT, TSS, ring-0 stack, and double-fault IST stack are static kernel data; exception stubs, dispatch code, and diagnostic strings must remain mapped too. The CPU’s descriptor-table/task-register state refers to these objects. The existing handlers are fatal, so a page fault during or just after a transition must not leave their required mappings absent. See [`src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs:98-105`](src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs) and [`src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs:141-221`](src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs).
4. **Loader request/response data while it is still used:** response pointers and memory-map entries are read during `capture_boot_information`; the copied snapshot is what later code consumes. Keep the request section and loader objects mapped through capture, and do not reclaim bootloader-reclaimable memory wholesale. See [`src/boot.rs:191-222`](src/boot.rs) and [`src/boot.rs:262-315`](src/boot.rs).
5. **Page-table access mappings:** table frames allocated from `Usable` need a way to be initialized and later accessed. If using the HHDM after switching, the candidate root must include the required HHDM coverage with the intended permissions/cache type. The old root and its backing pages must remain intact during inspection/building; do not mutate the active root in place. See [`docs/architecture/memory.md:27-38`](docs/architecture/memory.md).
6. **The transition’s machine-mode assumptions:** use the active 4- or 5-level paging format; do not casually change LA57 while paging is enabled. NXE must actually be enabled before relying on NX. For read-only supervisor mappings to enforce the intended W^X policy, establish `CR0.WP`; current CPU reporting does not capture it. Current code records PCID/LA57-related information but not enough paging-control state to settle global-page/TLB-flush behavior. In particular, stale global translations or reuse of a PCID could undermine assumptions about the new root. See [`src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs:62-104`](src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs) and [`docs/architecture/memory.md:30-38`](docs/architecture/memory.md).
7. **Serial diagnostics:** COM1 itself uses port I/O and needs no MMIO mapping, but the kernel code/data needed to print transition or exception diagnostics still must be mapped. The project currently has no framebuffer mapping.

A new root should also avoid a writable HHDM alias of kernel text/rodata; the documented initial policy excludes the kernel image from the generic HHDM and uses RW/NX for ordinary RAM. The existing live Limine HHDM is documented as RWX, so do not infer that it already satisfies the future W^X policy.

## Small, implementable sequence

1. **Make transition prerequisites explicit and fail closed.** Require a valid decoded root and known address widths before any table access. Record or validate the active paging depth, NXE, `CR0.WP`, and the PCID/global-page/TLB policy. Retain the current PAT/MTRR gates: if active cache state cannot be validated, do not claim the intended effective mapping type.
2. **Add only a checked HHDM access path for owned frames.** Start with one allocated `Usable` frame: validate membership, full-page bounds, physical width, and checked HHDM arithmetic; initialize and read it back without touching CR3. Keep the unsafe boundary and the Limine trust premise explicit. Do not generalize this into a physical-memory accessor.
3. **Inspect the inherited tables read-only.** First validate root-page map membership; then walk only with a bounded, fail-closed walker using the active paging depth. Validate each table-frame address and entry encoding before following it. Account for present/absent entries and inherited large-page leaves; don’t assume the old hierarchy is 4 KiB-only. Use this to check the critical virtual ranges and their live permissions/cache selections, not to reclaim or modify old tables.
4. **Build a private candidate hierarchy from owned frames, without switching.** Keep ownership of every table frame explicit, use only supported leaf sizes, initialize frames before linking them, reject W+X, and make allocation/table-capacity failure transactional. Test that a software walk of the candidate yields exactly the requested mappings. Budget table-frame demand before attempting a large HHDM: mapping large RAM extents with 4 KiB pages can consume substantial memory.
5. **Verify the candidate’s policy and aliases.** Compare every critical mapping against the linker/boot inventory; check HHDM aliases for permission and cache-type conflicts, including PAT/MTRR boundaries. Preserve the documented rule that the kernel image has no writable direct-map alias.
6. **Treat any eventual CR3 switch as a separate, gated change.** Before it, prove that the candidate covers the kernel image, current stack/`BootInfo`, GDT/TSS/IDT and both exception stacks, all still-needed loader data, and the mappings used to access page tables and diagnostics. Define PCID/global-TLB handling and the pre-switch failure path. Keep the inherited root/backing pages intact until the new root has demonstrably taken over.

## Concrete tests to require

- **Host tests:** frame-to-HHDM arithmetic at aligned and unaligned region boundaries, overflow and noncanonical addresses, unknown physical width, and rejection of frames not owned by a `Usable` range. Test that invalid root/child locations and malformed table entries fail closed.
- **Frame/table ownership tests:** duplicate allocation authority is prevented or explicitly rejected; failed table creation or map insertion returns all newly allocated frames and leaves the candidate unchanged; unmapping does not free a table still referenced by another mapping; allocator exhaustion and metadata exhaustion preserve ownership/accounting.
- **Walker tests:** synthetic 4- and 5-level hierarchies; absent entries; 4 KiB and inherited large-page leaves; reserved bits and out-of-width physical addresses; shared/cyclic references and bounded-walk exhaustion.
- **Cache tests:** inspect actual PTE-selected PAT indices for each extent and detect incompatible aliases; verify MTRR transition handling and fail closed on unsupported/invalid cache state. The existing selector tests policy calculations, not live PTEs.
- **QEMU before any switch:** allocate a `Usable` frame, access it via the checked HHDM path, and verify write/read/zero behavior; inspect the inherited root read-only and compare critical mappings with the inventory.
- **QEMU after a separately approved switch:** confirm normal boot and shell/serial output; exercise read-only and NX permission faults with expected CR2/error bits; test mapping/unmapping, TLB behavior, and allocation rollback/reclamation. Also rerun the existing fatal exception smoke paths. `just verify` and `just fault-smoke` are the documented relevant workflows; neither alone proves physical-hardware behavior.

This was a read-only review; I did not edit files or run tests.

```rustix/src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs
    44	        None
```

```rustix/docs/architecture/memory.md
    11	`src/paging.rs` adds pure, host-tested 4 KiB mapping groundwork and decodes the inherited CR3 root address plus its low-bit interpretation. The CR3 decoder validates the physical-address width and reserved bits and interprets the low 12 bits according to the active `CR4.PCIDE` state; it does not dereference the root. The mapping-range validator requires a known physical-address width, checked aligned bounds, canonical virtual endpoints in one canonical half, and rejects writable-executable permissions. A validated range can encode the raw bits of one 4 KiB leaf PTE, including supervisor/user and write permissions, NX when the caller confirms EFER.NXE, and a bounded three-bit PAT index. `PatLayout` parses a supplied `IA32_PAT` value and selects WB, UC, or WC indices. `MtrrMemoryType`, `VariableMtrr`, `FixedMtrrRanges`, and `MtrrLayout` resolve MTRR types at one physical address, including fixed-range priority and defined variable-overlap rules; undefined overlaps fail closed. `MtrrRegisters::validated_layout` additionally validates captured capability/default-type reserved bits, register counts and fixed-range presence, WC support, and variable-mask shape/alignment before producing an owned `ValidatedMtrrLayout`. It supports contiguous power-of-two variable masks; Intel permits discontinuous masks on some CPUs, but Rustix rejects them explicitly as unsupported rather than approximating their coverage. The layout combines the address-specific MTRR type with a selected PAT entry according to Intel SDM Table 11-7, but only when `CR0.CD` and `CR0.NW` are clear. Host tests cover all 30 documented MTRR/PAT type pairs and reject invalid indexes, malformed snapshots, out-of-range addresses, and non-normal caching mode. A pure range selector now returns the lowest PAT index that produces one requested effective type throughout a nonempty, aligned physical range, checking fixed- and variable-MTRR transition boundaries rather than iterating every page. It rejects the range if no single index works throughout. `ValidatedMappingRange::select_cache_attributes` composes that selector with a validated mapping extent and returns range-bound PAT attributes; those attributes can encode each 4 KiB leaf in that extent without reselecting per page. This is still policy-only: it trusts the supplied PAT/MTRR and normal-caching state, does not inspect existing PTEs or cache aliases, and does not establish frame ownership. Boot reads CR0 without modifying it, validates supported captured MTRR/PAT state, and reports a diagnostic resolution at physical address zero using PAT index 0; this does not inspect the inherited PTE or assert that the live mapping uses that index. The raw MTRR capture remains bounded to 32 variable pairs and reports capacity overflow without partial state. Its footnotes distinguish UC selected by an MTRR from UC selected by a page-table entry (the latter involves cache snooping and aliasing concerns); they also identify combinations that older manual editions called undefined but current processors supporting both PAT and MTRRs resolve as shown. If the CPU does not report a physical width, the physical-bound check is skipped and no mapping caller may treat the bound as known. Rustix still does not dereference physical memory through the HHDM. Rustix-owned mappings should be non-executable by default; executable kernel text must be explicit.     19	## Mapping inventory before a CR3 transition
    20	
    21	The current runtime has several mappings that a future page-table transition must preserve. The address sources and remaining gaps are:
    22

The memory-map `ExecutableAndModules` entries remain illustrative, not an authoritative kernel-image extent.

Under the SysV entry convention the synthetic return slot occupies 8 bytes, so `RSP + 8` is the exclusive stack top. The protocol guarantees at least 64 KiB (without a Stack Size request); `BootInfo` records that minimum virtual span, translates it through the HHDM, and requires it to fit within a single `BootloaderReclaimable` physical region. The full loader allocation may be larger, and neither its exact bounds nor a guard page are known. Preserve the inherited mapping; do not infer a guard page.

Exception entry also requires the handler code and the TSS/IDT references to remain mapped. Preserve the complete relevant data/BSS pages and stack pages.

Response objects and the memory-map pointer array are bootloader-reclaimable; `capture_boot_information` copies the values used later, and the shell does not retain those pointers. Keep them mapped until the copy and validation finish; any later reclaim must be explicit rather than reclaiming the whole bootloader-reclaimable class.

    31	
    32	A first Rustix-owned x86_64 root should use 4 KiB pages only and require NX support; if NX is unavailable, abort before switching. Exclude the complete physical kernel-image span from the generic HHDM in the first implementation so no writable direct-map alias can undermine text or rodata permissions. Ordinary RAM HHDM mappings should be RW/NX and WB.

The boot report validates captured registers and computes a diagnostic effective type from the active PAT/MTRR values under normal caching. A separate pure selector can choose an index whose effective type remains uniform across an aligned physical range, but neither checks inherited PTEs nor detects cache-type aliases. The pure combination follows Intel SDM Table 11-7; it is not a generic rule for legacy PCD/PWT-only selection or model-specific combinations. Under Limine base revision 3 on x86_64, use PAT index 0 for WB, index 3 for UC, and index 5 for WC only after the target physical range and active PAT/MTRR interaction are verified.     37	
    38	Never modify Limine's active page tables in place. Build a separate candidate root from owned frames, leave the inherited root and its backing memory intact, and do not switch CR3 until every transition-critical mapping has been preserved and checked. Any pre-switch failure must discard the candidate root and return its frames without changing the active root. This policy is not yet implemented; Rustix does not inspect the inherited root or replace CR3.
    39	
    40	## Planned memory layers
    41	
    42	1. **Validated physical regions:** implemented as a fixed-capacity owned snapshot; allocator ownership and reclaim policy remain future work.

    44	3. **Kernel virtual memory:** Rustix still runs on inherited Limine page tables.      1	# Boot protocol and kernel entry
```
```rustix/docs/architecture/boot.md
     2	
     3	## Current boot contract
     4	
     5	Rustix currently expects a Limine-compatible x86_64 handoff. Limine is an external loader; it does not implement Rustix's kernel services. The kernel requests protocol base revision 3, the higher-half direct-map (HHDM) offset, the executable physical/virtual base addresses, and the memory map.
     6	
     7	Requests are kept in `.limine_requests_start`, `.limine_requests`, and `.limine_requests_end` by `linker.ld`. The response-bearing request records are mutable and the output `.limine_requests` section is placed in a writable load segment because Limine fills their response pointers before entering Rustix. The ELF entry symbol is `_start`.
     8	
     9	### Entry sequence
    10	
    11	1. Limine loads the ELF and transfers control to the assembly `_start` shim under the x86_64 Limine protocol. The shim captures the entry `RSP`, aligns the stack for a SysV call, and invokes `rustix_start`.
    12	2. `rustix_start` configures the legacy COM1 UART for polling output and input.
    13	3. The kernel disables maskable interrupts and installs its bootstrap GDT, TSS, and fatal-exception IDT. This does not initialize IRQ delivery.
    14	4. The kernel reads CR0 caching-control state, CPU address widths, active `CR4.PCIDE`, and raw CR3. It decodes CR3's physical root address and low-bit meaning against those CPU properties, without dereferencing the root. It reads EFER.NXE only when CPUID reports NX, `IA32_PAT` only when CPUID reports PAT, and MTRR registers only when CPUID reports MTRR support; these reads do not change CPU state. The MTRR snapshot is bounded to 32 variable pairs and reports an explicit capacity-exceeded state without retaining partial registers. It copies the HHDM, executable-address, and memory-map responses into an owned `BootInfo` snapshot, validates pointers against the active linear width, derives and validates the linker-defined kernel image span and its page-aligned text/rodata/data segment spans from Limine's executable bases, and derives the protocol-guaranteed minimum initial-stack span from the captured entry `RSP`. It validates physical bounds, stack HHDM arithmetic/coverage, and page-rounded HHDM arithmetic for protocol-mapped memory types. It then builds a frame allocator only from validated usable ranges and rejects malformed metadata before starting the shell.
    15	5. The kernel reports raw CR3 and its decoded physical root/low bits when the reported width permits, physical and virtual kernel-image spans, linker-defined text RX, rodata R/NX, and data RW/NX segment spans, minimum protocol-guaranteed stack span, validated memory ranges, frame counts, CPU features/address widths, NXE and normal-caching state, the active PAT value plus recognized WB/UC/WC indices, and a summary of captured MTRR state. It also reports whether the captured PAT/MTRR registers validate and a diagnostic effective type at physical address zero for PAT index 0; this is not a page-table inspection or a live mapping claim. It then seeds a volatile RAM filesystem and enters Crabshell on the serial console.
    16	6. The shell busy-polls COM1 because no scheduler or UART interrupt handler exists yet. The kernel does not return to the loader.
    17	
    18	The linker exports page-aligned virtual bounds for each of the kernel's three load segments. Boot validates their order, contiguity, coverage of the rounded image span, and derived physical ranges, then reports them with the permissions intended by `linker.ld`. Boot also decodes CR3's root physical address and active low-bit interpretation. These are validated linker/boot metadata only: Rustix does not inspect the inherited page tables, so it has not established that the segments are mapped or that their live permissions match the ELF flags.
    19	
    20	The memory-map snapshot stores physical regions as checked half-open ranges `[start, end)` and retains Limine's known classifications plus unknown type values. It does not authorize Rustix to access every region, reclaim loader memory, or mutate the current page tables. Rustix checks physical bounds and calculates canonical HHDM ranges for memory types covered by the requested base revision, but does not dereference physical memory through the HHDM or verify the inherited page tables. These metadata checks cannot prove that a Limine-provided non-null pointer is readable; that remains an explicit handoff trust boundary.
    21	
    22	## Link and target configuration
    23	
    24	- Rust target: `x86_64-unknown-none`
    25	- Linker script: `linker.ld`
    26	- Kernel virtual base: `0xffffffff80000000`
    27	- Required code-generation constraints: kernel code model, static relocation, and disabled red zone
    28	- Rust panic strategy: abort; the panic handler logs and halts
    29	
    30	See [`../development/building.md`](../development/building.md) for commands and toolchain setup.
    31	
    32	## Failure behavior and limitations
    33	
    34	Missing responses, bad pointers/alignment, invalid HHDM values, invalid image or segment bounds, invalid initial-stack spans, excessive counts, null entries, address arithmetic overflow, and invalid or overlapping physical ranges reject the complete boot snapshot. `_start` halts before starting Crabshell rather than continuing with partial memory metadata. Structural checks cannot establish that a non-null loader pointer is mapped and readable; that remains an explicit trust assumption of the Limine handoff. The installed exception handlers print fatal context and halt; no fault recovery or maskable IRQ delivery is provided. COM1 writes use a bounded polling loop so a non-responsive UART does not block forever.
    35	
    36	The repository includes a Limine v12.9.3 binary archive pin with SHA-256 verification, a hybrid ISO recipe, and a bounded QEMU serial smoke test that checks Crabshell's prompt. On 2026-10-16, `just verify` passed in WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 on both the working tree and a clean detached worktree with an empty `target` directory; the clean run fetched and built the pinned Limine host utility, created the image, and QEMU reported boot metadata before reaching the prompt. Milestone 0's local exit criteria are met. Hosted CI has not been observed. There is still no framebuffer console, reboot/shutdown interface, or broader boot-protocol compatibility test. The available serial and keyboard drivers do not imply a general device model.
    37	
    38	## Future boot work
    39	
    40	The kernel now snapshots and validates the Limine map and preserves firmware and loader-reclaimable classifications without reclaiming them. No region is considered Rustix-owned or free for allocation yet. Loader-reclaimable memory must remain unavailable until Rustix has copied any needed boot data and explicitly reaches a documented reclaim point; ACPI reclaimable memory needs the ACPI tables to be copied or parsed first. Frame allocation, page-table replacement, and ownership transfer remain future work.
```

```
//! Allocation-free validation for virtual addresses and physical memory maps.

/// Limine's memory-map type for ordinary usable RAM.
pub const MEMORY_MAP_USABLE: u64 = 0;
/// Maximum number of memory regions retained in the boot snapshot.
pub const MAX_MEMORY_REGIONS: usize = 256;
/// Minimum x86_64 initial stack size guaranteed by the Limine protocol.
pub const LIMINE_X86_64_MIN_STACK_SIZE: u64 = 64 * 1024;

/// Check whether an address is canonical for a sign-extended virtual width.
///
/// Widths outside `1..=64` are rejected. A 64-bit width accepts every address.
pub const fn is_canonical_virtual_address(address: u64, address_bits: u8) -> bool {
    if address_bits == 0 || address_bits > 64 {
        return false;
    }
    if address_bits == 64 {
        return true;
    }

    let sign_bit = (address >> (address_bits - 1)) & 1;
    let upper_bits = address >> address_bits;
    let expected_upper_bits = if sign_bit == 0 {
        0
    } else {
        u64::MAX >> address_bits
    };
    upper_bits == expected_upper_bits
}

/// Check that a non-empty half-open physical range fits an address width.
pub const fn physical_range_fits_address_width(start: u64, end: u64, address_bits: u8) -> bool {
    if start >= end || address_bits == 0 || address_bits > 64 {
        return false;
    }
    address_bits == 64 || end <= (1u64 << address_bits)
}

/// Return the physical end of the linker-defined kernel image span, if valid.
///
/// Limine reports the load bases while the linker supplies the virtual span.
/// This validates that both sources agree on the virtual base and that the
/// relocated half-open physical range fits the known address widths.
pub const fn kernel_image_physical_end(
    physical_base: u64,
    reported_virtual_base: u64,
    linked_virtual_start: u64,
    linked_virtual_end: u64,
    physical_bits: Option<u8>,
    virtual_bits: u8,
) -> Option<u64> {
    if linked_virtual_start != reported_virtual_base
        || linked_virtual_start >= linked_virtual_end
        || physical_base & 0xfff != 0
        || linked_virtual_start & 0xfff != 0
    {
        return None;
    }

    let virtual_last = linked_virtual_end - 1;
    if !is_canonical_virtual_address(linked_virtual_start, virtual_bits)
        || !is_canonical_virtual_address(virtual_last, virtual_bits)
    {
        return None;
    }
    let sign_bit = 1u64 << (virtual_bits - 1);
    if linked_virtual_start & sign_bit != virtual_last & sign_bit {
        return None;
    }

    let image_size = linked_virtual_end - linked_virtual_start;
    let Some(physical_end) = physical_base.checked_add(image_size) else {
        return None;
    };
    if let Some(bits) = physical_bits {
        if !physical_range_fits_address_width(physical_base, physical_end, bits) {
            return None;
        }
    }
    Some(physical_end)
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct KernelImageVirtualSegments {
    pub text: (u64, u64),
    pub rodata: (u64, u64),
    pub data: (u64, u64),
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct KernelImageSegment {
    pub virtual_start: u64,
    pub virtual_end: u64,
    pub physical_start: u64,
    pub physical_end: u64,
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct KernelImageSegments {
    pub text: KernelImageSegment,
    pub rodata: KernelImageSegment,
    pub data: KernelImageSegment,
}

/// Validate page-aligned PT_LOAD mapping spans and translate them to physical ranges.
///
/// The three spans must be contiguous, ordered text/rodata/data ranges that cover
/// the linker-defined image after rounding its final byte to a 4 KiB boundary.
/// This validates linker metadata; it does not prove that inherited page tables
/// map these ranges or that their backing frames are owned by Rustix.
pub const fn kernel_image_segments(
    physical_base: u64,
    reported_virtual_base: u64,
    image_virtual_start: u64,
    image_virtual_end: u64,
    virtual_segments: KernelImageVirtualSegments,
    physical_bits: Option<u8>,
    virtual_bits: u8,
) -> Option<KernelImageSegments> {
    let Some(_) = kernel_image_physical_end(
        physical_base,
        reported_virtual_base,
        image_virtual_start,
        image_virtual_end,
        physical_bits,
        virtual_bits,
    ) else {
        return None;
    };

    let (text_start, text_end) = virtual_segments.text;
    let (rodata_start, rodata_end) = virtual_segments.rodata;
    let (data_start, data_end) = virtual_segments.data;
    if text_start != image_virtual_start
        || text_start >= text_end
        || text_end != rodata_start
        || rodata_start >= rodata_end
        || rodata_end != data_start
        || data_start >= image_virtual_end
        || image_virtual_end > data_end
    {
        return None;
    }

    let Some(rounded_image_end) = image_virtual_end.checked_add(0xfff) else {
        return None;
    };
    let rounded_image_end = rounded_image_end & !0xfff;
    if data_end != rounded_image_end
        || text_start & 0xfff != 0
        || text_end & 0xfff != 0
        || rodata_start & 0xfff != 0
        || rodata_end & 0xfff != 0
        || data_start & 0xfff != 0
        || data_end & 0xfff != 0
    {
        return None;
    }

    let mapped_last_virtual = data_end - 1;
    if !is_canonical_virtual_address(image_virtual_start, virtual_bits)
        || !is_canonical_virtual_address(mapped_last_virtual, virtual_bits)
    {
        return None;
    }
    if virtual_bits < 64
        && ((image_virtual_start ^ mapped_last_virtual) & (1u64 << (virtual_bits - 1))) != 0
    {
        return None;
    }

    let Some(mapped_physical_end) = physical_base.checked_add(data_end - image_virtual_start)
    else {
        return None;
    };
    if let Some(bits) = physical_bits {
        if !physical_range_fits_address_width(physical_base, mapped_physical_end, bits) {
            return None;
        }
    }

    let Some(text_physical_start) = physical_base.checked_add(text_start - image_virtual_start)
    else {
        return None;
    };
    let Some(text_physical_end) = physical_base.checked_add(text_end - image_virtual_start) else {
        return None;
    };
    let Some(rodata_physical_start) = physical_base.checked_add(rodata_start - image_virtual_start)
    else {
        return None;
    };
    let Some(rodata_physical_end) = physical_base.checked_add(rodata_end - image_virtual_start)
    else {
        return None;
    };
    let Some(data_physical_start) = physical_base.checked_add(data_start - image_virtual_start)
    else {
        return None;
    };

    Some(KernelImageSegments {
        text: KernelImageSegment {
            virtual_start: text_start,
            virtual_end: text_end,
            physical_start: text_physical_start,
            physical_end: text_physical_end,
        },
        rodata: KernelImageSegment {
            virtual_start: rodata_start,
            virtual_end: rodata_end,
            physical_start: rodata_physical_start,
            physical_end: rodata_physical_end,
        },
        data: KernelImageSegment {
            virtual_start: data_start,
            virtual_end: data_end,
            physical_start: data_physical_start,
            physical_end: mapped_physical_end,
        },
    })
}

/// Derive Limine's protocol-guaranteed minimum initial x86_64 stack span.
///
/// The SysV entry stack has an 8-byte return-address slot, so `entry_rsp + 8`
/// is the exclusive top. The function returns the 64 KiB minimum span below it.
pub const fn limine_x86_64_stack_bounds(entry_rsp: u64, virtual_bits: u8) -> Option<(u64, u64)> {
    if entry_rsp & 0xf != 8 {
        return None;
    }
    let Some(stack_end) = entry_rsp.checked_add(8) else {
        return None;
    };
    let Some(stack_start) = stack_end.checked_sub(LIMINE_X86_64_MIN_STACK_SIZE) else {
        return None;
    };
    let stack_last = stack_end - 1;
    if !is_canonical_virtual_address(stack_start, virtual_bits)
        || !is_canonical_virtual_address(stack_last, virtual_bits)
    {
        return None;
    }
    let sign_bit = 1u64 << (virtual_bits - 1);
    if stack_start & sign_bit != stack_last & sign_bit {
        return None;
    }
    Some((stack_start, stack_end))
}

/// Validate the page-rounded HHDM span for one Limine base-revision-3 region.
///
/// `physical_bits` is `None` only when CPUID does not report the width. This
/// checks arithmetic and canonicality, not whether the inherited page tables
/// actually contain the mapping.
pub const fn limine_v3_hhdm_range_is_valid(
    offset: u64,
    physical_start: u64,
    physical_end: u64,
    physical_bits: Option<u8>,
    virtual_bits: u8,
) -> bool {
    const PAGE_SIZE: u64 = 4096;
    const PAGE_MASK: u64 = !(PAGE_SIZE - 1);

    if physical_start >= physical_end
        || offset & (PAGE_SIZE - 1) != 0
        || (virtual_bits != 48 && virtual_bits != 57)
        || !is_canonical_virtual_address(offset, virtual_bits)
    {
        return false;
    }
    if let Some(bits) = physical_bits {
        if !physical_range_fits_address_width(physical_start, physical_end, bits) {
            return false;
        }
    }

    let mapped_start = physical_start & PAGE_MASK;
    let Some(rounded_end) = physical_end.checked_add(PAGE_SIZE - 1) else {
        return false;
    };
    let mapped_end = rounded_end & PAGE_MASK;
    if mapped_start >= mapped_end {
        return false;
    }
    if let Some(bits) = physical_bits {
        if !physical_range_fits_address_width(mapped_start, mapped_end, bits) {
            return false;
        }
    }

    let Some(virtual_start) = offset.checked_add(mapped_start) else {
        return false;
    };
    let Some(virtual_last) = offset.checked_add(mapped_end - 1) else {
        return false;
    };
    if !is_canonical_virtual_address(virtual_start, virtual_bits)
        || !is_canonical_virtual_address(virtual_last, virtual_bits)
    {
        return false;
    }

    let sign_bit = 1u64 << (virtual_bits - 1);
    virtual_start & sign_bit == virtual_last & sign_bit
}

/// Classification of a physical memory region from the Limine memory map.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum RegionKind {
    Usable,
    Reserved,
    AcpiReclaimable,
    AcpiNvs,
    BadMemory,
    BootloaderReclaimable,
    ExecutableAndModules,
    Framebuffer,
    Unknown(u64),
}

impl RegionKind {
    /// Whether Limine base revision 3 includes this type in the HHDM.
    pub const fn is_mapped_by_limine_v3_hhdm(self) -> bool {
        matches!(
            self,
            Self::Usable
                | Self::BootloaderReclaimable
                | Self::ExecutableAndModules
                | Self::Framebuffer
        )
    }

    const fn from_limine(kind: u64) -> Self {
        match kind {
            0 => Self::Usable,
            1 => Self::Reserved,
            2 => Self::AcpiReclaimable,
            3 => Self::AcpiNvs,
            4 => Self::BadMemory,
            5 => Self::BootloaderReclaimable,
            6 => Self::ExecutableAndModules,
            7 => Self::Framebuffer,
            unknown => Self::Unknown(unknown),
        }
    }
}

/// Unvalidated region fields copied from a boot protocol response.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct RawMemoryRegion {
    pub base: u64,
    pub length: u64,
    pub kind: u64,
}

/// Validated half-open physical address range `[start, end)`.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct PhysicalRegion {
    start: u64,
    end: u64,
    kind: RegionKind,
}

impl PhysicalRegion {
    const EMPTY: Self = Self {
        start: 0,
        end: 0,
        kind: RegionKind::Unknown(0),
    };

    pub const fn start(&self) -> u64 {
        self.start
    }

    pub const fn end(&self) -> u64 {
        self.end
    }

    pub const fn length(&self) -> u64 {
        self.end - self.start
    }

    pub const fn kind(&self) -> RegionKind {
        self.kind
    }
}

/// Errors produced when a memory map is malformed or exceeds kernel capacity.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum MemoryMapError {
    EmptyMap,
    TooManyRegions,
    EmptyRegion { index: usize },
    AddressOverflow { index: usize },
    OverlappingRegions { first: usize, second: usize },
    UsableTotalOverflow,
}

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum HhdmAddressError {
    UnknownPhysicalAddressWidth,
    EmptyRange,
    UnalignedRange,
    AddressOverflow,
    NotUsable,
    InvalidHhdmRange,
}

/// Validated, allocation-free snapshot of the physical memory map.
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct MemoryMap {
    regions: [PhysicalRegion; MAX_MEMORY_REGIONS],
    region_count: usize,
    usable_bytes: u64,
}

impl MemoryMap {
    const EMPTY: Self = Self {
        regions: [PhysicalRegion::EMPTY; MAX_MEMORY_REGIONS],
        region_count: 0,
        usable_bytes: 0,
    };

    pub fn from_raw(regions: &[RawMemoryRegion]) -> Result<Self, MemoryMapError> {
        let mut builder = MemoryMapBuilder::new();
        for region in regions {
            builder.push(region.base, region.length, region.kind)?;
        }
        builder.finish()
    }

    pub fn regions(&self) -> &[PhysicalRegion] {
        &self.regions[..self.region_count]
    }

    pub fn range_is_within_region_kind(&self, start: u64, end: u64, kind: RegionKind) -> bool {
        start < end
            && self
                .regions()
                .iter()
                .any(|region| region.start <= start && end <= region.end && region.kind == kind)
    }

    /// Calculate the Limine base-revision-3 HHDM address of a page-aligned
    /// extent wholly contained in one validated `Usable` region.
    ///
    /// This validates metadata and relies on the Limine handoff contract for the
    /// actual mapping; it does not inspect inherited page tables or make the
    /// returned integer safe to dereference by itself.
    pub fn usable_hhdm_address(
        &self,
        hhdm_offset: u64,
        physical_start: u64,
        length: u64,
        physical_address_bits: Option<u8>,
        virtual_address_bits: u8,
    ) -> Result<u64, HhdmAddressError> {
        const PAGE_SIZE: u64 = 4096;

        let physical_address_bits =
            physical_address_bits.ok_or(HhdmAddressError::UnknownPhysicalAddressWidth)?;
        if length == 0 {
            return Err(HhdmAddressError::EmptyRange);
        }
        if (physical_start | length) & (PAGE_SIZE - 1) != 0 {
            return Err(HhdmAddressError::UnalignedRange);
        }
        let physical_end = physical_start
            .checked_add(length)
            .ok_or(HhdmAddressError::AddressOverflow)?;
        if !self.range_is_within_region_kind(physical_start, physical_end, RegionKind::Usable) {
            return Err(HhdmAddressError::NotUsable);
        }
        if !limine_v3_hhdm_range_is_valid(
            hhdm_offset,
            physical_start,
            physical_end,
            Some(physical_address_bits),
            virtual_address_bits,
        ) {
            return Err(HhdmAddressError::InvalidHhdmRange);
        }
        hhdm_offset
            .checked_add(physical_start)
            .ok_or(HhdmAddressError::InvalidHhdmRange)
    }

    pub const fn usable_bytes(&self) -> u64 {
        self.usable_bytes
    }
}

/// Incremental validator used to copy loader entries without an intermediate heap.
pub struct MemoryMapBuilder {
    map: MemoryMap,
}

impl MemoryMapBuilder {
    pub const fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            map: MemoryMap::EMPTY,
        }
    }

    pub fn push(&mut self, base: u64, length: u64, raw_kind: u64) -> Result<(), MemoryMapError> {
        let index = self.map.region_count;
        if index == MAX_MEMORY_REGIONS {
            return Err(MemoryMapError::TooManyRegions);
        }
        if length == 0 {
            return Err(MemoryMapError::EmptyRegion { index });
        }
        let end = base
            .checked_add(length)
            .ok_or(MemoryMapError::AddressOverflow { index })?;
        let kind = RegionKind::from_limine(raw_kind);

        for (other_index, other) in self.map.regions().iter().enumerate() {
            if base < other.end && other.start < end {
                return Err(MemoryMapError::OverlappingRegions {
                    first: other_index,
                    second: index,
                });
            }
        }

        let usable_bytes = if kind == RegionKind::Usable {
            self.map
                .usable_bytes
                .checked_add(length)
                .ok_or(MemoryMapError::UsableTotalOverflow)?
        } else {
            self.map.usable_bytes
        };

        self.map.regions[index] = PhysicalRegion {
            start: base,
            end,
            kind,
        };
        self.map.region_count += 1;
        self.map.usable_bytes = usable_bytes;
        Ok(())
    }

    pub fn finish(self) -> Result<MemoryMap, MemoryMapError> {
        if self.map.region_count == 0 {
            Err(MemoryMapError::EmptyMap)
        } else {
            Ok(self.map)
        }
    }
}

impl Default for MemoryMapBuilder {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self::new()
    }
}

/// Add an already-validated usable region length to a running total.
///
/// Non-usable regions leave the total unchanged. `None` signals arithmetic
/// overflow so callers can report malformed or unrepresentable maps.
pub const fn add_usable_bytes(total: u64, region_kind: u64, region_length: u64) -> Option<u64> {
    if region_kind == MEMORY_MAP_USABLE {
        total.checked_add(region_length)
    } else {
        Some(total)
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use core::assert_eq;

    use super::{
        add_usable_bytes, is_canonical_virtual_address, kernel_image_physical_end,
        kernel_image_segments, limine_v3_hhdm_range_is_valid, limine_x86_64_stack_bounds,
        physical_range_fits_address_width, HhdmAddressError, KernelImageSegment,
        KernelImageSegments, KernelImageVirtualSegments, MemoryMap, MemoryMapBuilder,
        MemoryMapError, RawMemoryRegion, RegionKind, MAX_MEMORY_REGIONS, MEMORY_MAP_USABLE,
    };

    #[test]
    fn canonical_virtual_addresses_follow_the_selected_width() {
        assert!(is_canonical_virtual_address(0x0000_7fff_ffff_ffff, 48));
        assert!(!is_canonical_virtual_address(0x0000_8000_0000_0000, 48));
        assert!(is_canonical_virtual_address(0xffff_8000_0000_0000, 48));
        assert!(!is_canonical_virtual_address(0xffff_7fff_ffff_ffff, 48));

        assert!(is_canonical_virtual_address(0x00ff_ffff_ffff_ffff, 57));
        assert!(!is_canonical_virtual_address(0x0100_0000_0000_0000, 57));
        assert!(is_canonical_virtual_address(0xff00_0000_0000_0000, 57));
        assert!(!is_canonical_virtual_address(0xfeff_ffff_ffff_ffff, 57));
        assert!(!is_canonical_virtual_address(0, 0));
        assert!(!is_canonical_virtual_address(0, 65));
    }

    #[test]
    fn physical_ranges_fit_the_reported_address_width() {
        assert!(physical_range_fits_address_width(0x1000, 1 << 40, 40));
        assert!(!physical_range_fits_address_width(
            0x1000,
            (1 << 40) + 1,
            40
        ));
        assert!(!physical_range_fits_address_width(1, 1, 40));
        assert!(!physical_range_fits_address_width(0, 1, 0));
        assert!(!physical_range_fits_address_width(0, 1, 65));
        assert!(physical_range_fits_address_width(
            u64::MAX - 1,
            u64::MAX,
            64
        ));
    }

    #[test]
    fn relocates_and_validates_the_linker_defined_kernel_image_span() {
        let virtual_base = 0xffff_ffff_8000_0000;
        let virtual_end = 0xffff_ffff_8002_5050;
        assert_eq!(
            kernel_image_physical_end(
                0x0fee_3000,
                virtual_base,
                virtual_base,
                virtual_end,
                Some(40),
                48,
            ),
            Some(0x0ff0_8050)
        );
        assert_eq!(
            kernel_image_physical_end(
                0x1000,
                virtual_base + 0x1000,
                virtual_base,
                virtual_end,
                Some(40),
                48,
            ),
            None
        );
        assert_eq!(
            kernel_image_physical_end(0x1000, virtual_base, virtual_base, virtual_base, None, 48),
            None
        );
        assert_eq!(
            kernel_image_physical_end(
                0xffff_ffff_ffff_f000,
                virtual_base,
                virtual_base,
                virtual_base + 0x2000,
                None,
                48,
            ),
            None
        );
        assert_eq!(
            kernel_image_physical_end(
                0x1001,
                virtual_base,
                virtual_base,
                virtual_base + 0x1000,
                None,
                48,
            ),
            None
        );
        assert_eq!(
            kernel_image_physical_end(
                (1 << 40) - 0x1000,
                virtual_base,
                virtual_base,
                virtual_base + 0x2000,
                Some(40),
                48,
            ),
            None
        );
        assert_eq!(
            kernel_image_physical_end(
                0x1000,
                0x0000_7fff_ffff_f000,
                0x0000_7fff_ffff_f000,
                0xffff_8000_0000_1000,
                None,
                48,
            ),
            None
        );
    }

    #[test]
    fn validates_and_relocates_page_aligned_kernel_load_segments() {
        let virtual_start = 0xffff_ffff_8000_0000;
        let virtual_end = 0xffff_ffff_8000_5050;
        let segments = kernel_image_segments(
            0x20_0000,
            virtual_start,
            virtual_start,
            virtual_end,
            KernelImageVirtualSegments {
                text: (virtual_start, virtual_start + 0x2000),
                rodata: (virtual_start + 0x2000, virtual_start + 0x4000),
                data: (virtual_start + 0x4000, virtual_start + 0x6000),
            },
            Some(40),
            48,
        )
        .unwrap();

        assert_eq!(
            segments,
            KernelImageSegments {
                text: KernelImageSegment {
                    virtual_start,
                    virtual_end: virtual_start + 0x2000,
                    physical_start: 0x20_0000,
                    physical_end: 0x20_2000,
                },
                rodata: KernelImageSegment {
                    virtual_start: virtual_start + 0x2000,
                    virtual_end: virtual_start + 0x4000,
                    physical_start: 0x20_2000,
                    physical_end: 0x20_4000,
                },
                data: KernelImageSegment {
                    virtual_start: virtual_start + 0x4000,
                    virtual_end: virtual_start + 0x6000,
                    physical_start: 0x20_4000,
                    physical_end: 0x20_6000,
                },
            }
        );
    }

    #[test]
    fn rejects_invalid_page_aligned_kernel_load_segments() {
        let virtual_start = 0xffff_ffff_8000_0000;
        let virtual_end = virtual_start + 0x5050;
        let valid = KernelImageVirtualSegments {
            text: (virtual_start, virtual_start + 0x2000),
            rodata: (virtual_start + 0x2000, virtual_start + 0x4000),
            data: (virtual_start + 0x4000, virtual_start + 0x6000),
        };
        assert_eq!(
            kernel_image_segments(
                0x20_0000,
                virtual_start,
                virtual_start,
                virtual_end,
                KernelImageVirtualSegments {
                    rodata: (virtual_start + 0x3000, virtual_start + 0x4000),
                    ..valid
                },
                Some(40),
                48,
            ),
            None
        );
        assert_eq!(
            kernel_image_segments(
                0x20_0000,
                virtual_start,
                virtual_start,
                virtual_end,
                KernelImageVirtualSegments {
                    text: (virtual_start, virtual_start + 0x2001),
                    rodata: (virtual_start + 0x2001, virtual_start + 0x4000),
                    ..valid
                },
                Some(40),
                48,
            ),
            None
        );
        assert_eq!(
            kernel_image_segments(
                0x20_0000,
                virtual_start,
                virtual_start,
                virtual_end,
                KernelImageVirtualSegments {
                    data: (virtual_start + 0x4000, virtual_start + 0x5000),
                    ..valid
                },
                Some(40),
                48,
            ),
            None
        );
    }

    #[test]
    fn derives_protocol_guaranteed_initial_stack_bounds() {
        let entry_rsp = 0xffff_8000_0001_fff8;
        assert_eq!(
            limine_x86_64_stack_bounds(entry_rsp, 48),
            Some((0xffff_8000_0001_0000, 0xffff_8000_0002_0000))
        );
        assert_eq!(
            limine_x86_64_stack_bounds(0x0000_7fff_ffff_fff8, 48),
            Some((0x0000_7fff_ffff_0000, 0x0000_8000_0000_0000))
        );
        assert_eq!(
            limine_x86_64_stack_bounds(entry_rsp, 57),
            Some((0xffff_8000_0001_0000, 0xffff_8000_0002_0000))
        );
        assert_eq!(limine_x86_64_stack_bounds(entry_rsp & !0xf, 48), None);
        assert_eq!(limine_x86_64_stack_bounds(u64::MAX - 7, 64), None);
        assert_eq!(limine_x86_64_stack_bounds(0x0000_8000_0000_0008, 48), None);
        assert_eq!(
            limine_x86_64_stack_bounds(0x10008, 48),
            Some((0x10, 0x10010))
        );
    }

    #[test]
    fn validates_page_rounded_limine_hhdm_ranges_without_accessing_them() {
        let offset = 0xffff_8000_0000_0000;
        assert!(limine_v3_hhdm_range_is_valid(
            offset,
            0x1234,
            0x2345,
            Some(40),
            48
        ));
        assert!(limine_v3_hhdm_range_is_valid(
            offset, 0x1234, 0x2345, None, 48
        ));
        assert!(!limine_v3_hhdm_range_is_valid(
            offset,
            0x1234,
            (1 << 40) + 1,
            Some(40),
            48
        ));
        assert!(!limine_v3_hhdm_range_is_valid(
            u64::MAX - 0x0fff,
            0x1000,
            0x2000,
            None,
            48
        ));
        assert!(!limine_v3_hhdm_range_is_valid(
            0x0000_8000_0000_0000,
            0x1000,
            0x2000,
            None,
            48
        ));
        assert!(!limine_v3_hhdm_range_is_valid(
            0,
            0x0000_7fff_ffff_f000,
            0x0000_8000_0000_1000,
            Some(64),
            48
        ));
        assert!(!limine_v3_hhdm_range_is_valid(
            offset, 0x1000, 0x2000, None, 46
        ));
    }

    #[test]
    fn calculates_usable_hhdm_addresses_only_for_validated_owned_ranges() {
        let map = MemoryMap::from_raw(&[
            RawMemoryRegion {
                base: 0x10_0000,
                length: 0x3000,
                kind: 0,
            },
            RawMemoryRegion {
                base: 0x10_3000,
                length: 0x1000,
                kind: 1,
            },
        ])
        .unwrap();
        let offset = 0xffff_8000_0000_0000;

        assert_eq!(
            map.usable_hhdm_address(offset, 0x10_1000, 0x1000, Some(40), 48),
            Ok(offset + 0x10_1000)
        );
        assert_eq!(
            map.usable_hhdm_address(offset, 0x10_3000, 0x1000, Some(40), 48),
            Err(HhdmAddressError::NotUsable)
        );
        assert_eq!(
            map.usable_hhdm_address(offset, 0x10_0001, 0x1000, Some(40), 48),
            Err(HhdmAddressError::UnalignedRange)
        );
        assert_eq!(
            map.usable_hhdm_address(offset, 0x10_0000, 0, Some(40), 48),
            Err(HhdmAddressError::EmptyRange)
        );
        assert_eq!(
            map.usable_hhdm_address(offset, 0x10_0000, 0x1000, None, 48),
            Err(HhdmAddressError::UnknownPhysicalAddressWidth)
        );
        assert_eq!(
            map.usable_hhdm_address(offset, u64::MAX & !0xfff, 0x1000, Some(64), 48),
            Err(HhdmAddressError::AddressOverflow)
        );
        assert_eq!(
            map.usable_hhdm_address(0x0000_8000_0000_0000, 0x10_0000, 0x1000, Some(40), 48),
            Err(HhdmAddressError::InvalidHhdmRange)
        );
    }

    #[test]
    fn classifies_limine_v3_hhdm_region_types() {
        assert!(RegionKind::Usable.is_mapped_by_limine_v3_hhdm());
        assert!(RegionKind::BootloaderReclaimable.is_mapped_by_limine_v3_hhdm());
        assert!(RegionKind::ExecutableAndModules.is_mapped_by_limine_v3_hhdm());
        assert!(RegionKind::Framebuffer.is_mapped_by_limine_v3_hhdm());
        assert!(!RegionKind::Reserved.is_mapped_by_limine_v3_hhdm());
        assert!(!RegionKind::AcpiReclaimable.is_mapped_by_limine_v3_hhdm());
        assert!(!RegionKind::AcpiNvs.is_mapped_by_limine_v3_hhdm());
        assert!(!RegionKind::BadMemory.is_mapped_by_limine_v3_hhdm());
        assert!(!RegionKind::Unknown(99).is_mapped_by_limine_v3_hhdm());
    }

    #[test]
    fn counts_only_usable_regions() {
        assert_eq!(add_usable_bytes(4096, MEMORY_MAP_USABLE, 2048), Some(6144));
        assert_eq!(add_usable_bytes(4096, 1, 2048), Some(4096));
    }

    #[test]
    fn reports_total_overflow() {
        assert_eq!(add_usable_bytes(u64::MAX - 4, MEMORY_MAP_USABLE, 8), None);
    }

    #[test]

        }

            Err(MemoryMapError::TooManyRegions)
        );
    }
```
