## Milestone 3 — IRQs, time, and kernel scheduling

Do not enable interrupts as a side effect of installing exception gates. IRQ delivery needs its own controller, acknowledgement, masking, ownership, and synchronization design.

### Planned work

- [ ] Select and document the initial interrupt controller policy for QEMU and target hardware (for example, legacy PIC compatibility versus local I/O APIC; do not enable both accidentally).
- [ ] Add IRQ vector allocation, controller masking/unmasking, end-of-interrupt acknowledgement, spurious-interrupt handling, and a policy for unexpected IRQs.
- [ ] Add a calibrated/verified timer source and monotonic timekeeping; test interval arithmetic and drift assumptions.
- [ ] Establish interrupt-safe lock primitives and rules for code callable from normal, exception, and IRQ contexts. No allocator or blocking console operation may run in an unsafe interrupt context.
- [ ] Add a minimal kernel-thread context and lifecycle model, stack ownership/guard policy, context-switch tests, and emulator scheduling tests.
- [ ] Add preemption only after lock, stack, timer, and interrupt-return invariants have deterministic tests.
- [ ] Keep application-processor startup/SMP as a separate sub-milestone after per-CPU state, TLB invalidation, and lock semantics exist.

**Exit criteria:** tested IRQ acknowledgement and timer behavior, deterministic thread lifecycle/context-switch tests, and bounded QEMU tests under repeated timer interrupts. No `sti` before the design and tests are ready.

---

## Milestone 4 — isolated processes and syscall ABI

Userspace begins only after page tables, exception handling, scheduling, and controlled memory allocation are trustworthy. The syscall ABI is a product interface and must not emerge accidentally from internal functions.

### Planned work

- [ ] Decide and document the x86_64 user-entry/syscall mechanism, register convention, selector/MSR setup, per-CPU state requirements, and safe return path.
- [ ] Add user/kernel page permissions and process-owned address spaces, including teardown and TLB invalidation rules.
- [ ] Implement copy-in/copy-out helpers that validate lengths, arithmetic, canonical ranges, permissions, and faults; never form a kernel reference directly from a user pointer.
- [ ] Specify version discovery, stable syscall numbers, argument layouts, error encoding, partial-I/O behavior, interruption/restart, and compatibility policy before exposing calls.
- [ ] Add initial process lifecycle and descriptor-table semantics: create/load, exit, wait, close, duplication/inheritance, and process cleanup.
- [ ] Load a deliberately small documented executable format with bounds/segment/permission checks; reject malformed binaries safely.
- [ ] Build adversarial tests for bad pointers, overflow, invalid mappings, process teardown, descriptor misuse, and failed exec.

### First user-visible target

A small controlled `init` process should start from a reproducible image, write through a descriptor, exit with a status, and be waited on by a kernel test harness. Do not claim userspace or process isolation from ring-0 tasks that merely use process-shaped structs.

**Exit criteria:** an isolated init process runs in user mode and uses a versioned, documented syscall subset; invalid user pointers and process teardown are tested without corrupting the kernel.

---

## Milestone 5 — VFS, storage, and device ownership

Keep the current RAM filesystem as a bootstrap/test implementation. Persistence and device drivers require explicit block ownership, error handling, and recovery behavior.

### Planned work

- [ ] Define VFS node, mount, path, metadata, and file-descriptor contracts independently of a particular disk format.
- [ ] Preserve volatile RAMFS as a test backend and add tests for mount/path errors, capacity, partial I/O, and object lifetime.
- [ ] Add a narrowly scoped block-device interface with request validation, timeout/error reporting, and a QEMU-supported initial device driver (such as virtio-blk after PCI discovery is ready).
- [ ] Choose and document the first on-disk filesystem format. Specify partition discovery, byte order, block size, metadata limits, corruption handling, and read-only/recovery behavior before writable support.
- [ ] Add persistent write/read/remount/reboot integration tests; never claim persistence from an in-memory cache alone.
- [ ] Add a driver ownership and DMA policy before any device can write into arbitrary kernel memory.
- [ ] Define file descriptors and basic process I/O semantics before exposing them to applications.

**Exit criteria:** a reproducible image mounts a documented on-disk filesystem, user-visible tools can create/read files across reboot, and corruption/I/O errors fail safely.

---

## Milestone 6 — initial userspace and command-line utilities

Crabshell is currently an in-kernel parser/frontend. The long-term terminal application should reuse its parser model without linking kernel internals or bypassing syscalls.

### Planned work

- [ ] Start a user-mode `init` process and establish executable search, environment, current directory, descriptor inheritance, and process startup rules.
- [ ] Port or adapt Crabshell into a userspace terminal application that uses only the documented syscall/VFS interfaces.
- [ ] Add a small utility set with explicit scope: file listing, text output, create/remove/copy/move, and system information.
- [ ] Add command-line quoting, escaping, history, redirection, and pipelines only with parser tests and process/descriptor/pipe semantics to support them.
- [ ] Add integration tests that launch tools from the filesystem image and exercise them through syscalls; keep unsupported features explicit.

**Exit criteria:** shell and basic tools run as isolated user processes from a reproducible image; no shell command directly calls kernel-private VFS internals.

---

## Milestone 7 — graphical console and GUI (long-term)

A GUI is intentionally downstream of stable memory management, interrupts/input, process isolation, drivers, and userspace. Keep Crabshell's parser independent so a graphical terminal frontend can reuse it.

### Planned work

- [ ] Add validated framebuffer discovery and memory ownership; implement a minimal text/graphics console without compromising serial panic diagnostics.
- [ ] Establish an input subsystem that separates raw device events from key mapping and terminal policy. Plan PS/2 and USB HID support separately; do not treat the current raw scancode poller as a keyboard driver stack.
- [ ] Define a graphics buffer ownership/presentation API, clipping rules, pixel format, and bounds/overflow checks.
- [ ] Implement a minimal compositor/windowing policy only after process isolation and input routing are ready.
- [ ] Run Crabshell as a terminal application in a GUI window using the same parser and userspace services as the serial/TTY path.
- [ ] Preserve serial as a headless recovery/debug console and add repeatable QEMU display/input tests.

**Exit criteria:** a documented GUI session starts from userspace, renders a terminal, accepts tested input, and does not require direct kernel-private VFS access.

---

## Milestone 8 — networking (long-term, after drivers and process isolation)

Networking is not implied by the current device drivers. The initial target should be a tightly scoped virtual-device path with clear ownership and bounded buffers.

### Planned work

- [ ] Complete PCI/device discovery and define DMA buffer ownership, address translation, cache synchronization, and reset/error behavior.
- [ ] Implement one virtual NIC driver with bounded queues and timeouts; test against QEMU user networking.
- [ ] Choose and document a minimal link/network protocol scope before implementation. Keep packet parsing length-checked and fuzzable on the host.
- [ ] Add interface configuration, routing, socket/descriptor ownership, and per-process access policy.
- [ ] Add adversarial packet tests and integration tests for link loss, malformed packets, queue exhaustion, and device reset.
- [ ] Add higher-level transports/services only when the required protocol semantics, entropy source, and security model are designed.

**Exit criteria:** documented user processes can communicate through a tested virtual NIC/network stack, with malformed input and resource exhaustion handled safely. Do not claim internet, TLS, or POSIX sockets merely from a packet driver.

---

## Cross-cutting acceptance gates

Every milestone should include the relevant subset of these gates:

1. **Design:** documented ownership, invariants, resource limits, error semantics, and unsupported cases.
2. **Tests:** host tests for pure policy and malformed/boundary input; integration tests for hardware-facing behavior.
3. **Safety:** review unsafe blocks, pointer provenance/access, integer overflow, privilege boundaries, concurrency, and cleanup/rollback paths.
4. **Build:** format, host tests, target check, and final ELF link as appropriate.
5. **Boot/integration:** QEMU tests for changes to boot, paging, descriptors, interrupts, drivers, processes, or persistence.
6. **Documentation/status:** update architecture and roadmap docs; never check off a criterion without evidence.
7. **Compatibility:** claim Unix/POSIX behavior only for the exact documented subset with conformance-style tests.

## Working rule

Prefer a small end-to-end vertical slice over broad, unbootable scaffolding. A source file, interface, or architecture document is not proof that the corresponding subsystem is operational. When a check cannot run, record the exact environment blocker and leave that acceptance gate pending.

# Rustix roadmap

This roadmap describes an incremental path from the current bare-metal kernel to a useful Unix-like operating system. It is a dependency plan, not a schedule or a claim of compatibility. Features become current only after the implementation, tests, and exit criteria below agree.

## How to read status

- A checked box means the source/design work exists; it does **not** imply the code compiled, linked, booted, or passed an integration test.
- A milestone is not complete until its stated exit criteria are met and the evidence is recorded.
- Hardware work needs target build and emulator evidence. Host tests cannot validate privileged instructions, bootloader pointers, page tables, device I/O, or exception-entry assembly.
- Future work is intentionally not represented by placeholder APIs or dummy implementations.

## Current status

- **Milestone 0: local exit criteria met from a clean detached worktree; hosted CI pending.** On 2026-10-16, `just verify` passed in WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 from both the working tree and a clean detached worktree with an empty `target` directory. The clean run downloaded and compiled the pinned Limine host utility, formatted and tested the workspace, checked and built the target, created the image, and passed the 20-second QEMU prompt smoke test. Hosted CI has not been observed.
- **Milestone 1: validation criteria met for the current Limine path.** The bounded boot snapshot, memory-range classification, and CPUID reporting were covered by host tests and QEMU reporting; the Limine pointer-readability trust boundary remains explicit.
- **Milestone 2: in progress, not complete.** The boot path owns and activates a clone of Limine's reachable page-table hierarchy, preserves inherited mappings, hardens kernel HHDM aliases to R/NX or RW/NX while retaining PAT attributes, and retains table-frame tokens. QEMU has exercised the 256 KiB requested stack, active CR3 transition, fixed BSS heap alignment/reuse/exhaustion, frame probes, and fatal exception diagnostics. The bounded heap does not grow from frames; broad mapping policy, reclamation, IRQ-safe allocation, and physical-hardware validation remain outstanding.
- **Milestones 3 and later: planned.** There is no general IRQ system, scheduler, userspace, syscall ABI, persistent filesystem, GUI, or networking stack.

## Dependency path

```text
Reliable boot
    -> validated boot state
    -> owned mappings + frame allocation + heap + fault diagnostics
    -> timer/IRQ model + scheduler
    -> isolated processes + syscall ABI
    -> VFS/storage + userland utilities
    -> graphical terminal and other optional services
```

Some device-driver work can proceed in parallel after the core ownership, locking, and testing rules exist. It must not bypass them with direct, unreviewed hardware access.

## Milestone 3 — IRQs, time, and kernel scheduling

Do not enable interrupts as a side effect of installing exception gates. IRQ delivery needs its own controller, acknowledgement, masking, ownership, and synchronization design.

### Planned work

- [ ] Select and document the initial interrupt controller policy for QEMU and target hardware (for example, legacy PIC compatibility versus local I/O APIC; do not enable both accidentally).
- [ ] Add IRQ vector allocation, controller masking/unmasking, end-of-interrupt acknowledgement, spurious-interrupt handling, and a policy for unexpected IRQs.
- [ ] Add a calibrated/verified timer source and monotonic timekeeping; test interval arithmetic and drift assumptions.
- [ ] Establish interrupt-safe lock primitives and rules for code callable from normal, exception, and IRQ contexts. No allocator or blocking console operation may run in an unsafe interrupt context.
- [ ] Add a minimal kernel-thread context and lifecycle model, stack ownership/guard policy, context-switch tests, and emulator scheduling tests.
- [ ] Add preemption only after lock, stack, timer, and interrupt-return invariants have deterministic tests.
- [ ] Keep application-processor startup/SMP as a separate sub-milestone after per-CPU state, TLB invalidation, and lock semantics exist.

**Exit criteria:** tested IRQ acknowledgement and timer behavior, deterministic thread lifecycle/context-switch tests, and bounded QEMU tests under repeated timer interrupts. No `sti` before the design and tests are ready.

---

## Milestone 4 — isolated processes and syscall ABI

Userspace begins only after page tables, exception handling, scheduling, and controlled memory allocation are trustworthy. The syscall ABI is a product interface and must not emerge accidentally from internal functions.

### Planned work

- [ ] Decide and document the x86_64 user-entry/syscall mechanism, register convention, selector/MSR setup, per-CPU state requirements, and safe return path.
- [ ] Add user/kernel page permissions and process-owned address spaces, including teardown and TLB invalidation rules.
- [ ] Implement copy-in/copy-out helpers that validate lengths, arithmetic, canonical ranges, permissions, and faults; never form a kernel reference directly from a user pointer.
- [ ] Specify version discovery, stable syscall numbers, argument layouts, error encoding, partial-I/O behavior, interruption/restart, and compatibility policy before exposing calls.
- [ ] Add initial process lifecycle and descriptor-table semantics: create/load, exit, wait, close, duplication/inheritance, and process cleanup.
- [ ] Load a deliberately small documented executable format with bounds/segment/permission checks; reject malformed binaries safely.
- [ ] Build adversarial tests for bad pointers, overflow, invalid mappings, process teardown, descriptor misuse, and failed exec.

### First user-visible target

A small controlled `init` process should start from a reproducible image, write through a descriptor, exit with a status, and be waited on by a kernel test harness. Do not claim userspace or process isolation from ring-0 tasks that merely use process-shaped structs.

**Exit criteria:** an isolated init process runs in user mode and uses a versioned, documented syscall subset; invalid user pointers and process teardown are tested without corrupting the kernel.

---

## Milestone 5 — VFS, storage, and device ownership

Keep the current RAM filesystem as a bootstrap/test implementation. Persistence and device drivers require explicit block ownership, error handling, and recovery behavior.

### Planned work

- [ ] Define VFS node, mount, path, metadata, and file-descriptor contracts independently of a particular disk format.
- [ ] Preserve volatile RAMFS as a test backend and add tests for mount/path errors, capacity, partial I/O, and object lifetime.
- [ ] Add a narrowly scoped block-device interface with request validation, timeout/error reporting, and a QEMU-supported initial device driver (such as virtio-blk after PCI discovery is ready).
- [ ] Choose and document the first on-disk filesystem format. Specify partition discovery, byte order, block size, metadata limits, corruption handling, and read-only/recovery behavior before writable support.
- [ ] Add persistent write/read/remount/reboot integration tests; never claim persistence from an in-memory cache alone.
- [ ] Add a driver ownership and DMA policy before any device can write into arbitrary kernel memory.
- [ ] Define file descriptors and basic process I/O semantics before exposing them to applications.

**Exit criteria:** a reproducible image mounts a documented on-disk filesystem, user-visible tools can create/read files across reboot, and corruption/I/O errors fail safely.

---

## Milestone 6 — initial userspace and command-line utilities

Crabshell is currently an in-kernel parser/frontend. The long-term terminal application should reuse its parser model without linking kernel internals or bypassing syscalls.

### Planned work

- [ ] Start a user-mode `init` process and establish executable search, environment, current directory, descriptor inheritance, and process startup rules.
- [ ] Port or adapt Crabshell into a userspace terminal application that uses only the documented syscall/VFS interfaces.
- [ ] Add a small utility set with explicit scope: file listing, text output, create/remove/copy/move, and system information.
- [ ] Add command-line quoting, escaping, history, redirection, and pipelines only with parser tests and process/descriptor/pipe semantics to support them.
- [ ] Add integration tests that launch tools from the filesystem image and exercise them through syscalls; keep unsupported features explicit.

**Exit criteria:** shell and basic tools run as isolated user processes from a reproducible image; no shell command directly calls kernel-private VFS internals.

---

## Milestone 7 — graphical console and GUI (long-term)

A GUI is intentionally downstream of stable memory management, interrupts/input, process isolation, drivers, and userspace. Keep Crabshell's parser independent so a graphical terminal frontend can reuse it.

### Planned work

- [ ] Add validated framebuffer discovery and memory ownership; implement a minimal text/graphics console without compromising serial panic diagnostics.
- [ ] Establish an input subsystem that separates raw device events from key mapping and terminal policy. Plan PS/2 and USB HID support separately; do not treat the current raw scancode poller as a keyboard driver stack.
- [ ] Define a graphics buffer ownership/presentation API, clipping rules, pixel format, and bounds/overflow checks.
- [ ] Implement a minimal compositor/windowing policy only after process isolation and input routing are ready.
- [ ] Run Crabshell as a terminal application in a GUI window using the same parser and userspace services as the serial/TTY path.
- [ ] Preserve serial as a headless recovery/debug console and add repeatable QEMU display/input tests.

**Exit criteria:** a documented GUI session starts from userspace, renders a terminal, accepts tested input, and does not require direct kernel-private VFS access.

---

## Milestone 8 — networking (long-term, after drivers and process isolation)

Networking is not implied by the current device drivers. The initial target should be a tightly scoped virtual-device path with clear ownership and bounded buffers.

### Planned work

- [ ] Complete PCI/device discovery and define DMA buffer ownership, address translation, cache synchronization, and reset/error behavior.
- [ ] Implement one virtual NIC driver with bounded queues and timeouts; test against QEMU user networking.
- [ ] Choose and document a minimal link/network protocol scope before implementation. Keep packet parsing length-checked and fuzzable on the host.
- [ ] Add interface configuration, routing, socket/descriptor ownership, and per-process access policy.
- [ ] Add adversarial packet tests and integration tests for link loss, malformed packets, queue exhaustion, and device reset.
- [ ] Add higher-level transports/services only when the required protocol semantics, entropy source, and security model are designed.

**Exit criteria:** documented user processes can communicate through a tested virtual NIC/network stack, with malformed input and resource exhaustion handled safely. Do not claim internet, TLS, or POSIX sockets merely from a packet driver.

---

## Cross-cutting acceptance gates

Every milestone should include the relevant subset of these gates:

1. **Design:** documented ownership, invariants, resource limits, error semantics, and unsupported cases.
2. **Tests:** host tests for pure policy and malformed/boundary input; integration tests for hardware-facing behavior.
3. **Safety:** review unsafe blocks, pointer provenance/access, integer overflow, privilege boundaries, concurrency, and cleanup/rollback paths.
4. **Build:** format, host tests, target check, and final ELF link as appropriate.
5. **Boot/integration:** QEMU tests for changes to boot, paging, descriptors, interrupts, drivers, processes, or persistence.
6. **Documentation/status:** update architecture and roadmap docs; never check off a criterion without evidence.
7. **Compatibility:** claim Unix/POSIX behavior only for the exact documented subset with conformance-style tests.

## Working rule

Prefer a small end-to-end vertical slice over broad, unbootable scaffolding. A source file, interface, or architecture document is not proof that the corresponding subsystem is operational. When a check cannot run, record the exact environment blocker and leave that acceptance gate pending.

# Testing and verification

## Current checks

`just verify` runs the standard development verification sequence:

1. `just fmt` — fail on formatting differences across the workspace.
2. `just test` — run host-side memory-map, mapping-range/PTE-bit policy, frame-allocator, RAM-filesystem, and Crabshell parser tests.
3. `just check` — check the `x86_64-unknown-none` kernel target.
4. `just smoke` — build the pinned hybrid ISO, boot it in QEMU, and check that Crabshell reaches its prompt within a deadline.

`just frame-smoke` builds an opt-in kernel variant that allocates one `Usable` frame, validates its HHDM address, writes and reads the whole page, clears it, returns the frame, and checks the prompt in QEMU. It reads the inherited root, walks all pages in the kernel image segments and requested 256 KiB stack span, compares effective PAT/MTRR types for kernel-image/HHDM aliases, and exercises a separate candidate map/unmap/release. The normal boot path in this image also clones the full reachable inherited hierarchy, hardens kernel-image HHDM aliases to text/rodata R/NX and data RW/NX while retaining PAT bits, switches CR3, verifies the active root and critical mappings, and exercises the global heap's alignment, reuse, and deterministic exhaustion. The workflow restores the default release kernel and ISO. These probes rely on Limine's HHDM contract and do not inventory every unrelated mapping or prove physical-hardware correctness. `just fault-smoke` separately builds opt-in kernel variants that deliberately trigger a page fault and an invalid opcode. It requires each QEMU run to report the expected exception (and CR2 for the page fault), avoid the shell prompt, and remain halted until timeout. It then rebuilds and restores the default release kernel and ISO. These are fatal-path diagnostics, not exception recovery tests; diagnostic Cargo features are disabled by default and mutually exclusive.

Keep the Crabshell parser, VFS, memory-map validator, paging policy helpers, frame allocator, and fixed heap independent of hardware so syntax, path handling, address and leaf-PTE bit policy, PAT/MTRR policy, storage semantics, frame ownership, HHDM/root-range calculations, allocation alignment, reuse, and exhaustion can be tested without booting. Pure tests validate captured MTRR register snapshots, resolve the Intel SDM Table 11-7 PAT/MTRR combinations for one physical address, select a PAT index that remains uniform across MTRR boundaries in an aligned range, bind that selection to validated mapping metadata before encoding leaves, and walk synthetic four-/five-level page tables including large-page leaves. Host tests also exercise the candidate builder's owned-table walk, clone ownership, 4-/5-level mapping, 2 MiB/1 GiB splitting, permission/cache-bit preservation, active-state mutation/release guard, transactional allocation/prepare rollback, and retryable frame-release failure. Heap tests cover alignment, exact-layout free/reuse, zero-sized rejection, metadata exhaustion, and arena exhaustion. Tests reject malformed state, unsupported discontinuous masks, invalid indexes/ranges, out-of-range addresses, mismatched physical widths, and non-normal caching mode. The pure inherited-table walker does not access hardware tables; the opt-in QEMU reader and candidate backend use checked HHDM addresses. Boot-time QEMU checks a subset of live kernel/HHDM aliases but does not inventory all aliases or prove complete transition safety. Boot separately captures the registers and CR0 caching mode read-only and reports a diagnostic resolution; this is not a page-table or mapping test. The GDT/TSS/IDT and CPU-register paths are privileged kernel code; QEMU boot and fault-injection checks complement, but do not replace, static review and target builds. Add tests for boundaries and failure behavior when introducing new pure kernel helpers. The kernel binary is not a host test target.

## What current checks do not prove

- `cargo check` does not perform a final target link.
- A successful ELF link does not prove the boot protocol is recognized or `_start` is reached.
- Host unit tests do not validate privileged instructions, UART behavior, memory-map pointer validity, page tables, interrupts, or actual hardware. The QEMU boot path exercises the gated EFER/PAT reads and bounded MTRR capture and prints diagnostic summaries, but the prompt smoke assertion does not make those facts a mapping-safety proof.
- The automated QEMU prompt smoke test asserts the cloned CR3 transition, kernel HHDM alias permissions/cache preservation, heap probe, and shell prompt. `just frame-smoke` additionally exercises one allocator-owned frame, inherited paths, kernel/HHDM cache aliases, and a separate candidate mapping through Limine's HHDM contract. The clone preserves Limine's complete reachable hierarchy, but there is no clean-room mapping policy or exhaustive audit of unrelated aliases; emulator tests do not establish physical-hardware behavior. `just fault-smoke` exercises only the controlled page-fault and invalid-opcode fatal paths; it does not test every exception vector or recovery.
- A separate manual QEMU session exercised directory navigation and file create/write/append/read/copy/move/remove operations, including `cp` replacing an existing destination and rejection of `rmdir` on a nonempty directory. This is not exhaustive shell coverage and does not prove persistence across reboot.
- There is no on-disk filesystem integration test, syscall/userspace test, fuzz target, or physical-hardware test.

## Validation policy

For changes to the kernel entry, linker script, boot requests, architecture code, shell, or VFS, run `just verify`. For memory-management and ABI code, add negative tests for overflow, malformed ranges, permission failures, and invalid user pointers before exposing those paths to userspace.

Record commands actually run and any environment limitation in change summaries; never call an unexecuted build “passing.”

# Boot protocol and kernel entry

## Current boot contract

Rustix currently expects a Limine-compatible x86_64 handoff. Limine is an external loader; it does not implement Rustix's kernel services. The kernel requests protocol base revision 3, a 256 KiB x86_64 stack, the higher-half direct-map (HHDM) offset, the executable physical/virtual base addresses, and the memory map.

Requests are kept in `.limine_requests_start`, `.limine_requests`, and `.limine_requests_end` by `linker.ld`. The response-bearing request records are mutable and the output `.limine_requests` section is placed in a writable load segment because Limine fills their response pointers before entering Rustix. The ELF entry symbol is `_start`.

### Entry sequence

1. Limine loads the ELF and transfers control to the assembly `_start` shim under the x86_64 Limine protocol. The shim captures the entry `RSP`, aligns the stack for a SysV call, and invokes `rustix_start`.
2. `rustix_start` configures the legacy COM1 UART for polling output and input.
3. The kernel disables maskable interrupts and installs its bootstrap GDT, TSS, and fatal-exception IDT. This does not initialize IRQ delivery.
4. The kernel reads CR0 caching-control state, CPU address widths, active `CR4.PCIDE`, and raw CR3. It decodes CR3's physical root address and low-bit meaning against those CPU properties, without dereferencing the root. It reads EFER.NXE only when CPUID reports NX, `IA32_PAT` only when CPUID reports PAT, and MTRR registers only when CPUID reports MTRR support; these reads do not change CPU state. The MTRR snapshot is bounded to 32 variable pairs and reports an explicit capacity-exceeded state without retaining partial registers. It requires and validates the stack-size response, copies the HHDM, executable-address, and memory-map responses into an owned `BootInfo` snapshot, validates pointers against the active linear width, derives and validates the linker-defined kernel image span and its page-aligned text/rodata/data segment spans from Limine's executable bases, and derives the requested 256 KiB initial-stack span from the captured entry `RSP`. It validates physical bounds, stack HHDM arithmetic/coverage, and page-rounded HHDM arithmetic for protocol-mapped memory types. It then builds a frame allocator only from validated usable ranges and rejects malformed metadata before starting the shell.
5. The kernel reports raw CR3 and its decoded physical root/low bits when the reported width permits, physical and virtual kernel-image spans, linker-defined segment permissions, the requested stack span, validated memory ranges, frame counts, CPU features/address widths, NXE and normal-caching state, the active PAT value plus recognized WB/UC/WC indices, and a summary of captured MTRR state. It also reports a diagnostic effective type at physical address zero for PAT index 0; this is not a live mapping claim.
6. Before entering the shell, the kernel clones the reachable inherited hierarchy into allocator-owned frames, makes the kernel-image HHDM aliases R/NX or RW/NX while preserving PAT bits, verifies critical mappings, switches CR3, and verifies the active root. It retains ownership tokens for the lifetime of the active root and probes the fixed heap.
7. The kernel seeds a volatile RAM filesystem and enters Crabshell. The shell busy-polls COM1 because no scheduler or UART interrupt handler exists; the kernel does not return to the loader.

The linker exports page-aligned virtual bounds for each of the kernel's three load segments. Boot validates their order, contiguity, coverage of the rounded image span, and derived physical ranges, then reports the permissions intended by `linker.ld`. Boot also decodes CR3's root physical address and active low-bit interpretation. The opt-in `just frame-smoke` path reads the 512 root entries and follows every page in the kernel image segments and requested stack span. The default boot transition clones the complete reachable table graph, applies and checks kernel HHDM alias permissions while preserving PAT bits, and verifies the candidate and active critical paths. This is a clone of Limine's mapping graph, not a clean-room mapping policy or exhaustive validation of unrelated aliases.

The memory-map snapshot stores physical regions as checked half-open ranges `[start, end)` and retains Limine's known classifications plus unknown type values. It does not authorize Rustix to access every region or reclaim loader memory. Rustix checks physical bounds and calculates canonical HHDM ranges for memory types covered by the requested base revision. The active cloned root leaves the inherited root and loader-owned leaf frames untouched. The opt-in `just frame-smoke` probe writes one allocator-issued frame contained in a validated `Usable` region and reads the inherited root page after checking that it is bootloader-reclaimable; both accesses rely on the Limine mapping contract after checked address arithmetic. It does not prove full live page-table coverage. These metadata checks cannot prove that a Limine-provided non-null pointer is readable; that remains an explicit trust assumption of the Limine handoff.

## Link and target configuration

- Rust target: `x86_64-unknown-none`
- Linker script: `linker.ld`
- Kernel virtual base: `0xffffffff80000000`
- Required code-generation constraints: kernel code model, static relocation, and disabled red zone
- Rust panic strategy: abort; the panic handler logs and halts

See [`../development/building.md`](../development/building.md) for commands and toolchain setup.

## Failure behavior and limitations

Missing responses (including the stack-size response), bad pointers/alignment, invalid HHDM values, invalid image or segment bounds, invalid requested-stack spans, excessive counts, null entries, address arithmetic overflow, and invalid or overlapping physical ranges reject the complete boot snapshot. `_start` halts before starting Crabshell rather than continuing with partial memory metadata. Structural checks cannot establish that a non-null loader pointer is mapped and readable; that remains an explicit trust assumption of the Limine handoff. The installed exception handlers print fatal context and halt; no fault recovery or maskable IRQ delivery is provided. COM1 writes use a bounded polling loop so a non-responsive UART does not block forever.

The repository includes a Limine v12.9.3 binary archive pin with SHA-256 verification, a hybrid ISO recipe, and a bounded QEMU serial smoke test that checks Crabshell's prompt. On 2026-10-16, `just verify` passed in WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 on both the working tree and a clean detached worktree with an empty `target` directory; the clean run fetched and built the pinned Limine host utility, created the image, and QEMU reported boot metadata before reaching the prompt. Milestone 0's local exit criteria are met. Hosted CI has not been observed. There is still no framebuffer console, reboot/shutdown interface, or broader boot-protocol compatibility test. The available serial and keyboard drivers do not imply a general device model.

## Future boot work

The kernel snapshots and validates the Limine map and preserves firmware and loader-reclaimable classifications without reclaiming them. The frame allocator manages only validated `Usable` regions; cloned page-table frames are retained as owned tokens. Loader-reclaimable memory remains unavailable until Rustix has copied any needed boot data and explicitly reaches a documented reclaim point; ACPI reclaimable memory needs the ACPI tables to be copied or parsed first.

# Rustix agent instructions

These instructions apply to every coding agent working in this repository. Read this file before changing code. For the architecture and detailed subsystem contracts, use the linked documents under `docs/`; this file summarizes the rules agents must preserve.

## Project mission

Rustix is an experimental 64-bit, Unix-like operating system with its own Rust kernel. Limine is the external boot protocol/loader only. Do not describe Limine, a host shell, or a userspace project as the Rustix kernel.

The kernel is `no_std` and targets `x86_64-unknown-none`. Rust is the implementation language for kernel and OS components. The repository currently uses a Python standard-library script only to assemble and smoke-test the boot image; it does not replace kernel or OS functionality.

Unix-like behavior is a long-term design goal, not a claim of POSIX compatibility. Make unsupported behavior explicit rather than approximating it silently.

## Current project status — read before planning

The source contains:

- A Limine-based x86_64 kernel entry, linker layout, serial diagnostics, and boot-memory reporting.
- A separate allocation-free `no_std` `crabshell` parser crate and a kernel-mode COM1 shell frontend.
- A volatile, fixed-capacity RAM filesystem used by the shell.
- A validated, fixed-capacity boot memory-map snapshot, CPUID/address-width reporting, read-only CR0 caching-mode reporting, and gated read-only EFER.NXE/IA32_PAT/MTRR reporting.
- A fixed-capacity physical frame allocator retained in `BootInfo`; Crabshell's `meminfo` command reports counts. The opt-in `probe-hhdm-frame` QEMU feature allocates, validates, writes, reads, clears, and returns one `Usable` frame through Limine's HHDM contract. `src/paging.rs` has a bounded candidate-root builder that owns allocator-issued table/leaf tokens and maps/unmaps 4 KiB leaves transactionally. The default boot path clones and activates the full reachable inherited hierarchy, hardens kernel-image HHDM aliases to R/NX or RW/NX while preserving PAT bits, and retains the active table tokens. A 256 KiB BSS-backed global heap is installed; it has fixed capacity and does not grow from frames.
- Pure 4 KiB mapping-range validation, leaf-PTE bit encoding, PAT layout parsing, and host-tested MTRR/PAT policy in `src/paging.rs`; these helpers check alignment, address widths, canonical virtual ranges, W^X, NXE input, PAT indices, captured-register validity, MTRR overlap rules, and Intel SDM Table 11-7 effective types under normal caching. Discontinuous variable-MTRR masks are explicitly unsupported. A pure selector chooses a PAT index only when its effective type remains uniform across all MTRR boundaries in an aligned physical range, and range-bound selected attributes can encode 4 KiB leaves. The bounded candidate builder stores its unique mutable table-memory backend borrow, uses allocator-issued `Frame` tokens for table pages and leaf mappings, restricts walks to owned tables, and rolls back failures. Active candidates reject mutation and release. Boot captures CR0 caching mode, EFER.NXE, `IA32_PAT`, and a bounded MTRR snapshot read-only when supported, validates the captured state, and reports a diagnostic PA 0 resolution. QEMU checks the requested 256 KiB stack, active CR3 clone, kernel-image HHDM alias permissions/cache preservation, and heap allocation behavior; the old root and its leaf frames are not reclaimed.
- Bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT setup and fatal exception handlers for vectors 0–31. Double faults use an IST stack and page faults report CR2. Opt-in QEMU tests inject a page fault and invalid opcode and verify diagnostics plus fatal halt; maskable IRQs remain disabled and exceptions are not recoverable.

Important incomplete work:

- Milestone 0's local exit criteria were met on 2026-10-16: `just verify` passed from both the working tree and a clean detached worktree in WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04. The detached worktree had an empty `target` directory, so the run exercised fresh Limine download/host-tool compilation, formatting, 19 host tests, target check, optimized build, image creation, and the 20-second QEMU prompt smoke test. Hosted CI has not been observed.
- A separate interactive `just run` session exercised directory navigation and create/write/append/read/copy/move/list/remove operations; `cp` replaced an existing destination, `rmdir` rejected a nonempty directory and succeeded after its child was removed, and unsupported `memtest` was rejected as expected. Boot snapshot tests and QEMU boot-metadata reporting were exercised. Structural checks still cannot prove that a Limine-provided non-null pointer is mapped or readable; that remains a loader trust boundary.
- Milestone 2 is **in progress**, not complete pending the final full validation and review. The frame allocator specifies token ownership and preserves the token on failed deallocation; unique allocator-instance use is still caller-enforced. The active root is an allocator-owned clone of Limine's reachable hierarchy, with critical translations checked and kernel-image HHDM aliases set R/NX or RW/NX while PAT bits are preserved. QEMU has exercised the 256 KiB requested stack, CR3 transition, fixed BSS heap alignment/reuse/exhaustion, and fatal page-fault/invalid-opcode paths. Host tests cover clone/table ownership, huge-page splitting, active-state guards, frame rollback, and heap behavior. The old root and inherited leaf frames are retained. There is no clean-room address-space policy, active general mapping service, frame reclamation, IRQ-safe heap path, or physical-hardware validation.
- There is no scheduler, userspace, syscall ABI, persistent filesystem, user/kernel isolation, or general IRQ subsystem.

Never advance status or check off a roadmap item merely because source code or an interface exists. Update `docs/roadmap/README.md` only to reflect implementation and validation actually achieved.

## Source-of-truth documents

Consult the relevant documentation before modifying a subsystem:

- [`docs/index.md`](docs/index.md) — documentation entry point and current status.
- [`docs/roadmap/README.md`](docs/roadmap/README.md) — milestone sequencing and exit criteria.
- [`docs/architecture/overview.md`](docs/architecture/overview.md) — current architecture and intended layers.
- [`docs/architecture/boot.md`](docs/architecture/boot.md) — Limine requests, boot snapshot, and trust boundary.
- [`docs/architecture/memory.md`](docs/architecture/memory.md) — memory ownership, frame allocator, and paging direction.
- [`docs/architecture/crabshell.md`](docs/architecture/crabshell.md) — parser/kernel boundary and shell/VFS contract.
- [`docs/architecture/drivers.md`](docs/architecture/drivers.md) — current driver scope and limitations.
- [`docs/security.md`](docs/security.md) — unsafe boundaries and security policy.
- [`docs/development/building.md`](docs/development/building.md) and [`docs/development/testing.md`](docs/development/testing.md) — supported commands and validation expectations.

When code and documentation disagree, inspect the implementation, resolve the discrepancy deliberately, and update the relevant documentation in the same change.

## Repository map

- `src/main.rs` — freestanding entry, boot snapshot acquisition, panic path, and shell handoff.
- `src/boot.rs` — mutable Limine requests, structural response/range validation, owned `BootInfo`, and boot diagnostics.
- `src/memory.rs` — allocation-free memory-map, address-width, canonical-address, Limine HHDM-range, and linker-defined kernel segment validation.
- `src/frame.rs` — bounded physical-frame allocator core; it only uses validated `Usable` ranges, reserves the first MiB, and has fixed range metadata.
- `src/paging.rs` — checked mapping/cache policy, inherited page-table walking, and a bounded candidate-root builder. The default boot path activates a cloned hierarchy and retains its owned table tokens; the HHDM backend accesses only complete allocator-owned `Usable` frames after checked address derivation.
- `src/shell.rs` — serial line editor and kernel-side Crabshell executor.
- `src/vfs.rs` — fixed-capacity volatile RAM filesystem and host-side tests.
- `crates/crabshell/` — separate `no_std` parser crate. It has no terminal, filesystem, or kernel dependencies.
- `src/arch/x86_64/serial.rs` — polling COM1 driver for shell input/output.
- `src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs` — bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT, assembly stubs, and fatal exception diagnostics.
- `src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs` — CPUID identification and selected feature reporting.
- `src/arch/x86_64/keyboard.rs` — raw, non-blocking PS/2-compatible scancode polling; not an input subsystem.
- `src/arch/x86_64/io.rs` — narrow port-I/O wrappers.
- `linker.ld`, `.cargo/config.toml`, `rust-toolchain.toml` — target, linker, and toolchain configuration.
- `limine.conf`, `scripts/boot.py` — boot configuration and pinned image/emulator workflow.
- `justfile` — supported development commands.
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — CI validation workflow.

## Engineering rules

### Keep changes incremental and coherent

1. Inspect the relevant source, tests, docs, and call sites before editing.
2. State assumptions, invariants, and failure behavior for new kernel interfaces.
3. Prefer small vertical slices that compile and can be tested over broad scaffolding or placeholder APIs.
4. Update tests and documentation alongside behavior changes.
5. Do not change unrelated code, rename files gratuitously, add speculative features, or rewrite project history.
6. Do not commit or create branches unless the user explicitly asks.

### Rust and dependency policy

- Preserve the kernel's `no_std`/freestanding constraints. Do not introduce `std` into kernel code.
- Prefer `core` and existing in-tree abstractions. Do not add third-party Rust dependencies without a concrete need and compatibility/security review.
- Keep the Crabshell parser independent of kernel I/O and VFS implementation. Kernel execution belongs in `src/shell.rs` or an appropriate kernel service.
- Do not add allocation-dependent APIs before a real heap exists. Fixed-capacity structures must document their limits and exhaustion behavior.
- Respect the workspace structure and the host-testable `rustix-kernel` library versus freestanding `rustix` binary boundary.

### Unsafe and hardware code

Unsafe code is expected only at explicit hardware, boot-protocol, assembly, or raw-memory boundaries. Keep each unsafe block narrow and document the invariant that makes it sound. Do not add broad `unsafe impl`, mutable global references, unchecked pointer arithmetic, or unreviewed inline/global assembly.

Before changing boot or memory code, account for these facts:

- Limine fills response pointers before `_start`; the request records must remain writable in the ELF image.
- Rustix validates nullness, alignment, counts, arithmetic, and physical ranges, but cannot prove that a non-null bootloader pointer is readable.
- Physical ranges are half-open `[start, end)` and must use checked arithmetic.
- Only regions classified `Usable` may enter the frame allocator. ACPI, bootloader-reclaimable, framebuffer, reserved, unknown, and other types are not free frames.
- A `Frame` is a physical address, not a dereferenceable pointer. HHDM access is allowed only through checked full-frame token-based paths that rely on the documented Limine contract; never access arbitrary physical addresses. Do not change CR3 until a complete, reviewed transition mapping policy and ownership proof exist.
- The kernel currently inherits Limine's page tables. Do not casually replace or mutate them: preserve the executing kernel, boot stack, `BootInfo`, request/response data, exception stacks, and mappings needed to continue execution.
- The exception setup is fatal-only. It does not enable maskable interrupts, configure a PIC/APIC, or provide recovery. Do not call `sti` or claim interrupt support without an IRQ design and tests.
- The shell and VFS run in ring 0 and are not isolated or secure.

For hardware changes, document assumptions about CPU mode, selectors, stacks, page permissions, interrupt state, and failure handling. Avoid new architecture mechanisms that cannot be statically reviewed or validated.

### Shell and filesystem contract

- Crabshell is presently a kernel-mode serial shell, not a userspace program or a POSIX shell.
- Its parser is a separate `no_std`, allocation-free crate; retain that boundary.
- The RAM filesystem is volatile and bounded. Preserve explicit errors and test capacity, path, and mutation edge cases.
- Do not imply persistence, permissions, links, process launching, or shell features that do not exist.
- Update the parser tests and `docs/architecture/crabshell.md` when adding or changing commands.

## Validation workflow

Run the narrowest relevant checks first, then broaden them. From the repository root, the supported commands are:

```sh
just fmt
just test
just check
just build
just image
just smoke
just verify
```

`just test` runs host-side library tests (memory-map validation, frame allocator, VFS, and Crabshell parser). `just check` checks `x86_64-unknown-none`; `just build` links the optimized ELF. `just verify` includes formatting, host tests, target check, pinned Limine image creation, and QEMU prompt smoke test. Image/boot checks need Python, `xorriso`, QEMU, the Rust target, and network access for the first pinned Limine download; Linux/WSL also needs `cc` to build Limine's host utility.

For changes to `src/main.rs`, `src/boot.rs`, linker/request configuration, `src/arch/x86_64/`, `src/frame.rs`, or paging/heap code, the intended full validation is `just verify`. If the environment does not permit a check, report the exact blocker and leave the corresponding roadmap criterion pending.

Do not claim a check passed unless it was run and its successful result was observed. Editor diagnostics are useful but are not a substitute for `cargo test`, a target build, or QEMU. A target check is not a final link; a linked ELF is not proof of boot; a prompt smoke test is not proof of interactive shell behavior or physical-hardware correctness.

## Completion criteria for agent changes

Before reporting work complete:

- Ensure source, tests, docs, and call sites agree.
- Review unsafe and hardware assumptions, including error paths and capacity limits.
- Run appropriate formatting/tests/build/boot checks, or clearly state why they could not run.
- Report files changed, behavior delivered, validation actually observed, and remaining risks.
- Keep milestone status accurate. A subsystem is not complete just because it has code.

# Architecture overview

## Goals

Rustix is a from-scratch operating system project with its own kernel, written in Rust. The intended initial platform is 64-bit x86 (`x86_64`), with a Unix-like process and file-descriptor model. The kernel should eventually own machine initialization, physical and virtual memory management, interrupt handling, scheduling, system calls, and device policy. A bootloader is a transport into the kernel, not a replacement for those facilities.

Unix-like is a compatibility direction. It does **not** mean the current kernel is POSIX-compliant, nor does it commit the project to a particular existing kernel's internals. Compatibility profiles and a userland should be defined only after the underlying process, descriptor, and syscall semantics are implemented and tested.

## Current implementation

1. Cargo builds a `no_std`, `no_main` ELF for `x86_64-unknown-none` and uses Limine for the boot handoff.
2. `_start` initializes COM1 and exception diagnostics, captures a validated boot snapshot and frame-allocator state, reports memory/CPU information, initializes a fixed-capacity RAM filesystem, and enters Crabshell.
3. Crabshell reads an ASCII command line from the serial UART and supports basic navigation, directory creation/listing, and text-file operations.
4. The separately packaged `crabshell` `no_std` crate parses commands without allocation or dependence on kernel I/O, making that layer reusable by a future graphical frontend.
5. The kernel library contains checked memory accounting and the bounded VFS implementation, both covered by host-side unit tests.

The current shell and filesystem run in kernel mode. Files exist only in RAM and disappear at reboot. Bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT setup and fatal exception handlers for vectors 0–31 exist, but maskable IRQs remain disabled and exception recovery is not implemented. The active page tables are an owned clone of Limine's reachable hierarchy, and a bounded 256 KiB BSS heap is installed. There is no clean-room address-space policy, general active mapping service, frame reclamation, IRQ-safe allocation, general IRQ subsystem, scheduler, user/kernel isolation, syscall ABI, on-disk filesystem, network stack, or userspace process.

## Intended layers (planned)

```text
User programs and system utilities
        | versioned syscall ABI
Kernel services: processes, descriptors, VFS, IPC, signals
        | explicit ownership and authorization checks
Core kernel: scheduler, virtual memory, physical frames, interrupts
        | narrow architecture abstractions
x86_64 platform: paging, exceptions, timers, AP startup, drivers
        | Limine boot handoff only
Firmware and hardware
```

The diagram is a target decomposition, not a claim that those layers are implemented. Architecture-independent policy should live in safe Rust where possible; privileged instructions and raw device access should stay in small, reviewed architecture modules.

## Design constraints

- **Freestanding:** kernel code does not link `std`; allocation must be introduced deliberately after a physical-frame and heap strategy exists.
- **Explicit unsafe boundaries:** raw pointers from boot protocol responses and x86 port I/O are unsafe. Each use must document its preconditions and remain short-lived.
- **Fail visibly:** early boot failures should produce serial diagnostics where possible and then halt, rather than continue with invalid machine state.
- **Checked arithmetic:** physical ranges, sizes, and address translations must reject overflow.
- **No premature ABI:** userspace interfaces stay unstable until process lifetime, error conventions, copy-in/copy-out, and versioning are designed together.
- **Hardware-independent tests:** parsing, range arithmetic, and policy should be testable as ordinary host-side Rust wherever possible.

## Boot and CPU assumptions

The current target is x86_64, with a 4 KiB page-oriented linker layout and no red zone. Limine performs the initial platform setup required by its protocol. Rustix must not assume that receiving a memory-map response means it owns the loader's page tables or can overwrite reserved regions. The current bootstrap does not enable interrupts or start application processors.

See [Boot protocol](boot.md), [Memory management](memory.md), [x86_64 drivers](drivers.md), [Crabshell](crabshell.md), and [the roadmap](../roadmap/README.md) for subsystem boundaries and planned acceptance criteria.

# Memory-management direction

## What exists now

`src/memory.rs` contains an allocation-free `MemoryMapBuilder` that copies Limine ranges into validated half-open physical regions. It rejects empty ranges, `base + length` overflow, overlapping ranges, empty maps, and maps exceeding the fixed 256-region capacity. Known Limine types remain distinct, and unknown type values are preserved. Host-side tests cover range validation/classification, canonical-address boundaries, physical-width bounds, and HHDM range arithmetic. `src/boot.rs` stores the resulting map in an owned boot snapshot and reports usable bytes.

`src/frame.rs` provides a fixed-capacity allocator core with host-side tests. It only manages complete 4 KiB frames inside validated `Usable` regions, reserves the first MiB, and coalesces adjacent free ranges. The ownership contract assumes one allocator instance per physical map: within that instance, each eligible frame is owned either by its free-range table or by a non-copyable `Frame` token while allocated. The public constructor does not enforce unique instances, so callers must not initialize multiple allocators for the same physical map; the boot path retains one allocator in `BootInfo`. `allocate` returns `None` when no free frame remains. `deallocate` consumes the token only on success; on any error, including free-range-table exhaustion, it returns a `DeallocationError` containing the original token and leaves allocator state unchanged. The range tables each have a fixed `MAX_FRAME_RANGES` capacity, so fragmentation can prevent a frame from being returned until nearby ranges coalesce. The active cloned page-table hierarchy owns its page-table frames; the frame allocator is otherwise not yet a general-purpose virtual-memory service.

`Frame::address()` is a physical address value, not a dereferenceable pointer and not a proof that the frame is mapped. CPU diagnostics now read `CR4.LA57` to report the active linear-address width (48 or 57 bits) and query `CPUID.80000008H` for physical and maximum linear-address widths when available. Boot-protocol pointers are checked against the active width, with host tests for 48- and 57-bit canonical boundaries. These facts do not prove that any physical address is mapped.

`src/paging.rs` contains host-tested mapping and cache policy plus a bounded candidate-root builder. The CR3 decoder validates physical-address width and reserved bits and interprets its low 12 bits according to active `CR4.PCIDE`; it does not dereference the root. The mapping-range validator requires known physical width, checked aligned bounds, canonical virtual endpoints in one canonical half, and rejects writable-executable permissions. It can encode one 4 KiB leaf PTE with supervisor/user and write permissions, NX when EFER.NXE is confirmed, and a bounded PAT index. `PatLayout` parses supplied `IA32_PAT` values and selects WB, UC, or WC indexes. `MtrrMemoryType`, `VariableMtrr`, `FixedMtrrRanges`, and `MtrrLayout` resolve address-specific MTRR types, including fixed-range priority and defined variable-overlap rules; undefined overlaps fail closed. `MtrrRegisters::validated_layout` validates captured capability/default-type bits, register counts and fixed-range presence, WC support, and variable-mask shape/alignment before producing an owned layout. Rustix supports contiguous power-of-two variable masks and explicitly rejects unsupported discontinuous masks. The layout combines address-specific MTRR type and PAT selection according to Intel SDM Table 11-7 only when `CR0.CD` and `CR0.NW` are clear. Host tests cover all 30 documented MTRR/PAT pairs and malformed inputs. A pure range selector chooses an index only when its effective type is uniform throughout all fixed/variable MTRR boundaries in an aligned extent; selected attributes remain bound to that physical extent. The selector itself does not inspect PTEs, aliases, or frame ownership. Boot reads CR0 without modifying it, validates captured MTRR/PAT state, and reports a diagnostic PA 0 resolution; this does not assert the live PTE's type. MTRR capture is bounded to 32 variable pairs and rejects excess capacity without partial state.

`CandidatePageTables` owns a separate root, bounded to 32 table frames and 256 explicitly mapped leaf frames. It accepts only allocator-issued `Frame` tokens, requires NXE, supports four- and five-level paths, and holds one exclusive mutable borrow of its unsafe memory backend so prepared handles cannot be mixed across backends. The default boot path clones the complete reachable Limine hierarchy, rewrites inherited kernel HHDM aliases to text/rodata R/NX and data RW/NX while preserving PAT bits, verifies critical translations, activates the cloned CR3, and retains the candidate tokens for the active root's lifetime. Active candidates reject mapping, unmapping, and release; the type never writes CR3. Host tests cover clone ownership, huge-page splitting, cache-bit preservation, mutation guards, transactional map rollback, and retryable release failure. The QEMU adapter derives table pointers only from complete allocator-owned `Usable` frames through checked HHDM arithmetic.

The opt-in `just frame-smoke` probe reads the inherited root and follows paths for every page in kernel text/rodata/data and the requested stack span. The transition clones every reachable present table and preserves leaf mappings, then rewrites and validates the kernel-image HHDM aliases. The kernel and HHDM aliases retain the same PAT index; MTRR state is unchanged. This is not a fresh address-space policy or a hardware-level exhaustive inventory, and it does not reclaim the inherited root or bootloader memory.

The effective-type resolver follows [Intel SDM Vol. 3A §11.5.2.2, Table 11-7](https://cdrdv2-public.intel.com/671447/325384-sdm-vol-3abcd.pdf), which applies when normal caching is enabled (`CR0.CD=0`, `CR0.NW=0`). Its footnotes distinguish UC selected by an MTRR from UC selected by a page-table entry (the latter involves cache snooping and aliasing concerns); they also identify combinations that older manual editions called undefined but current processors supporting both PAT and MTRRs resolve as shown. The resolver does not cover legacy PCD/PWT-only selection or model-specific combinations outside that table.

The requested Limine base revision is 3. Its protocol maps only `Usable`, `BootloaderReclaimable`, `ExecutableAndModules`, and `Framebuffer` memory-map regions into the HHDM; reserved, ACPI, bad, and unknown regions are not in that mapping set. HHDM mappings use at least 4 KiB granularity and may cover page-aligned bytes beyond unaligned region boundaries. Limine's inherited HHDM mappings are supervisor RWX, normally write-back cached, with framebuffer mappings write-combining when PAT is available. Before activating the cloned root, Rustix splits inherited huge pages where needed and changes the kernel image HHDM aliases to the matching R/NX or RW/NX policy while retaining PAT bits. The rest of the HHDM remains inherited; an HHDM offset is not a blanket physical-memory access grant. See the [Limine base revision 3 protocol](https://github.com/limine-bootloader/limine-protocol/blob/trunk/PROTOCOL.md#base-revision-3) and its memory-layout/caching sections.

The boot snapshot now rejects physical map ranges beyond the reported CPUID physical-address width when that CPUID leaf is available. For base revision 3 HHDM-mapped types, it also validates the page-rounded physical span, checked `offset + address` arithmetic, and canonical endpoints in the active linear-address width. If the CPU does not report a physical width, the physical-bound check is skipped and no mapping caller may treat the bound as known. These checks are derived from metadata and Limine's protocol contract; they do not inspect page tables or prove that a non-null loader pointer is readable. HHDM dereferences are limited to the opt-in QEMU frame probe and candidate-table backend. Both first validate a complete allocator-owned `Usable` frame and its checked HHDM address, then rely narrowly on Limine's base-revision-3 guarantee; this is not a general physical-memory access service. Rustix-owned mappings should be non-executable by default; executable kernel text must be explicit. MMIO requires an explicit device range and cache policy, and guard regions must remain unmapped. A page-table transition must preserve the kernel image, active stacks, boot data, descriptor tables, and any loader mappings still needed. Rustix does not reclaim bootloader memory or provide a general-purpose physical-memory service. It owns the page-table frames of the active cloned hierarchy but leaves inherited leaf frames and the old root unreclaimed. The initial 256 KiB global heap is a bounded BSS arena and does not grow from physical frames. Bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT setup and fatal exception diagnostics live in `src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs`; they do not enable maskable IRQs.

## Active-root preservation and remaining limits

The transition clones the complete reachable inherited hierarchy rather than building a clean address space. It preserves all reachable present leaves and non-present entries, owns each cloned intermediate table, and fails closed on malformed entries, unsupported page sizes, cross-level table aliases, or fixed-capacity exhaustion. Kernel text/rodata/data HHDM aliases are then adjusted to avoid writable-executable aliases. Limine's original root and leaf frames remain intact.

- **Kernel ELF image:** `linker.ld` places `.text`, `.rodata`, `.limine_requests`, `.data`, `.bss`, and `.got` in three `PT_LOAD` segments: RX text, read-only rodata, and RW data/BSS. It exports `__kernel_start` and `__kernel_end` around the complete loadable image, plus page-aligned bounds for each segment. `BootInfo` checks that Limine's reported virtual base matches the linker start, validates ordered contiguous segment bounds covering the rounded image, derives corresponding half-open physical ranges from the executable physical base with checked arithmetic, and validates canonical virtual and reported physical address widths. The release ELF and QEMU runtime report both showed the three aligned ranges on 2026-10-21. The RX, R/NX, and RW/NX labels describe the linker segment intent; these are linker/boot metadata, not proof that the inherited page tables map every page or enforce those permissions, nor proof that loader pointers are readable. The memory-map `ExecutableAndModules` entries remain illustrative, not an authoritative kernel-image extent.
- **Active stack and `BootInfo`:** The assembly `_start` shim captures Limine's entry `RSP` before any Rust prologue. Under the SysV entry convention the synthetic return slot occupies 8 bytes, so `RSP + 8` is the exclusive stack top. Rustix requests a 256 KiB Limine stack and requires the stack-size response; `BootInfo` records and validates that requested span through the HHDM, including its `BootloaderReclaimable` backing. The loader may allocate more, and no guard page is inferred. QEMU transition tests walk all 64 requested stack pages.
- **Kernel static data:** `RAM_FILESYSTEM`, GDT, IDT, TSS, the ring-0 stack, and double-fault IST stack are static BSS/data in the kernel image. Exception entry also requires the handler code and the TSS/IDT references to remain mapped. Preserve the complete relevant data/BSS pages and stack pages.
- **Limine request data:** request records are in the kernel's writable `.limine_requests` segment. Response objects and the memory-map pointer array are bootloader-reclaimable; `capture_boot_information` copies the values used later, and the shell does not retain those pointers. Keep them mapped until the copy and validation finish; any later reclaim must be explicit rather than reclaiming the whole bootloader-reclaimable class.
- **Inherited page tables:** Limine places its page tables in bootloader-reclaimable memory, but their layout is unspecified. `BootInfo` captures raw CR3 and validates the decoded root address and active low-bit mode. The default boot path clones all reachable page-table pages into allocator-owned frames and preserves all leaf entries, then changes only the kernel-image HHDM alias permission bits while retaining cache attributes. It verifies kernel segments, the requested stack span, and the candidate-root HHDM alias before switching; afterward it verifies CR3 and the critical paths again. The inherited root and its backing pages remain untouched and are not reclaimed.
- **Devices:** COM1 uses x86 port I/O and needs no MMIO virtual mapping. Rustix does not currently request or use a framebuffer. Any future framebuffer or device-register mapping needs an explicit physical range and cache policy.

## Permissions and cache policy of the active clone

The active root preserves Limine's inherited kernel virtual mappings and their cache attributes. Before switching, Rustix requires NXE and enforces the linker permissions for every kernel-image HHDM alias: text and rodata are read-only/NX, and data/BSS/GOT are RW/NX. This prevents writable-executable aliases without discarding the HHDM alias. Huge-page leaves are split as necessary; unaffected entries retain their mappings and PAT/MTRR effective types. The remainder of the HHDM and all non-kernel aliases remain as Limine supplied them, so this is not yet a comprehensive Rustix mapping policy.

Preserve the inherited PAT/MTRR configuration during the first transition. The boot report validates captured registers and computes a diagnostic effective type from the active PAT/MTRR values under normal caching. A separate pure selector can choose an index whose effective type remains uniform across an aligned physical range; the selector itself does not inspect PTEs or aliases. The opt-in `just frame-smoke` probe now compares effective types of the inherited kernel and HHDM aliases for kernel-image pages, but it is not a full alias inventory. The pure combination follows Intel SDM Table 11-7; it is not a generic rule for legacy PCD/PWT-only selection or model-specific combinations. The active transition retains the inherited PAT and MTRR state and changes no cache-selection bits. The page-table split copies large-page PAT selection to the equivalent 4 KiB/2 MiB entries. Future MMIO mappings must still use explicit device ranges and a verified cache policy; do not infer MMIO from generic reserved memory-map entries. COM1 uses port I/O and requires no MMIO mapping.

Do not use huge pages in the first root; add them only when physical coverage, permissions, and cache attributes are uniform across the entire huge-page extent. Future Rustix-owned downward-growing stacks should have at least one 4 KiB unmapped guard page below them. The Limine bootstrap stack has no known guard, so none may be assumed there.

Never modify Limine's active page tables in place. `src/paging.rs` builds an owned clone in allocator-issued frames, can split inherited large pages to update leaf permissions, and supports transactional 4 KiB map/unmap operations before activation. The default boot path validates critical translations and kernel alias permissions, switches CR3, verifies the active root, and retains its frame tokens for the active lifetime. The inherited root and backing memory remain intact. This preserves inherited mappings rather than constructing a new address space; broader mapping inventory, non-kernel permission policy, reclamation, and a general mapping service remain future work.

## Planned memory layers

1. **Validated physical regions:** implemented as a fixed-capacity owned snapshot; allocator ownership and reclaim policy remain future work.
4. **Frame allocator integration:** the bounded core is initialized from `BootInfo`; the active cloned hierarchy owns its table frames, while the opt-in QEMU frame probe is the only general frame allocation test. Add active mapping services only after a TLB and mapping-lifetime policy exists.
3. **Kernel virtual memory:** Rustix runs on an active cloned hierarchy whose page-table frames it owns. The clone preserves Limine's mappings and applies R/NX or RW/NX permissions to kernel-image HHDM aliases. It is not a clean address-space rebuild, and general mapping/unmapping after activation is deliberately rejected without a TLB policy.
4. **Heap:** an initial global allocator uses a fixed 256 KiB BSS arena and at most 128 live allocations. It has deterministic exhaustion and exact-layout free semantics, does not grow from frames, and must not be called in interrupt context.
5. **Process address spaces:** isolate userspace; define copy-in/copy-out helpers and never treat user pointers as kernel references.

## Invariants to preserve

- Physical ranges use checked arithmetic and the half-open convention `[start, end)`.
- Only complete frames in validated `Usable` regions enter the allocator; the first MiB remains reserved. Firmware and loader-reclaimable regions are not silently promoted to free memory.
- Under the single-allocator-per-physical-map contract, a frame is represented by one allocator-free range or one caller-owned, non-copyable `Frame` token. Only a successful `deallocate` transfers the token back to the allocator; errors return the token and leave allocator ranges and accounting unchanged. The current public constructor relies on callers to enforce unique allocator instances.
- `allocate` returns `None` on frame exhaustion. Metadata-capacity exhaustion is an explicit error, never silent loss of a frame.
- A `Frame` address is physical, not directly dereferenceable. HHDM translation and table access are limited to checked full-frame token-based paths that rely on Limine's documented mapping contract. Candidate mutations are allowed only before activation and only in owned tables. The active cloned root retains its ownership tokens and rejects mutation/release until an explicit, reviewed CR3 transition away from it.
- Mapping changes validate alignment, canonical addresses, ownership, and permissions before touching tables.
- User-controlled addresses are validated on every syscall boundary; prior validation is not a substitute for access checks during later copies.
- Tests cover unaligned edges, exact-boundary allocations, arithmetic overflow, overlaps, exhaustion, and unchanged state/ownership on failure.

The active root is a full clone of Limine's reachable hierarchy with kernel HHDM alias W^X hardening, not a clean-room Rustix address space. The fixed BSS heap is bounded and non-growing. General mapping policy, broader alias/MMIO coverage, frame reclamation, and physical-hardware validation remain outstanding.

```rustix/docs/architecture/memory.md
     1	# Memory-management direction
     2	
     3	## What exists now
     4	
     5	`src/memory.rs` contains an allocation-free `MemoryMapBuilder` that copies Limine ranges into validated half-open physical regions. It rejects empty ranges, `base + length` overflow, overlapping ranges, empty maps, and maps exceeding the fixed 256-region capacity. Known Limine types remain distinct, and unknown type values are preserved. Host-side tests cover range validation/classification, canonical-address boundaries, physical-width bounds, and HHDM range arithmetic. `src/boot.rs` stores the resulting map in an owned boot snapshot and reports usable bytes.
     6	
     7	`src/frame.rs` provides a fixed-capacity allocator core with host-side tests. It only manages complete 4 KiB frames inside validated `Usable` regions, reserves the first MiB, and coalesces adjacent free ranges. The ownership contract assumes one allocator instance per physical map: within that instance, each eligible frame is owned either by its free-range table or by a non-copyable `Frame` token while allocated. The public constructor does not enforce unique instances, so callers must not initialize multiple allocators for the same physical map; the boot path retains one allocator in `BootInfo`. `allocate` returns `None` when no free frame remains. `deallocate` consumes the token only on success; on any error, including free-range-table exhaustion, it returns a `DeallocationError` containing the original token and leaves allocator state unchanged. The range tables each have a fixed `MAX_FRAME_RANGES` capacity, so fragmentation can prevent a frame from being returned until nearby ranges coalesce. The active cloned page-table hierarchy owns its page-table frames; the frame allocator is otherwise not yet a general-purpose virtual-memory service.
     8	
     9	`Frame::address()` is a physical address value, not a dereferenceable pointer and not a proof that the frame is mapped. CPU diagnostics now read `CR4.LA57` to report the active linear-address width (48 or 57 bits) and query `CPUID.80000008H` for physical and maximum linear-address widths when available. Boot-protocol pointers are checked against the active width, with host tests for 48- and 57-bit canonical boundaries. These facts do not prove that any physical address is mapped.
    10	
    11	`src/paging.rs` contains host-tested mapping and cache policy plus a bounded candidate-root builder. The CR3 decoder validates physical-address width and reserved bits and interprets its low 12 bits according to active `CR4.PCIDE`; it does not dereference the root. The mapping-range validator requires known physical width, checked aligned bounds, canonical virtual endpoints in one canonical half, and rejects writable-executable permissions. It can encode one 4 KiB leaf PTE with supervisor/user and write permissions, NX when EFER.NXE is confirmed, and a bounded PAT index. `PatLayout` parses supplied `IA32_PAT` values and selects WB, UC, or WC indexes. `MtrrMemoryType`, `VariableMtrr`, `FixedMtrrRanges`, and `MtrrLayout` resolve address-specific MTRR types, including fixed-range priority and defined variable-overlap rules; undefined overlaps fail closed. `MtrrRegisters::validated_layout` validates captured capability/default-type bits, register counts and fixed-range presence, WC support, and variable-mask shape/alignment before producing an owned layout. Rustix supports contiguous power-of-two variable masks and explicitly rejects unsupported discontinuous masks. The layout combines address-specific MTRR type and PAT selection according to Intel SDM Table 11-7 only when `CR0.CD` and `CR0.NW` are clear. Host tests cover all 30 documented MTRR/PAT pairs and malformed inputs. A pure range selector chooses an index only when its effective type is uniform throughout all fixed/variable MTRR boundaries in an aligned extent; selected attributes remain bound to that physical extent. The selector itself does not inspect PTEs, aliases, or frame ownership. Boot reads CR0 without modifying it, validates captured MTRR/PAT state, and reports a diagnostic PA 0 resolution; this does not assert the live PTE's type. MTRR capture is bounded to 32 variable pairs and rejects excess capacity without partial state.
    12	
    13	`CandidatePageTables` owns a separate root, bounded to 32 table frames and 256 explicitly mapped leaf frames. It accepts only allocator-issued `Frame` tokens, requires NXE, supports four- and five-level paths, and holds one exclusive mutable borrow of its unsafe memory backend so prepared handles cannot be mixed across backends. The default boot path clones the complete reachable Limine hierarchy, rewrites inherited kernel HHDM aliases to text/rodata R/NX and data RW/NX while preserving PAT bits, verifies critical translations, activates the cloned CR3, and retains the candidate tokens for the active root's lifetime. Active candidates reject mapping, unmapping, and release; the type never writes CR3. Host tests cover clone ownership, huge-page splitting, cache-bit preservation, mutation guards, transactional map rollback, and retryable release failure. The QEMU adapter derives table pointers only from complete allocator-owned `Usable` frames through checked HHDM arithmetic.
    14	
    15	The opt-in `just frame-smoke` probe reads the inherited root and follows paths for every page in kernel text/rodata/data and the requested stack span. The transition clones every reachable present table and preserves leaf mappings, then rewrites and validates the kernel-image HHDM aliases. The kernel and HHDM aliases retain the same PAT index; MTRR state is unchanged. Its footnotes distinguish UC selected by an MTRR from UC selected by a page-table entry (the latter involves cache snooping and aliasing concerns); they also identify combinations that older manual editions called undefined but current processors supporting both PAT and MTRRs resolve as shown. The rest of the HHDM remains inherited; an HHDM offset is not a blanket physical-memory access grant.     21	The boot snapshot now rejects physical map ranges beyond the reported CPUID physical-address width when that CPUID leaf is available.
